title: Working on the platform
subtitle: The core platform course: how a report is built, where the data is computed and where trust in a number comes from

units.title: Foundations: the report as an artifact
units.subtitle: What a report is on this platform, where it lives, who sees it, and what happens at the moment it is opened

lessons.title: What a report is on this platform
lessons.summary: By the end of this chapter you understand why the unit of delivery here is a single self-contained file, how the platform infers a report's type from its markup, and why a sandbox without allow-same-origin makes postMessage the only channel.

cards.heading: The unit of delivery is a file, not an application
cards.text:
A report on OnePage is a single self-contained HTML file. All the CSS, all the JavaScript and all the fonts live inside it; a finished report has not a single external network dependency. The platform specification states this as a contract, not a wish: the targets are at most 300 KB of markup, full initialization in under one second, no main-thread task longer than 50 ms, zero external requests and zero console errors.

What this decision saves you is not elegance but an entire class of problems. A file has no build, no dependencies that can drift apart, no server-side runtime that needs upgrading. Publishing is writing bytes to disk plus a row in the database. Rolling back is the previous version directory, which never went anywhere.

Compare this with an ordinary web application: there a report is a route, a template, a data-access layer and a frontend build, and each of the four parts lives its own life and needs a coordinated rollout. Here the unit of delivery coincides with the unit of understanding: the file you opened with a double click is exactly what the reader will see.

cards.heading: What exactly the platform does with the file
cards.text:
The platform does not build the report and does not execute its code on its own side. It does exactly four things: it stores the bytes by version, decides whom to show them to, injects its own service scripts into the markup at serve time, and serves the result from a cache. Everything the user sees was drawn by your file in their browser.

The service scripts are a height reporter, so the frame can fit the content, and dormant controllers for annotations, colors and text edits: they are present in every report but wake up only for someone who has the right to turn them on. Your code does not need to know about them, but you must not override postMessage and localStorage or install a global message handler that swallows other message types — otherwise you will break them silently.

From this follows a simple consequence worth accepting right away: the perceived speed of a report is almost entirely the size of your file and the quality of your JavaScript. The server side is measured in microseconds (that is the subject of chapter five), whereas parsing a megabyte of markup in the browser takes hundreds of milliseconds.

cards.heading: Three types and how the type is inferred
cards.text: The platform does not ask the author for the report type. It determines the type with regular expressions over the raw text of the file — including comments and string literals inside JavaScript:
cards.code_text:
def detect_type(html: str) -> str:
    if _RE_SNAPSHOT.search(html):      # <script id="bootstrap-snapshot">
        return DASH_SNAPSHOT
    if _RE_FILE_INPUT.search(html):    # <input type="file">
        return DASH_INTERACTIVE
    return DASH_STATIC

cards.text: The order of the checks sets the priority, and it matters: a file that contains both the snapshot tag and a file input will be snapshot, not interactive. The type is not a label on a card but a decision about what the platform injects into your file at serve time, so a wrong type silently changes how data is delivered. What each type means:
list: snapshot — data comes from a separate slot file or from the bootstrap-snapshot tag, which the platform fills with fresh JSON at serve time; this is the default type and the most refreshable scheme
interactive — the markup contains input type=file and the user supplies the file themselves; the platform injects a bridge, and the file reaches the report as an ordinary change event
static — neither of the above: a report with no data, or with a trivial amount hard-coded right into the markup

cards.note: Detection works on text, not on the DOM. The string '<input type="file"' inside your JavaScript — even in a comment — will make the report interactive. The type changes what the platform injects into the file, so an accidental match is not visible right away: the report simply stops receiving data the way you expected.

cards.heading: Origin isolation: the foundation
cards.text:
Browser security rests on the notion of an origin — the triple of scheme, host and port. Documents with the same triple count as one origin; documents with different triples are different origins, and the same-origin policy forbids them from reading each other's data. Cross-origin writes and embedding are usually allowed; cross-origin reads are not. This is precisely what stops a stranger's site from reading your mail or your internal portal while you are logged into them.

A special case is the opaque origin: a document whose origin matches nobody's, including that of its own source. Such a document always fails the same-origin check.

cards.heading: A report lives in an opaque origin
cards.text: A report opens inside an iframe with a sandbox attribute that lists permissions but does not include allow-same-origin:
cards.code_text: sandbox="allow-scripts allow-forms allow-downloads allow-popups allow-modals"

cards.text: The absence of one token changes everything. The document gets an opaque origin, and from that follow hard facts about the environment that every report author has to take into account:
list: cookies are unavailable — document.cookie is useless inside a report
a fetch to the platform API returns 401: the request carries no session, and the report cannot go and get data by itself
the real localStorage is blocked; the platform injects a transparent proxy, but it is meant for settings of up to 4 KB, not for data
the browser HTTP cache is partitioned per opening, and the document itself is served with no-store — “it will be cached after the first time” does not exist here

cards.heading: Why relaxing it would be a hole
cards.text:
The temptation is clear: add allow-same-origin and the report could call the API by itself, no bridges needed. The MDN documentation warns explicitly that combining allow-scripts and allow-same-origin for a same-origin document makes the sandbox pointless: a script inside can remove the sandbox attribute from its own frame.

The threat here is not abstract. A report is someone else's code running in the reader's browser under the reader's session. A model wrote it at a colleague's request, and it was uploaded without review. As long as the origin is opaque, the worst this code can do is spoil its own picture. With allow-same-origin it would gain access to cookies, storage and the platform API on behalf of whoever opened the report.

cards.heading: The only channel is postMessage
cards.text: Since there is no direct access, everything that crosses the boundary crosses it as messages. The contract is small and worth memorizing:

head: Message
Direction
Purpose
rows: the report has loaded and lists the slots it needs
contents of a slot file as an ArrayBuffer
a modified file to be saved (interactive)
content height for auto-sizing the frame

cards.note: The message handler on the parent page has no origin check — and none could be useful: the controller injected by the platform and the report's own scripts share one window, and their messages are indistinguishable. That is why nothing that arrives via postMessage goes into innerHTML without escaping, and numeric fields are coerced with Number() on input.

cards.text: And one last consequence that is often mistaken for a whim: the ban on CDNs, external fonts and any absolute external URLs. This is not a matter of style. A report runs in an opaque origin inside a closed network perimeter where the external network may be blocked, and there has already been an incident that got the Google Fonts stylesheet removed from the platform: page rendering stalled while waiting for an unreachable CDN. Self-containment is not aesthetics; it is the condition for the report opening at all.

takeaways: The unit of delivery is one self-contained HTML file; the platform stores, authorizes and serves it, but never builds or executes it on its own side.
The report type is inferred by a regular expression over the raw text: bootstrap-snapshot first, then input type=file, otherwise static.
An iframe without allow-same-origin gives the report an opaque origin: no cookies, no API, no real localStorage.
Adding allow-same-origin is not an option — a script inside could remove the sandbox itself, and a report is by definition someone else's code under the reader's session.
The only channel across the boundary is postMessage; the ban on external links follows directly from isolation and the closed perimeter, it is not a matter of taste.

checks.q: An author is writing a snapshot report. Their JavaScript contains a hint string: const HINT = 'drag a file here or click <input type="file">';. They forgot to insert the inline bootstrap-snapshot tag. What type will the platform assign to this file, and what will happen?
options: interactive: the detector matches a substring of the raw text, so the file gets the slot bridge, not a snapshot
snapshot: the detector builds a DOM and checks elements, and a string literal inside a script is not an element
static: the signals conflict, and in that case the platform picks the type with the smallest amount of injection
The upload will be rejected: the platform treats two mutually exclusive signals in one file as a 409 error
checks.why: detect_type works with regular expressions over the raw text of the file, including comments and string literals, and never builds a DOM. There is no bootstrap-snapshot tag, but the file-input substring is there — so the snapshot branch does not fire and interactive is returned. The platform will inject the slot bridge and change events instead of substituting fresh JSON, and the report will be left without data even though the file looks correct. The platform returns 409 only when the type of an already existing report changes, not on the first upload.

checks.q: Suppose allow-same-origin were added to the sandbox attribute so that the report could fetch data by itself. Which of the following becomes possible?
options: Nothing dangerous: the remaining sandbox tokens still restrict the report, and they cannot be removed from inside
Only a speed-up: data would come over a direct fetch, and the postMessage bridge would no longer be needed for slots
The report's script can remove the sandbox from its own frame and call the API on behalf of whoever opened it
Access to data would appear, but not to the session: the cookie is HttpOnly and stays out of the script's reach
checks.why: MDN warns that allow-scripts together with allow-same-origin for a same-origin document lets the embedded document remove the sandbox attribute itself, after which the sandbox protects against nothing. The HttpOnly flag prevents JavaScript from reading the cookie, but it does not stop the browser from attaching it to fetch requests — so the report would call the platform API under the reader's session. That is exactly the difference between “someone else's code draws a picture” and “someone else's code acts on your behalf”.

checks.q: An author asks to allow one external link in a report — a minified charting library from a public CDN, “only 90 KB”. Which decision is consistent with the platform's invariants?
options: Allow it: the same 90 KB arrive faster over the network, because the CDN cache is shared by all reports
Allow it on condition of https and a pinned version: then the library contents cannot be swapped in transit
Allow it only for static reports: they hold no data, so there is nothing to leak through an external host
Embed the library code in the file or put it in a separate slot, and do not use an external URL
checks.why: The external network inside the perimeter may be blocked — the precedent with the Google Fonts stylesheet, which stalled page rendering, is recorded in the repository, and fonts have been self-hosted ever since. On top of that, a shared CDN cache does not work here at all: the report document is served with no-store, and its HTTP cache is partitioned per opening of the opaque origin. Https changes neither the reachability of the host nor the partitioning, and the report type has nothing to do with network dependencies.

checks.q: A snapshot report shows the user an endless “Loading data…” spinner. The console has a single line: a request to /api/dashboards/…/files/0 returned 401. What happened?
options: The user's session expired: until they log in again, both the page and the nested frame respond with 401
The report called the API itself, but its origin is opaque and no session cookie was attached to the request
The owner never uploaded the slot file, and for a missing index the server answers 401 instead of the expected 404
The user lacks the can_update_data right, and reading a slot is checked against exactly that right
checks.why: From an opaque origin any fetch to the platform API returns 401 by construction: the request carries no session cookie, because the document does not belong to the platform's origin. The correct path is to wait for op_file: the parent page fetches the slot itself and passes it to the report as an ArrayBuffer. An expired session would show up on the report page itself, not only inside the frame; a missing file gives 404; can_update_data governs writing, not reading.

checks.q: You need to persist the selected tab of a report between openings. What is correct on this platform?
options: Write to document.cookie: the approach is portable and does not depend on platform injections
Put the state into the document URL via history.pushState: the frame's URL survives closing the tab
Use localStorage as usual: the platform injects a transparent proxy and stores the setting
Keep the selection in memory only: in an opaque origin there is nowhere to persist it
checks.why: The real localStorage is blocked in an opaque origin, but the platform replaces it with a transparent proxy and persists the state on its side via op_save_ls — provided these really are settings, up to 4 KB: the state is inlined into the document on every render and bloats it. Cookies are unavailable because of the same isolation. The report document's URL belongs to the frame, not to the page, and it will not survive between openings.

lessons.title: Address, version, immutability
lessons.summary: By the end of this chapter you understand why versions are never overwritten, how content addressing makes caching safe, and why a fresh response from the cache once showed yesterday's numbers.

cards.heading: Three addresses of one report
cards.text: A report has a permanent identifier and several addresses, each standing for a different thing. Do not mix them up: they have different authorization and different caching rules.

head: Address
What it is
Who gets in
rows: the viewing page: report frame, docs, panels
the report document itself — the bytes the frame sees
the page behind an external link

cards.text:
A report's identifier never changes: not when a new version is uploaded, not on rename, not when it moves to another folder. That is what makes a link to a report fit for an email or a bookmark — the address points to the report, not to its contents as of today.

The canonical document address ends with a trailing slash; old addresses without it answer with a 307 redirect. The slash is not cosmetic: a relative link inside the report to a file x.js resolves to /render/{id}/x.js, and the platform serves it from the slot file with the matching name. A report that is “almost self-contained” is fixed by uploading the missing file into a slot, not by rewriting the markup.

cards.heading: A version is a new directory, not an edit
cards.text:
Replacing the markup does not overwrite the file. It creates the next version: a new v{n} directory on disk, a new row in the versions table with author and timestamp, and only after that is the report's current_version field switched over to it. Slot files are copied from the previous version so that the data is not lost.

There is also a guard against the most common mistake: if the new file changes the report type — say, instead of a full static export someone uploaded an application shell with an empty data slot — the platform refuses and asks you to confirm the intent. This is not pedantry: exactly this case has already produced a blank screen on the production server.

Old directories stay where they are. That is immutability in the practical sense: the published content of a version is never changed, it is replaced by a new version. The Lineage page can later honestly answer which version and which run produced specific numbers — precisely because nobody overwrote that version.

cards.heading: Idempotency and content addressing
cards.text:
Two concepts make this scheme work. An idempotent operation gives the same result whether it is performed once or five times; republishing the same version breaks nothing, because it changes nothing in place.

Content addressing (content-addressable storage) means the address of data is derived from the data itself rather than assigned by a person. Identical content has one address, different content has different addresses. The key property: an address cannot be “reused” for new content, so a response at such an address can be cached for as long as you like without the risk of going stale.

The prerequisite for both is determinism. Caching only makes sense for something that gives the same output for the same inputs; if the response depends on the time of day or on who is asking, the key has to be extended until it includes those inputs too. The report document here is deterministic by design: it is the same for everyone who has access, and everything that differs by viewer has been moved outside this document.

cards.heading: The version fingerprint as the cache key
cards.text: The platform caches the finished report document in process memory. The cache key is not the report identifier but a triple: identifier, version number and version fingerprint. The fingerprint is the modification times of all render inputs:
cards.code_text:
return (
    m(vdir / "dashboard.html"),
    m(vdir / "snapshot.json"),
    m(vdir / "theme.json"),
    m(vdir / "text.json"),
    m(vdir / "localstorage.json"),
    m(vdir / "files"),
)

cards.text:
Any edit to any of these inputs changes the fingerprint and therefore mints a new key. The old cache entry is not deleted; it simply becomes unreachable and is sooner or later evicted under the budget. The code comments put it plainly: invalidation here is key rotation, not partial deletion.

Why this beats “delete what is stale”: deletion is an operation you can forget to perform, perform incompletely, or perform in a race with a read. Key rotation cannot be done halfway: either you read by the new key and get the new content, or by the old key and get consistent old content. A single cache entry holds the raw bytes together with their compressed variants, all produced from the same content, so a mismatch between a variant and the original is structurally impossible.

cards.heading: A real case: a fresh response with yesterday's data
cards.text:
A report's data file was served with the header Cache-Control: max-age=300, must-revalidate. It looks careful: five minutes of lifetime and mandatory revalidation. In practice it turned out to be a bug, and it cost users wrong numbers.

The semantics of must-revalidate under RFC 9111 are these: a response may be stored and reused while it is fresh, and revalidation is mandatory only after it has gone stale. Until max-age expires, the browser does not ask the server anything. Meanwhile the slot address contains no version: publishing new data means a new file at the very same address.

It all came together. The generator ran and published new data. The user clicked “Show new report”, the page called location.reload() — and the browser answered the data request from its own cache with whatever had been sitting there for up to five minutes. The screen showed the previous report, and the button looked as if it had done nothing.
cards.note: The symptom of a caching bug almost never looks like a caching bug. It looks like “the button doesn't work” or “the generator didn't run”. That is why the regression is pinned by a test: this is exactly the class of defect that comes back if the rule is not written down.

cards.heading: How it was fixed
cards.text: The slot address was made content-based. Along with the name and size, the slot list now returns a short fingerprint v, derived from the same stat call that was already being made for the size: modification time and file length. The page puts it into the address as ?v=…, and the server answers immutable only when it matches.
cards.code_text:
Cache-Control: private, max-age=31536000, immutable   # ?v matches the fingerprint
Cache-Control: no-store, must-revalidate               # ?v is empty or stale

cards.text:
The logic here is strictly two-valued, and that is its virtue. If the fingerprint matches, the content at this address will never change again, so a one-year lifetime is safe and a repeat view costs not a single request. If it does not match, the response must not be stored at all, because an address without a version is reused by the next publication. The intermediate state of “probably still fresh” is gone, and that state was exactly the defect.

A strong ETag derived from stat was added at the same point: revalidation costs one lookup of the file's metadata, not reading several megabytes and computing a hash. Assets referenced by the report author directly cannot be rotated — their address was written into the markup by a human — so they are served as private, no-cache: one conditional request, closed by a 304 response.

cards.note: The browser does not cache the report document itself at all: it is served with no-store, must-revalidate. The cache here lives on the server, in process memory, and that is precisely why it can be controlled — a key on the server rotates instantly, whereas you cannot ask someone else's browser to forget a response.

takeaways: A report version is a new directory and a new row in the version log; published content is never edited in place.
The server cache key includes the version fingerprint — the modification times of all render inputs — so any edit mints a new key.
Invalidation here is key rotation, not deletion: it cannot be done halfway and cannot be forgotten.
max-age with must-revalidate does not revalidate while the response is fresh — and once showed the previous report's data after new data had been published.
Content addressing (?v = fingerprint) makes immutable safe: a fingerprint mismatch means no-store, and there are no intermediate states.

checks.q: The generator published new data at 10:00. A user opened the report at 10:01 and sees yesterday's numbers; at 10:06 the same numbers are replaced by fresh ones without any action. The response for the data file carried Cache-Control: max-age=300, must-revalidate. What happened?
options: The server render cache held the old entry: its key is refreshed on a schedule once every five minutes
The server served a stale file: the version fingerprint is recomputed by a background job with a delay
The copy sat in the corporate proxy cache, not in the browser, and the proxy refreshed it after exactly five minutes
The browser served its own copy while it was fresh: must-revalidate kicks in only after the response goes stale
checks.why: Under RFC 9111, must-revalidate requires checking a response only after it has become stale; within max-age=300 the browser answers from its own copy without asking the server. Hence the exactly five-minute window of divergence: 10:01 falls inside it, 10:06 does not. The server cache has nothing to do with it: its key contains the modification times of the inputs and rotates immediately after publication, and the fingerprint has no five-minute delay.

checks.q: Imagine the server render cache key were reduced to the pair (report identifier, version number), dropping the fingerprint. What error becomes possible?
options: Theme or text-replacement edits, or a slot swap, do not bump the version — the old entry is served
None: the version number is bumped on any edit to the report, including the theme and slot contents
The cache will take more memory: a short key distributes worse, and entries will stop being evicted on time
Different users will start receiving each other's entries: no access attribute will be left in the key
checks.why: Only replacing the markup bumps the version number; the theme, text replacements, saved state and the contents of the slot directory live inside the same version and change only file modification times. Without the fingerprint the key would stay the same, and the old entry would be served after every such edit. Memory is beside the point — the eviction budget does not depend on what the key consists of, and there is no user attribute in the key even now: the rendered document is the same for everyone who has access.

checks.q: You need to serve a data file so that a repeat view costs not a single request, yet publishing new data becomes visible immediately. Which solution is consistent with the platform's invariant?
options: A short max-age of 30 seconds: the window of divergence remains, but the reader won't notice it
An address carrying a content fingerprint: match — immutable for a year, mismatch — no-store
no-cache on every response: one conditional request per opening, but always up to date
A one-year max-age without a fingerprint, plus a “clear cache” button in the report UI
checks.why: Only content addressing achieves both goals at once: new content arrives at a new address, so the old response is never served in its place, and a fingerprint match guarantees immutability and removes the need to ask the server. A short max-age keeps the very window that already produced wrong numbers, merely shortening it. no-cache is honest, but pays a request for every opening. Clearing someone else's browser cache from the UI is impossible in principle — all we control is the address and the headers.

checks.q: A report with a 15 MB data file is opened 20 times a day. What does content addressing give, compared with the former max-age=300, in terms of bytes transferred?
options: Nothing: the file is downloaded again on every opening, only the response header changes
About 5% savings: roughly that share of openings used to fall into the old five-minute window
Almost all repeat openings stop pulling 15 MB, and new data becomes visible immediately
Savings for the owner only: other users are never given the address with the fingerprint
checks.why: With twenty openings a day, only a handful fell into the five-minute window of the previous response, meaning almost every opening pulled the full 15 MB again. With the fingerprint in the address the response is marked immutable for a year, and reopening the same content costs not a single byte until the data is republished. The header is not cosmetic here: it is what decides whether the browser goes to the network at all. The fingerprint is handed out in the slot list to everyone who opens the report, not only to the owner.

checks.q: A new file-serving route gained the line headers['Cache-Control'] = 'private, max-age=31536000, immutable', unconditionally, without checking the ?v parameter against the fingerprint. What will happen?
options: Old data will be shown at the same address for up to a year, and the server cannot fix that
Nothing bad: on publication the server sends a new ETag, and the browser picks up the update
The response becomes invalid: immutable cannot be combined with private and is discarded by the browser
Load will grow: immutable forces the browser to recheck the response on every page reload
checks.why: immutable means “while the response is fresh, it will not change”, and the browser will not recheck it even on a page reload; an ETag is presented only in a conditional request, and in this scenario there will be none. An address without a fingerprint is reused by the next publication, so the old content will stay on clients until the end of its lifetime, and clearing someone else's cache from the server is impossible. That is exactly why the code issues immutable only when ?v matches the fingerprint, and no-store otherwise.

lessons.title: How to ask a model
lessons.summary: By the end of this chapter you can state the intent before the code, you understand why a model needs the structure of the data rather than a description of it, and you know where the boundary runs for what leaves your computer at all.

cards.heading: The intent is an artifact, and it comes first
cards.text:
A report starts not with markup but with a statement: what decision is made from it, who reads it, which two or three numbers on it matter most. This text is an artifact in its own right. It outlives any particular file: when, six months from now, the report has to be redone for new data, you will ask the model again, and you will ask with the same intent.

A practical sign that the intent has been stated: you can read it aloud to a colleague, and they can tell you what is missing from the screen. If there is nothing to read, the model gets the task “make it look nice” and carries it out exactly as written.

It pays to keep the intent next to the report, not in a chat thread. Six months from now someone else will ask “why exactly these three metrics?”, and the answer should be a text, not a reconstruction from the code. It is the same discipline as with versions in the previous chapter: an artifact you can produce is cheaper than a memory you have to rebuild.

cards.heading: Context is a finite resource
cards.text:
Anthropic's engineering documentation calls the work on what you put into a request context engineering, and separates it from choosing wording: “Context engineering refers to the set of strategies for curating and maintaining the optimal set of tokens (information) during LLM inference” — that is, it is about the whole set of information, not about a well-turned phrase.

The same text records the observation that motivates the separation: a model has an “attention budget”, and every new token spends some of it; as the context grows, recall accuracy drops — an effect the text calls context rot. Hence a direct prescription: look for “the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximize the likelihood of some desired outcome”.

Let us turn this into practice for writing a report request. More is not better: a twenty-page methodology attached in full is read by the model just as attentively as your task, and dilutes it. What works is different:
list: hard requirements — as a list, in the imperative mood, with no “preferably”
the task — in one paragraph: what to show and what decision is made from it
the data — as a sample of rows, not as a description in words
anything the model can infer by itself — do not write at all

cards.heading: Structure instead of description
cards.text:
The most expensive mistake in a request is to describe the data in prose. “There is a sales export by region with dates and amounts” leaves the model a dozen decisions it will make for you: what the column is called, what type the date is stored as, what units the amount is in, what sits in an empty cell, how the decimal separator is written.

The same principle works the other way round: describe in words only what cannot be seen in the data — the meaning of a metric, the rounding rule, which value counts as bad. Everything that can be shown, show.

Five to ten rows of the export settle all these questions at once. The model will see the headers, see the formats, see that “Region” is sometimes empty and that “Customer code” is a string with leading zeros that must not be cast to a number. That is high signal density: a few rows carry more than a paragraph of description, and cost less.

cards.heading: What a working request consists of
cards.text: The ready-made template the platform gives an analyst is structured exactly this way — first the environment contract, then the task, then the data:
cards.code_text:
Write a self-contained HTML file — an analytical report.

HARD REQUIREMENTS
1. No external requests: all CSS, JS and fonts inside the file.
   If you need a library, embed its code in <script>; CDN links are forbidden.
2. The file must work offline when opened with a double click.
3. File size <= 2 MB. If there is more data, tell me and we will move it out.
4. Define all colors as CSS variables in :root and redraw the charts
   on window.addEventListener('op:theme', redraw).

TASK
[what the report should show and what decisions are made from it]

DATA
[paste 5-10 rows: column headers and sample values]

cards.text: The fourth item is in the requirements for a reason. The platform can recolor a published report, but it does so by rewriting the style rules and variables it can reach; a color hard-coded as a literal in a chart or baked into an image is beyond its reach. A format requirement is not pedantry; it is the condition for a later feature being applicable to your file at all.

cards.heading: The CDN ban is a consequence, not a whim
cards.text:
In the list of hard requirements, the ban on external links comes first, and it has two independent reasons. The first is the isolation from chapter one: the report runs in an opaque origin, and its network capabilities are deliberately cut back. The second is the perimeter: the external network may be closed from the corporate network, which has already been confirmed in practice, when a stylesheet from a public CDN blocked page rendering and the fonts had to be moved in-house.

By default a model writes differently — linking a library is simpler and shorter. That is why the requirement must be stated in the request explicitly: whatever you did not demand, you will get in its most common form.

cards.heading: The data boundary
cards.text:
What goes outside is a question that needs a precise answer, not a general statement. Separate two paths.

The platform path: for the report Q&A feature the rule is fixed in code, not in prose — cell values never go to the model. The request is built from definitions: the metric name, its definition, a few phrasings of the question, the list of dimensions, the author's prose description of a dimension (first 90 characters) and the glossary of terms. Not a single row is taken from the data, and the tests fail if even one value leaks into the request.

Your own path: when you open an external chat assistant and paste a sample of rows into it, you are the one drawing the boundary. The platform takes no part at that moment — none of its routes sees either your request or the model's answer — and that is exactly why the decision is entirely yours. The rule is simple: the sample must be a sample of structure, not an export. Real headers, neutral values: “Region”, “Customer code”, Sales_2026_w37.xlsx. Preserve the shape, though — length, case, leading zeros, decimal separator: it is the shape that carries the signal, not authenticity.

cards.note: Check a sample against a single criterion: can these rows identify a specific person, counterparty or deal? If yes, replace the values; the structure will not suffer. The model needs types, formats and edge cases, not authenticity.

cards.heading: How to read the model's answer
cards.text: The answer arrives confident and well formatted, and that is the main source of errors. Read it not as text but as a claim of conformance to the contract. A minimal check takes a couple of minutes:
list: search the file for http://, https://, googleapis — zero external-link matches
open the file with a double click and no network: the report must render completely
browser console: zero errors on normal data and a clear banner on empty data
type: does the text contain bootstrap-snapshot or input type=file, and is that the type you wanted
colors: defined as variables in :root, not as literals in the chart code

cards.text: If something does not match, do not rewrite the file by hand. Go back to the model with a precise description of the discrepancy — “item 1 is violated: a font is loaded from an external link; embed it or replace it with a system font stack”. That is cheaper and keeps the request and the file consistent: next time you ask with the same text, extended by one line.

takeaways: The intent is a separate artifact: it outlives the file and is reused every time the report is redone.
Context is a finite resource: look for the smallest set of high-signal information, not the largest.
Five to ten rows of the export replace a paragraph of description and settle the decisions about types, formats and empty values.
The CDN ban follows from isolation and the closed perimeter; it must be written into the request explicitly, otherwise the model will link the library.
The platform Q&A path sends not a single cell to the model; you are responsible for the contents of a sample you paste into an external chat.

sources.title: Anthropic — Effective context engineering for AI agents

checks.q: An analyst is preparing a report request. They have an 18-page methodology for calculating the metric, a two-paragraph task and an export of 400 thousand rows. What should go into the request?
options: The whole methodology and the task: the more context, the better the model will understand the calculation
The task, file requirements and 5–10 rows of the export; from the methodology, only the definitions
The task and the entire export: from complete data the model will infer the needed breakdowns and formats
The task only: the model will reconstruct the structure from the metric names in the text
checks.why: Anthropic's documentation describes context as an attention budget that gets spent and prescribes looking for the smallest set of high-signal tokens: eighteen pages of methodology dilute the task rather than sharpen it. A few rows of the export, by contrast, are dense — they establish column names, types, formats and edge cases. A full export is pointless twice over: it does not fit into the request and takes data outside for no reason, while the report receives the data later as a slot file anyway.

checks.q: The request says: “The data is an Excel file with sales: region, date, amount, customer. Make a dashboard with the trend and the top customers.” Which defect of this wording will show up in the finished file first?
options: The model won't realize HTML is needed and will return a Python notebook instead of a file
The report will be too heavy: without a size limit the model will embed the whole export in the markup
The model will pick the wrong report type, because the type has to be declared in the request in words
Formats and edge cases are not specified: parsing of dates, separators and codes will be guesswork
checks.why: The prose describes the entities but not their representation: in what form the date is written, which character separates the decimal part of the amount, whether the customer code is a string with leading zeros, what sits in an empty cell. The model will make each of these decisions itself, and the mismatch will surface on the very first real file. A five-row sample settles all of this at once. The report type, incidentally, is not declared in words at all — the platform infers it from the markup.

checks.q: The item about colors in CSS variables and redrawing on the op:theme event was removed from the requirements in the request. What will stop working in the finished report?
options: Nothing: the platform recolors the report by overriding style rules on top of any declared colors
The report will stop opening in the dark theme and show the reader a white screen instead of charts
Recoloring of the published report: the platform cannot change color literals in the chart code
Only the preview in the report grid will break; the file itself will still open correctly
checks.why: The recoloring mechanism works with what it can reach: variables and style rules, and for charts, their own interfaces; a color written as a literal in the drawing code or baked into a raster stays as it was. The report will still open and render — what breaks is not the display but a later platform feature, and that will be discovered months later, when redoing the file is already expensive.

checks.q: An analyst is about to paste 8 rows of an export into an external chat: managers' surnames, counterparty names, deal amounts. Formally this is “the structure of the data”. What is the right way?
options: Replace the values with neutral ones, keeping headers, types, formats and edge cases
Paste as is: without the real values the model won't see the real formats
Paste no rows at all and describe the columns in prose — the only way not to cross the line
Paste them, but ask the model not to remember this data and not to use it afterwards
checks.why: The model needs column names, types, formats and edge cases — authentic values add nothing to that. Replacing surnames and counterparties with neutral ones, while preserving length, case and separators, keeps all the useful signal and removes the disclosure of information about people and companies. Falling back to a prose description is overpaying: you lose exactly what the sample is for. A request to “not remember” gives no guarantees and is not a boundary.

checks.q: The model returned a report that loads a font from an external link. What should you do?
options: Delete the line with the link by hand: it is one line, no need to rewrite the request
Leave it: inside the perimeter the font won't load, and the browser will quietly use a system one
Upload the font file into a report slot and keep the external link in the markup as a fallback
Go back to the model with a precise statement of the violated requirement and get a new file
checks.why: A manual edit diverges from the request: next time the same text will give you the same error, and keeping intent and file consistent is the very reason the request is kept at all. Leaving the link is not an option: an unreachable external stylesheet does not degrade quietly, it blocks rendering — exactly the case that forced the fonts to be moved onto the platform. An external fallback path is pointless when the local file is already there.

lessons.title: Access: who sees a report
lessons.summary: By the end of this chapter you can tell authentication from authorization, you know the four ways to grant access to a report on this platform, and you understand what exactly the perimeter closes off and what remains your responsibility.

cards.heading: Two different questions
cards.text:
Authentication answers the question “who are you” and ends with the system being confident of your identity. Authorization answers the question “what exactly are you allowed to do” and happens on every access to a resource. They are confused more often than any other pair of concepts in security, and the result is always the same: a system that outsiders cannot get into, but inside which everything is visible.

On this platform the separation is visible literally in the routes. Sign-in is single: a redirect to corporate SSO, parsing of a signed assertion, a lookup of the account. Access to a specific report is a separate function, called on every request.

cards.heading: Authorization models: the foundation
cards.text:
Historically, two major models emerged. Discretionary access control (DAC) leaves the decision to the owner of the object: whoever created the file hands out rights to it. Role-based access control (RBAC) attaches rights not to people but to roles, and gives people roles; it is easier to administer, because rights change in one place for a whole category of employees.

OnePage combines both. The role settles system-wide questions — an administrator sees everything, the right to upload and to manage folders is given to a narrow group. The fate of a specific report is decided by its owner: whom to show it to, whether to publish it, whether to issue an external link. That is the discretionary part, and it is deliberately left to people: whoever made the report knows who needs it.

cards.heading: Four ways to get access
cards.text: The access-check function is short, and it is worth reading in full — the whole list is in it:
cards.code_text:
if user.role == ROLE_ADMINISTRATOR: return dashboard
if dashboard.owner_id == user.id: return dashboard
if dashboard.is_public:            return dashboard
perm = <this user's permission row for this report>
if perm and dashboard.is_published: return dashboard
raise 403

cards.text: It reads like this, top to bottom, and the order is part of the meaning:
list: administrator — sees any report; this is a role, not a right to a specific object
owner — whoever uploaded the report; always sees it, even unpublished
“open to all signed-in users” (is_public) — access for anyone who has signed in; note that the published flag is not checked here
named colleagues — a permission row for a specific person, but only together with the “published” flag: not even someone it has already been granted to will see a draft

cards.note: “Open to all signed-in users” is not “open to the internet”. Sign-in is handled by corporate SSO, and the sign-in page can only be reached from inside the perimeter. But inside the company such a report is visible to every employee with an account, and that is exactly what to ask yourself about before turning the flag on.

cards.heading: The external link
cards.text:
A fifth path stands apart: a token link. The token is created by whoever manages the report; the link can have a lifetime and a note on why it was issued. From then on the token is the only thing that is checked: the platform does not know who opened the link.

Two restrictions follow from this, both deliberate. First: the page behind the link has not a single write handler — a visitor can save neither a snapshot, nor a file, nor state. Second: a report with per-viewer row-level filtering enabled does not hand out external links at all — there is nobody to filter for, so the link is disabled entirely. When a link is issued, the audit log stores only the first characters of the token: the full token grants access by itself and must not sit in a log.

cards.heading: The “can update data” right
cards.text:
Granted permissions carry a can_update_data flag, and its scope is a conscious decision by the platform owner, made on 4 September 2026. This flag opens up more than uploading the data file. A person with it gets the report's entire right-hand dock: settings, access, versions, links, annotations, colors, text, data — and the right to upload a new version of the markup.

Exactly one thing remains reserved for the owner and the administrator: deleting the report.

This is enforced on the server too, not only in the UI: the routes for changing settings, version, markup, theme, slot files, permissions, and all external-link routes accept such a user, while deletion does not. The right-hand dock in the template is shown on the same condition, so no gap arises between what is visible and what is permitted.

This is a conscious departure from the principle of least privilege, which calls for granting the minimum necessary. The reasoning was this: a colleague trusted to update the numbers updates the report itself as well, and splitting this into five flags means breeding roles that nobody will configure correctly. The price of the decision is stated plainly too: by granting this flag you grant almost everything except deletion.
cards.note: Practical conclusion: “can update data” is not a minor concession; it hands the report over into joint ownership. If you only need to show the numbers, ordinary read access is enough.

cards.heading: Sessions and revoking access
cards.text:
After sign-in an op_session cookie is issued: HTTP-only, with an eight-hour lifetime. The session itself is stored not in process memory but in the database: it is shared by all worker processes and survives an application restart.

This has an important operational consequence. Restarting the service logs nobody out. Revoking access means deleting session rows; an administrator deactivating or deleting a user does this explicitly. The rule to remember: as long as the session row is alive, so is access, no matter how many times the application is restarted.

Access decisions are made on the server on every request — the UI merely shows or hides buttons. The fast document-serving path holds the result of its checks in a one-second microcache, and that is the only place where a revocation arrives with a delay — at most one second, and only there; all other routes ask the database on every request.

cards.heading: The perimeter: what it closes and what it does not
cards.text:
The server is isolated: it can be reached only through the corporate VPN, and VPN sign-in uses the same directory account as SSO. Hence an organizational lever: revoking the account closes both the VPN and sign-in to OnePage in a single action.

This closes very specific gaps, and they are listed honestly. There is no Single Logout: signing out of the platform kills only the local session, the user remains signed in to SSO, and the next sign-in goes through silently. There is no rate limiting on sign-in attempts. External links live until they expire. All three are covered by the fact that without a directory account a request will never reach the platform, and revoking the account kills both network access and sign-in.

cards.note: The perimeter does not cover what happens inside it. An employee with a valid account is not an intruder as far as the perimeter is concerned, yet all the authorization inside is aimed precisely at them: the published flag, the list of named colleagues, the “open to all signed-in users” flag and the scope of the can_update_data right. The perimeter removes a class of external threats, not the duty to think about whom you have shown the report to.

takeaways: Authentication establishes identity once; authorization is checked on every access to a report.
Access is granted by four paths: the administrator role, ownership, “open to all signed-in users” and named colleagues, and the last also requires the published flag.
An external link is authorized by its token alone, which is why the page behind it has not a single write handler.
can_update_data opens the whole right-hand dock and uploading a new version; only deletion remains for the owner and the administrator.
Sessions live in the database and survive a restart: revoking access means deleting session rows, not restarting the service.
The perimeter (VPN plus SSO on one account) covers external threats and the leaver process, but says nothing about who can see a report inside it.

checks.q: A colleague has been granted access to a report; the report is not marked as published, and the “open to all signed-in users” flag is off. The colleague gets 403. The owner sees the report normally. What is going on?
options: The rights haven't applied because of the permission cache: it refreshes on a schedule once a day
The colleague lacks the can_update_data flag: without it, access is to metadata only
The right is granted, but the named-colleague branch also requires the published flag
The report hasn't been indexed since upload and is visible only to its owner for now
checks.why: In the check function the owner branch comes first and does not look at the published flag, so the author always sees the draft. The named-colleague branch is the only one where a granted right requires the paired condition is_published: until the report is published, the granted access has no effect. The microcache on the fast path lives for one second, there is no day to wait; can_update_data governs writing and has no effect on reading.

checks.q: Suppose sessions were moved from the database into process memory, with everything else left as is. What changes?
options: Nothing significant: the cookie, its lifetime and the checking rules all stay the same
A restart will log everyone out, and with several worker processes sessions break
Sign-in gets faster: SSO no longer goes to the database on every session check
Revocation becomes instant on all routes, including the fast document-serving path
checks.why: Storing sessions in the database gives exactly two properties: the session is shared by all worker processes and survives a restart. In process memory both are lost — with several processes the user will be “kicked out” every other request depending on which process took it, and a restart will reset everyone. The fast-path microcache lives its own life and lags by a second regardless of where sessions are stored.

checks.q: A colleague from a neighboring department needs to update the data file in your report once a week. Which approach fits how the platform works, and its price?
options: Grant a right with the can_update_data flag, knowing the colleague gets the whole right-hand dock
Turn on “open to all signed-in users”: it's simpler, and any employee will be able to update the data
Transfer ownership of the report to the colleague: in terms of rights it is exactly the same
Issue an external link with a long lifetime: the colleague will upload the file through it
checks.why: The can_update_data flag is the only standard way to entrust data updates, and its scope is stated plainly: the whole right-hand dock plus uploading a new version of the markup, without deletion. The “open to all signed-in users” flag is not about writing at all — it merely shows the report to everyone who has signed in. Transferring ownership would also hand over deletion. An external link has not a single write handler by construction, so nothing can be uploaded through it.

checks.q: An employee has left the company, their directory account has been disabled, but nobody deleted their session rows in the database. What can they do until the session expires?
options: Nothing: disabling the account in the directory immediately kills the platform's session rows as well
They can open reports for the full eight hours from any network: the session depends on nothing else
They can open only external token links; everything else requires re-authentication
The session is formally alive, but they can't reach the platform: network access is closed too
checks.why: The session lives in the database and survives even a service restart, so by itself it stays valid until it expires. But network access uses the same directory account as SSO, and revoking it closes both paths at once — the decision not to build a separate access layer rests precisely on this coincidence. The tidy form of revocation still applies: an administrator deactivating the user deletes the session rows explicitly.

checks.q: A report contains information that not every employee should see. The owner turned on “open to all signed-in users”, reasoning that the perimeter settles the question. Where is the mistake?
options: There is no mistake: without the VPN and a directory account the report is unreachable anyway
The perimeter covers outside threats; inside, every signed-in user passes the is_public branch
The mistake is that the flag only works for published reports, and this one is not published
The mistake is that this flag grants, along with access, the right to update the report's data
checks.why: The perimeter answers the question of who can reach the platform at all, not who can see a specific report; an employee with a valid account is not an intruder for the perimeter. The is_public branch sits above the published flag in the access check and requires nothing but a completed sign-in — meaning every signed-in user will see the report. This flag grants no write rights at all; those come from a separate right for a specific person.

task.text: Create an external view link to your report — the Share tab on the report page.
task.hint: No links yet. Open your report, go to the Share tab, click “Create link”.

lessons.title: What happens when you open a report
lessons.summary: By the end of this chapter you can trace a request from the cookie to the finished bytes, explain why the fast path never answers with an error, and read the platform's measured numbers correctly.

cards.heading: The path of one request
cards.text:
Opening a report, you make not one request but at least two: the viewing page and, inside it, the report document. The second one is the interesting one: it is the most frequent request in the system, and almost everything below is built around it.

The order of steps is exactly this: parse the cookie, get the session and the user in one database call, check access to the report, compute the version fingerprint, look up the cache entry by key and send the pre-assembled response. Not a single step here can be reordered: authorization must happen before even one byte of content leaves the process.

Notice what is not on this list. There is no reading of a file from disk, no injection of service scripts, no compression — all of that has already been done and sits in the cache entry. A miss turns the request into a different scenario: assembly in a thread pool, under a per-key lock, so that ten concurrent readers of a cold, heavy report build it once rather than ten times.

cards.heading: Session and user in a single query
cards.text:
The session and the account are read with one SQL statement joining the tables, not with two consecutive calls. This is not a micro-optimization for elegance's sake: on the hot path every database call is both latency and a risk of tying up the event loop.

Related decisions of the same kind: reads go over a separate read-only connection, so that exhausting the shared pool cannot block the loop; rare housekeeping writes such as the “last seen” mark are moved to a background thread; the session lifetime is checked on read, regardless of when the expired row gets deleted in the background.

cards.heading: The fast path
cards.text:
A warm cache hit is served by a separate layer — the fast path. It is written on the bare ASGI protocol and enters neither the web framework's routing nor its dependency system: cookie, session with user, access check, fingerprint, finished response. Headers and body for each “entry plus encoding” pair are assembled once, so a hit costs two sends.

The authorization rules on it are the same, word for word, as on the ordinary route; database calls are made on every request, and the results are held in a one-second microcache.

cards.note: The fast path never answers with an error. No cookie, an unknown session, no access, a cache miss, parameters in the URL, any exception — none of these is an answer; each is a fall-through to the ordinary route, which derives everything again by the canonical rules. This is not specific to it: a layer that duplicates logic for the sake of speed must be able to do only one thing — agree; saying “no” is the job of whoever owns the rules.

cards.heading: Compression off the event loop
cards.text:
The second rule of the hot path: no compression on the event loop. Bodies of report documents and slot files are compressed in a thread pool, bodies larger than 64 KB are streamed in 256 KB chunks, and the headers go out before compression starts — which is why time to first byte is about 2 ms.

The reason was measured. A 26 MB report source was compressed by the standard middleware right on the loop: 1.3 s of freeze for every concurrent request. Compression of slot files belongs in the same category: reopening a report with a multi-megabyte file cost about 255 ms of CPU time until the compressed variants started being stored in the same cache.

Another case of the same kind is rendering page templates. It is pure CPU work, and before it was moved to the thread pool it caused 25–56 ms of event-loop stall on every page open. The rule that follows transfers beyond the platform: in a single-threaded event loop, anything that computes for longer than a few milliseconds must be computed somewhere else.

cards.heading: Measured numbers
cards.text: Now the figures — and straight away with the caveats without which they lie. The first column is a microbenchmark on loopback in the development environment; the second is the same build in a container on the production server.

head: Span
Development, loopback
Production server (20 July 2026)
rows: serve_us p50 — from cache lookup to response
fast_us p50 — the whole fast path with authorization

cards.text:
The medians improved, and the direction matches expectations: the access log that was switched off cost 91–96 µs per request. The tails, however, cannot be compared, and the report says so explicitly: the “after” window starts at process start, it contains cold cache builds (hit rate 88% versus 96%) and requests for a 15 MB data file that did not exist in the old window at all. The growth of p99 is explained by the composition of the window, not by the build.

Both windows are short — 6 and 16 minutes — and have different request mixes. Their status is stated plainly: an indication, not a result that has passed the validity gates.

cards.heading: p50 versus p99, and why the mean lies
cards.text:
The median describes a typical opening; the 99th percentile describes what every hundredth request runs into. Google's book on operations gives an example worth keeping in mind: with a mean latency of 100 ms at a thousand requests per second, one percent of requests may easily take 5 s. The mean here is not merely imprecise — it actively hides the very thing you measure for.

The practical conclusion for this platform: users notice not the median but the tail. A median of 0.42 ms and a p99 of 22 ms are the same report; the gap between them is the actual subject of the work.

cards.heading: The latency budget
cards.text: You have to add up everything that stands between the intent and the picture on the screen, and compare the terms by order of magnitude.
list: server time for the document — tenths of a millisecond at the median
the runtime environment — production costs about 30 times more than bare metal: 216 µs versus 6.8 µs, and that is about the shared CPU and the container, not about the code
the network between data centers — plus 1.75–1.79 ms on a 60 KB body
the browser — parsing the markup and executing the report's scripts, hundreds of milliseconds on a heavy file; a task longer than 50 ms already blocks the response to user input

cards.text: From this follows the priority recorded in the platform's decisions. An application optimization of under a millisecond is invisible to a remote user — it is done for the sake of the CPU and the tails under load. And the most expensive multiplier is the environment: before saving microseconds in code, check whether they are worth hundreds of microseconds in the container and the network. The same reasoning gives a sensible order of work on a report: the server side already costs a fraction of a millisecond, while your file costs hundreds, and that is where the gain lies.
cards.note: And one last word on honest numbers. The real load on the platform is about 0.5 requests per second: 487 records in 16 minutes. Optimizations that make sense at two thousand requests per second simply have no addressee here, and that is recorded as a decision not to return to them without new measurements.

takeaways: The path of a document request: cookie, session with user in one SQL query, access check, version fingerprint, finished response from the cache.
The fast path does not answer with errors: any deviation from a clean warm hit falls through to the ordinary route with the canonical rules.
Compression and template rendering have been moved off the event loop: 26 MB compressed on the loop froze all concurrent requests for 1.3 s.
The median and the tail are different quantities; the mean hides the tail, and tails from different measurement windows cannot be compared.
The runtime environment costs about 30 times more than the code, and the network between data centers 1.75–1.79 ms; optimizations of under a millisecond are invisible to a remote user.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Monitoring Distributed Systems

checks.q: A user complains that a report takes about 11 seconds to open. Telemetry shows a server time of 0.4 ms for the document and a body size of 6 MB. Where should you look?
options: At the server cache: the request bypasses the entry and rebuilds the document on every opening
At the network: six megabytes over the link between data centers account for those eleven seconds
At authorization: the rights check runs on every request and gets costlier with each granted right
At the file: parsing six megabytes of markup and scripts in the browser is the only such term
checks.why: 0.4 ms on the server and eleven seconds differ by a factor of about 27 thousand — the server simply has no such time in it, and a cache miss would add milliseconds, not seconds. The network between data centers adds about 1.8 ms on a 60 KB body; even with a body a hundred times larger that is a few hundred milliseconds, not seconds. What remains is the browser: parsing the markup, building the DOM and executing scripts on a six-megabyte file — exactly the class of problem for which the specification demands no more than 300 KB.

checks.q: Suppose the fast path were taught to answer 403 by itself when access is missing — “why route a refusal through the whole framework”. What error becomes possible?
options: Refusals will come from a simplified copy of the rules in the microcache and drift from the canon
None: the authorization rules on the fast path are word for word the same as on the ordinary route
Refusal latency will grow: returning an error from bare ASGI costs more than going through the framework
External links will stop working: they carry no cookie and will get 403 instead of the page
checks.why: The fast path is a duplicate copy of the logic that exists for speed, and its results are held in a microcache for about a second. As long as it can only agree, the cost of a divergence is bounded: it hands anything unclear to the ordinary route, which derives the decision again by the canonical rules. Allow it to refuse, and you make the copy a source of negative decisions — and any divergence or second-old entry turns into a wrongful refusal for the user.

checks.q: Two telemetry windows of the same build are compared. The /render median improved from 0.67 to 0.42 ms, while p99 grew from 11.35 to 22.51 ms. The second window starts at process start: its cache hit rate is 88% versus 96% in the first, and it also includes requests for a 15 MB data file that did not exist before. The load in both windows is about 0.5 requests per second. How should this be read?
options: The build sped up the typical request at the cost of the tail — a classic optimization trade-off
Load grew, and the tail reflects a queue of requests that built up in the second window
The tails of these windows are not comparable: a cold start, 88% hits versus 96%, and a 15 MB file
p99 on short windows is computed with a different formula, so these numbers are incomparable by definition
checks.why: The growth of the tail here is explained by the composition of the window, not by the build: the “after” window starts at process start and contains cold cache builds, as the hit rate of 88% versus 96% shows, plus requests for the fifteen-megabyte data file that did not exist in the first window at all. The load in both windows is about 0.5 requests per second — there is nowhere for a queue to come from. To get a comparable tail, you need a window without a cold start.

checks.q: Someone proposes an optimization that reliably removes 75 µs of server time per request. Users work over a network between data centers that adds about 1.75 ms to the response; the load is about 0.5 requests per second. How should this be assessed?
options: Do it first: 75 µs saved on every request add up to a noticeable gain
The user won't notice: the network adds about 1.75 ms, roughly 23 times more
Never do it: savings of under a millisecond are pointless in any system
Re-measure first: 75 µs is within the margin of error of such a measurement
checks.why: The estimate is simple: 1.75 ms of network against 0.075 ms of savings is about 23 to one, so the gain drowns on the way to the user. Work like this pays off by relieving the CPU and the tails under load, but at 0.5 requests per second there is pressure of neither kind, which is exactly why the front-end rewrite has stayed postponed. The number itself was measured twice by independent mechanisms, so the issue is not the margin of error but the absence of an addressee.

checks.q: A handler needs to compress response bodies for files of several megabytes. Which solution matches how the platform is built?
options: Compress in a thread pool, stream the output, cache compressed variants next to the bytes
Compress on the event loop, but only bodies over 1 MB — small responses won't suffer from it
Don't compress at all: in this perimeter, CPU time is more expensive than link bandwidth
Compress on the loop, but lower the compression level — then the latency will be acceptable
checks.why: Compression on the event loop blocks all concurrent requests, not just its own: the measured case — 26 MB compressed by the standard middleware on the loop — gave 1.3 s of freeze for every neighboring request, and a size threshold does not change that, it merely chooses who gets unlucky. Lowering the compression level shortens the time but does not remove the blocking. The right form is already implemented: computation in a thread pool, streamed delivery in 256 KB chunks and caching of the compressed variants — so reopening costs not a single cycle on compression.

units.title: Data and computation: where to compute and what it costs
units.subtitle: Why a report is slow not because of the server, where the data lives, and who pays for every megabyte

lessons.title: The weight budget and where the time goes
lessons.summary: You will understand what the time to open a report is made of, why the server side barely figures in that budget, and which weight thresholds the platform applies automatically.

cards.heading: Two sides of one opening
cards.text:
When a reader opens a report, two machines do the work. The server finds the finished document and sends it. The browser receives the bytes, parses the markup, builds the document tree, executes scripts, computes the layout and paints pixels.

The costs of these two sides are not comparable. Warm delivery of the document on the production host was measured in the serve_us span at p50 207.2 µs, and the full server response on the render route at p50 0.42 ms. On a test bench without Docker and without shared cores the same code fits into a few microseconds. All the remaining time that the reader calls “opening” happens in their browser.

Hence a rule that the platform's reference guide states in one line: the server delivers a report in a fraction of a millisecond, so the only effective optimization is to shrink what the browser has to parse.

cards.heading: Amdahl's law on one example
cards.text:
Amdahl's law says a simple thing: the speed-up of the whole system is limited by the share you actually speed up. If a part takes a share p of the total time and you speed it up by a factor of k, the total time becomes (1 − p) + p / k. When p is small, any k is pointless.

Plug in the platform's numbers. The report opens in 11 s; the server span is 0.42 ms. The server's share p ≈ 0.42 / 11000 ≈ 0.00004. Even an infinite server speed-up gains about four hundredths of a percent. Rewriting the handler in another language, adding cores, raising the cache limit — none of it can mathematically produce a noticeable result.

The register of performance decisions records this as a separate line: the runtime environment costs about 30 times more than the code, and the network between data centers adds 1.75–1.79 ms p50 on a 60 KB body. Optimizations smaller than that are done for the sake of the CPU and the tails under load, not for what a remote reader will feel.

cards.heading: Thresholds the platform applies by itself
cards.text: A report's weight is not a matter of taste; two automatic thresholds hang on it.
list: Heavier than 1.5 MB (the threshold is configured as 1,500,000 bytes) — the report's card on the grid stops showing a live preview and draws a placeholder. A grid with a hundred cards cannot afford a hundred heavy frames.
Heavier than 2 MiB — the upload page warns the author before publication.
Hard publication limits: the html or a single slot file — at most 50 MB each, a generator bundle zip — at most 20 MB, an auxiliary input file — at most 10 MB.

cards.note: The preview threshold is not cosmetic. Since it was introduced, a full grid-viewing session costs about 10 MB of traffic versus 209 MB before: live previews used to load for all cards at once.

cards.heading: Why compression does not solve the parsing problem
cards.text:
Compression shrinks what travels over the network. It does not shrink what the browser parses. After decompression you have exactly the same bytes, and parsing costs exactly the same.

Separate the two bills. The transfer bill is proportional to the compressed size and the link bandwidth. The parsing bill is proportional to the decompressed size and the client's CPU speed. Compression pays only the first. The web.dev materials put it this way: transfer size is critical for slow networks, parse time for CPU-bound devices.

Concretely on the platform: parsing a ten-megabyte string with JSON.parse means hundreds of milliseconds of main-thread blocking and a three- to fivefold memory peak. Gzip such a file down to a megabyte and the hundreds of milliseconds stay put, because the parser will see the same ten megabytes.

The platform does its own compression carefully: bodies over 64 KB are streamed in 256 KB chunks, and each chunk is compressed in a thread pool, not on the event loop. The story that gave rise to this rule is telling: a 26-megabyte source compressed by middleware right on the loop froze every concurrent request for 1.3 s.

cards.heading: The critical rendering path
cards.text:
The browser paints nothing until it has built the document tree and the style object model. CSS is render-blocking by definition: a rule that arrives last can cancel everything before it, so an intermediate result cannot be shown. Scripts encountered during parsing stop the parser.

Now picture a typical “giant”: a small amount of visualization code plus megabytes of JSON inside the markup. Those megabytes cost twice. The first time as part of the document that the browser must parse before the first paint. The second time as a string that the script passes to JSON.parse, again on the main thread, again before anything appears on the screen.

The cure is structural, not cosmetic: data must not live in the markup. The HTML keeps an empty snapshot and the code; the data arrives as a separate file. How that works is the subject of the next chapter.

cards.heading: The latency budget as a sum of terms
cards.text:
It is worth writing out the budget for opening a report in a column once, with orders of magnitude, and never arguing about it in words again.

Looking up and sending the finished document on the server — hundreds of microseconds. Network transfer within one building — a few milliseconds; between data centers — plus about 1.75 ms for half the requests on a 60 KB body, and that is with an ideal link. Parsing markup and executing scripts on the reader's machine — from tens of milliseconds to seconds, depending on the weight and the CPU. Layout and painting — as much again if the document tree is large.

Three conclusions follow from this table at once. First: the terms differ by three to four orders of magnitude, so they cannot be added up “by eye” — you have to look at the largest. Second: the further a term is from the server, the less you control it and the wider the spread between readers; a corporate laptop with two cores and a developer workstation will give different seconds on the very same file. Third: the only term that the report author influences directly and strongly is the volume of what has to be parsed.

External measurements say the same: parsing a megabyte of decompressed code on an average mobile device takes two to five times longer than on a top-end one. The spread here is not noise but a property of the device fleet.

cards.heading: What to measure so as not to optimize the wrong thing
cards.text:
Before speeding anything up, break the budget into terms and find the largest. A practical order of steps for a report that “is slow”: check the file size; check how much of it is data; check the time to first paint in the browser tools; and only then look at the server numbers.

The platform makes the first step easier: it records the exact weight of the report itself after rendering and uses it to decide the fate of the preview. If the report has crossed the preview threshold, you already have the answer to “why is it heavy” — almost always it is data inside the markup.

The general rule carries over beyond OnePage. A latency budget is a sum of terms of very different magnitudes: microseconds on the server, milliseconds in the network, seconds in the client. Work on the term that dominates. Amdahl's law will zero out all other efforts for you.

takeaways: The server's share of report opening time is measured in hundreds of microseconds; everything the reader calls “slow” happens in their browser.
Amdahl's law turns this into arithmetic: speeding up a term with a share of 0.004% is pointless at any factor.
Compression pays for transfer but not for parsing: after decompression the parser sees the same bytes and spends the same time.
1.5 MB is the live-preview threshold on the grid, 2 MiB is the warning threshold on upload; 50 MB is the hard limit for publishing a file.
The right optimization for a heavy report is to move the data out of the markup, not to speed up what already costs a fraction of a millisecond.

checks.q: A report opens in 11 s. The server span of the render route is 0.42 ms. The file weighs 6 MB, of which 5.5 MB is a JSON array inside the markup. What will produce a real gain?
options: Rewrite the server handler in a compiled language and give the process more cores
Enable stronger compression for this response: the body will travel many times faster
Move the data into a separate slot file in a binary columnar format
Increase the size of the server's LRU render cache so the report is always warm
checks.why: The server's share of the budget is 0.42 ms out of 11,000 ms, about 0.004%: by Amdahl's law the ceiling on the gain from options 0 and 3 is roughly four hundredths of a percent. Compression shrinks only the transfer, and the browser will still parse the same 5.5 MB of decompressed JSON on the main thread.
