Removing those 5.5 MB from the markup is the only action that touches the dominant term.

checks.q: An author publishes a report weighing 1.7 MB. The platform draws a live preview on a grid card only for files lighter than 1,500,000 bytes, the upload page warns the author about weight starting at 2 MiB, and the hard publication limit is 50 MB. What will happen?
options: The grid card will show a placeholder instead of a live preview, with no warning
Nothing: 1.7 MB is below both the preview threshold and the upload warning threshold
The upload page will warn about the weight, but the live preview on the card will remain
Publication will be rejected: the file exceeds the permitted report weight limit
checks.why: The live-preview threshold is configured as 1,500,000 bytes, while the upload warning fires at 2 MiB, i.e. at about 2,097,000 bytes. 1.7 MB is above the first and below the second, so the preview disappears silently. The hard limit for publishing a file is 50 MB, still far away.

checks.q: The grid has about a hundred cards, among them reports weighing several megabytes each. What breaks if the preview threshold is removed and a live frame is drawn for every card regardless of weight?
options: Nothing: the browser itself will defer loading frames that are not on screen
Only server load will grow: sending bytes is cheaper than parsing them
The server render cache will stop working: previews will bypass its key
A grid-viewing session will grow from about 10 MB to 209 MB of traffic
checks.why: This is a measured effect: before the threshold was introduced, a full grid session cost 209 MB versus about 10 MB after. The browser will not defer anything on its own — a frame with a report starts loading and parsing immediately. The server cache will keep working; it will simply have to send dozens of times more bytes, and the client will pay for parsing them.

checks.q: A team complains that a heavy report opens slowly. Which solution is consistent with the platform's invariant?
options: Give the server more cores and memory so that document delivery gets faster
Split the report: an empty snapshot in the markup, the data as a separate slot file
Break the report into five separate reports by section and link them together
Ask readers to open the report in advance so it has time to land in the browser cache
checks.why: The platform's invariant is “data does not live in the markup”: the document must stay thin, because every reader's browser pays the cost. Server cores touch a term of 0.42 ms. Splitting the report moves the problem rather than removing it, and breaks the single view of the data. The browser cache does not help the first visit, and that is exactly what forms the impression.

checks.q: A report file was compressed with brotli from 8 MB to 900 KB. The time to first paint barely changed. Why?
options: Brotli takes longer to decompress than it saves on transferring a body like this
The server compresses right on the event loop and delays every response
The browser does not support brotli and requested the file again uncompressed
Compression cut the transfer, but the browser parses the same 8 MB once decompressed
checks.why: The transfer bill is proportional to the compressed size, the parsing bill to the decompressed size; compression pays only the first. Brotli decompression is orders of magnitude cheaper than parsing markup and JSON, so option 0 is wrong. Moreover, the platform does not compress on the event loop: bodies over 64 KB are compressed in 256 KB chunks in a thread pool.

lessons.title: Data outside the markup: slots, cache, binary formats
lessons.summary: You will understand how a report receives its data as a separate file, why that file's address changes together with its contents, and why large volumes need a columnar binary format instead of JSON.

cards.heading: An empty snapshot and a slot file
cards.text:
The invariant from the previous chapter — “data does not live in the markup” — is implemented on the platform by a concrete mechanism, not by a wish. It is worth taking apart precisely as a mechanism: it has a protocol, an addressing rule and a format.

The split looks like this. The markup keeps a small embedded snapshot — top-level aggregates that are enough for an instant first screen. The main dataset travels as a separate file, which the platform stores in a slot and hands to the report itself.

The platform can tell one from the other. On upload, a data file is promoted to the embedded snapshot only when the embedded snapshot in the markup is empty; if the author has already put something into it, the file stays an ordinary slot. The rule is simple, and it protects against accidentally overriding the author's intent.

A slot is also the report's file system. A relative link inside the markup resolves to the slot file with the matching name, so a report that is not self-contained is fixed by uploading the missing file, not by rewriting the markup.

cards.heading: The op_ready / op_file protocol
cards.text: A report lives in an isolated window with no right to call the platform API, so it cannot fetch the file by itself. Instead a short dialogue of two messages takes place: the report announces it is ready, and the platform answers with data.
cards.code_text:
<script>
  window.addEventListener('message', (e) => {
    const m = e.data;
    if (m && m.type === 'op_file' && m.slot === 0) {
      render(new Uint8Array(m.buf));   // ArrayBuffer from the platform
    }
  });
  parent.postMessage({ type: 'op_ready' }, '*');
</script>

cards.text:
What matters is not the shape of the messages but how the body is passed. The page sends the ArrayBuffer in the list of transferable objects: the memory is not copied but passes into the recipient's ownership, and on the sender's side the buffer becomes detached, with zero length. For megabytes of data this is the difference between moving a pointer and copying megabytes.

The same dialogue works over an external view link too: the external view page draws the same bridge whenever the report has slots.

cards.heading: The slot address changes together with the file
cards.text:
The platform appends a version fingerprint to the slot file's address — a value derived from the same file metadata it already reads anyway: the modification time in nanoseconds and the size. The page receives the fingerprint along with the slot list and substitutes it into the request.

From there a strict rule applies on the server. If the fingerprint matches, the response is marked immutable for a year, and a repeat view costs not a single request. If it does not match, or there is no fingerprint, the response is marked unfit for storage. There is deliberately no middle ground.

This is invalidation by key rotation: the content changed, so the address changed. The platform applies the same technique to the server render cache and to versioned static files.

The story that made the rule so strict is instructive. The response used to live for five minutes marked “revalidate”, and that did not work: under the caching standard a fresh response is not revalidated at all. After a report was recomputed, the browser spent five minutes answering the data request from its own cache, the page reloaded and showed the old numbers, and the “Show new report” button looked broken.

cards.note: The slot fingerprint is derived from the file's modification time and size, not from a hash of its contents. That is enough for invalidation — publication always creates a new file — but it is exactly the detail you need to know before transferring the technique to another system.

cards.heading: Why large volumes call for a columnar binary format
cards.text:
JSON stores data row by row: each row is an object, each object repeats the field names all over again, each number is written as text. Parsing such a string is linear in its length and happens entirely on the main thread, and the intermediate objects cause a three- to fivefold memory peak.

A columnar format flips the layout: first the whole first column, then the whole second. Three consequences. Homogeneous values compress several times better. A numeric column lies in memory as a contiguous region, over which a typed array is created without a single copy. And you can read only the columns you need without touching the rest.

Repeated strings are handled with dictionary encoding: unique values are moved out into a dictionary, and the column keeps integer codes. A “Region” column over hundreds of thousands of rows turns into a dozen dictionary strings plus an array of codes. This is a standard technique of industrial formats: both Arrow and Parquet describe dictionary encoding in their specifications with exactly this motivation.

Estimate the order of magnitude on an example. Half a million rows, a “Region” column, twelve distinct values of 10–15 characters each. Row-oriented JSON will write the field name and the value itself half a million times — tens of megabytes of text. Dictionary encoding writes twelve strings once and half a million four-byte codes: about 2 MB, an order of magnitude less, and without compression. Compression on top of that works even better, because the code array is homogeneous.

What the columnar format pays with matters too. Assembling one whole row from it is more expensive: the values sit in different regions of memory. For a report this is almost always a good trade — filters and aggregates read columns, while a whole row is shown rarely and one at a time.

cards.heading: What it looks like in the repository
cards.text: The platform has a working implementation of such a format — both sides, encoding and decoding, live in one module, so that what the server serves matches byte for byte what the generator published.
cards.code_text:
MAGIC "OPC1" | uint32 LE descriptor length | JSON descriptor (space-padded to 8)
                | columns back to back, each aligned to 8 bytes, little-endian

descriptor: {"rows": N,
             "cols": [{"name", "kind", "offset" [, "values" | "null"]}]}
kind: i32 | f32 | f64 | dict
  i32  carries "null": -2147483648 (int32 minimum)
  dict carries "values" — a list of strings, code = index in this list

cards.text:
Take the mechanics apart piece by piece. The signature at the start gives an honest refusal on a foreign or corrupted file instead of quietly producing an empty report. The descriptor length separates the header from the data. The 8-byte alignment is not aesthetics: a typed array throws a range error at an unaligned offset, and without this rule the format simply could not be read on the client. A dedicated null code for integer columns is declared explicitly in the descriptor rather than implied.

One detail of this format is a security lesson that carries over anywhere. When the server serves a filtered output, it rebuilds the dictionary from scratch, only from the rows that passed the filter. Reusing the source file's dictionary is not allowed: the values of other rows would leak through the descriptor, even if not a single such row remained in the output. Metadata is data too.

cards.heading: On the client: views instead of parsing
cards.text:
Decoding a columnar file is not parsing but creating views. You read a short JSON header, and then for each column you create a typed array over the same buffer, with the right offset and length. Not a single copy, not a single JSON.parse over megabytes.

The platform's practical guidelines. A slot file is uploaded pre-compressed, with a .bin.gz or .bin.br extension: the platform serves it with the right encoding header and the browser decompresses it transparently, whereas a raw file the server would compress itself, and the first visit after every replacement would pay for that. Filters materialize only the filtered subset, not the whole table. Pre-compressed JSON remains an acceptable option, but only while the decompressed volume fits within roughly 2 MB.

The server does not pay for compression twice either: the compressed variants of a raw slot sit in the same server cache and are tied to the same file metadata as the fingerprint. Before that, every opening of an interactive report recompressed its multi-megabyte data file — about 255 ms per view.

takeaways: Data reaches the report as a separate slot file: the markup keeps an empty snapshot, and the exchange takes two messages, op_ready and op_file.
The buffer is passed by transferring ownership, not by copying: on the sender's side it becomes detached.

The slot address carries a version fingerprint; match — the response is immutable for a year, mismatch — unfit for storage. The middle ground between them once showed readers data that was five minutes old.
A columnar layout plus string dictionaries give better compression, reading only the needed columns, and typed arrays without copying.
A dictionary in the metadata is data: a filtered output must build its own dictionary from scratch.

checks.q: In a columnar file's descriptor, a column of type f64 has "offset": 12. What will happen on the client?
options: Nothing: the offset is read as a number of bytes from the start of the data block
Creating the typed array will throw a range error: 12 is not a multiple of 8
The column will be read shifted by 12 rows relative to the neighboring columns
The file will be rejected by its signature before the descriptor is even read
checks.why: The format aligns every column to 8 bytes precisely because a typed array over a buffer requires an offset that is a multiple of the element size: for f64 that is 8 bytes, and 12 is not divisible by 8. The offset is indeed counted in bytes, but that is exactly what makes 12 invalid. The signature here is fine; the error will surface later — when the view is created.

checks.q: What would become possible if no version fingerprint were appended to the slot file's address, and the response were marked fresh for five minutes with a revalidation requirement?
options: Nothing: the “revalidate” directive makes the browser ask the server on every single request
The server would stop serving compressed variants of the slot and compress them per request
The report would lose access to slots: the bridge passes the file only at the exact address
After publication the browser would serve the old data from its cache for up to five minutes
checks.why: Under the caching standard, a response that still counts as fresh is not revalidated — the revalidation requirement takes effect only after it expires. That is exactly what happened: the address was the same before and after publication, so the browser served old data for five minutes and the refresh button looked broken. A fingerprint in the address removes the very possibility: new data means a new address.

checks.q: A report needs to show a table of 400,000 rows and 12 columns, four of which are repeating text categories. Which solution follows the platform's rules?
options: A columnar binary file with string dictionaries, read through typed arrays
Embed a JSON array in the markup and parse it when the report loads
Put pre-compressed JSON in a separate slot and parse it on the client with JSON.parse
Split the data into 12 slots, one per column, each in JSON format
checks.why: Data in the markup violates the core invariant and hits the time to first paint. Pre-compressed JSON is acceptable only up to roughly 2 MB after decompression, and 400,000 rows by 12 columns clearly exceed that threshold: parsing such a volume means hundreds of milliseconds of blocking and a three- to fivefold memory peak. Splitting into slots does not remove JSON.parse, it only multiplies requests; a columnar format with dictionaries removes both the parsing and the repetition of categories.

checks.q: The server serves a filtered version of a columnar file: 40 rows remain out of 100,000. Why can it not reuse the source file's dictionary, and why must it build a new one?
options: The old dictionary is written in a different byte order and the client can't read it
The codes in the filtered rows will change anyway, which makes the old dictionary useless
The dictionary sits in the descriptor as an open list, so other rows' values would leak
The file would grow: the dictionary would take more space than the remaining rows
checks.why: The dictionary is stored in the header as the full list of the column's unique values, and the header travels to the client in full. Keeping the source dictionary means handing over the list of all values, including those whose rows the filter cut out. Byte order and size have nothing to do with it, and the codes could even be kept as they were: the problem is not the codes, but that the list of values is itself data.

checks.q: A reader opens a report for the second time today; its data has not changed since the morning. How many server requests does loading the slot file cost?
options: One conditional request, which the server answers with “not modified”
Zero: the fingerprint in the address matched, and the response is marked immutable
One full request: under the platform's rules the browser doesn't store slot responses
Two: first a fingerprint check in the slot list, then the request for the body
checks.why: The fingerprint is derived from the file's modification time and size; since the file has not changed, the page substitutes the same address, and on a match the server marks the response immutable for a year. In this case the browser does not go to the server at all. The “not modified” option describes a neighboring mechanism — a strong version tag (ETag), which saves the body but still costs one round trip; it is used where the address cannot be rewritten.

lessons.title: Memory: why O(1) per file is a rule, not advice
lessons.summary: You will understand the streaming file-processing contract of a generator, know the measured memory ceilings of a browser tab, and be able to tell streaming aggregation from materialization.

cards.heading: A two-method contract
cards.text: A generator is a trusted Python package that the platform runs not on its own side but on the analyst's machine. Its contract with the engine fits into two methods: files arrive one at a time, and at the end the outputs are assembled.

The return value of add_file is not a status report but a command to the engine. A file marked as a service file is kept on disk by the engine until the outputs have been assembled: these are lookup tables and overrides that the calculation will come back to later. All other files are deleted immediately after add_file returns, so you must not store their path — by the time you use it, the file will be gone.

This is the formal statement of the streaming discipline. After add_file returns, only aggregates should remain of the file: sums, counters, dictionaries. Not data frames, not lists of rows, not “let's hold on to it for now and concatenate later”.

cards.heading: Measured numbers
cards.text: The ban on accumulating data frames looks like a formality right up until you look at the numbers from the pilot generator.

head: Implementation
Memory on a full year of data
Outcome
rows: Naive: frames into a list, concatenation in finish()

cards.text:
The word “flat” in the second row is essential. The disciplined version does not grow with the number of files: however many there are, the same aggregates live in memory. The naive one grows linearly, so its fate is decided not by today's folder but by the one the user brings in six months from now.

The ceiling that all of this runs into has been measured too. The tab's memory wall is about 2.75 GB, and the engine warns starting at 2.4 GiB. In generator acceptance this warning counts as a failure: there is too little left before the wall to rely on luck. Memory is measured on a full year of data, not on a sample, and the peak consumption of a native run is taken as a proxy.

cards.heading: The bounds within which all this lives
cards.text: The engine checks the bounds before starting: exceeding a limit yields a diagnostic, not a crash in the middle of the calculation.
list: Files across the connected folders in total — on the order of 500, total volume — on the order of 500 MB, a single file — on the order of 35 MB. These are recommendations: the engine shows a warning with the actual numbers and a button to continue, and the analyst makes the call.
Tab memory — a wall at about 2.75 GB, a warning from 2.4 GiB. This is a hard limit.
Device — at least 2 GB of RAM and at least 2 cores.
Engine start-up on a corporate laptop with two cores and 4 GB costs 9.8 s cold and 7.0 s warm — a fixed launch fee that every extra dependency inflates.

cards.note: Walking the folders costs about 63 ms per file on a network share. Five hundred files means half a minute on listing alone, before the first parse.

cards.heading: The aggregate cache: the price of a repeat run
cards.text:
Memory discipline pays off not only in the calculation not crashing. It has a direct consequence for speed too: if the calculation's state does not grow, a repeat run need not start from scratch. The second mechanism that keeps the calculation within bounds is the mandatory aggregate cache. The cache directory is mounted into the engine's file system and survives a browser reload.

The cache key is fixed and not open to invention: sha256 of the schema version, the file name, the modification time and the size. The schema version is a checksum of the generator's own code, so any code edit resets the cache automatically, and old aggregates cannot survive a change in the way they are computed.

What gets cached is the file's finished aggregates in compact binary form, not raw rows and not half-processed data. The effect has been measured: a warm run is 2.85–4.5 times faster than a cold one. At the same time the code must work without the cache too, losing only speed: the quota may run out, and private mode may not provide one.

cards.heading: The foundation: streaming aggregation versus materialization
cards.text:
The general knowledge that carries over beyond the platform is expressed in terms of the order of memory growth. Materialization holds O(N) of the input volume in memory: read everything first, then compute. Streaming aggregation holds O(1) or O(k), where k is the number of groups: read a chunk, update the state, forget the chunk.

Not every calculation reduces to streaming. Sum, count, minimum, maximum reduce trivially. Mean — via sum and count. The median and the exact number of distinct values in general require either all the data, or an approximation, or an external algorithm: sort in chunks to disk and merge. That is exactly why databases can spill intermediate results to disk, while an in-memory data frame cannot.

A browser tab has a harder ceiling than a server process, and not on a whim. The WebAssembly runtime works with linear memory — a growable buffer that in the classic 32-bit model is addressed with four bytes; on top of that, the browser allocates the tab's process its own budget. Taking “as much as the system has” is impossible here in principle.

This is visible in a comparison of the platform's two engines as well. The in-browser query engine holds 53,226 rows in about 41.2 MiB of the database's own memory and 12 MB of JavaScript heap — three orders of magnitude below the tab ceiling. And it has a property a data frame lacks: it can spill to disk instead of crashing.

cards.heading: Determinism as the prerequisite for a cache
cards.text:
Next to the memory rule, the contract contains a rule that at first glance has nothing to do with memory: identical inputs must give byte-identical outputs. Sort everything that comes from the operating system's sets and dictionaries, fix the column order, do not bake the generation time into the data.

This is neither aesthetics nor tidiness for tidiness' sake. A cache is the claim “I have already computed this and will get the same thing”. The claim holds only for a deterministic calculation. A non-deterministic calculation cannot be cached: you do not know what exactly you stored and whether it will match the next run.

Determinism is also what the equivalence gates during refactoring rest on: two runs on the same data are reconciled by the hashes of all outputs, and a new version of a report is reconciled with the old one element by element on aggregates and as multisets on detail rows. Without byte identity such a check turns into manual comparison, which is to say it ceases to exist.

The generalization carries over anywhere: determinism is the prerequisite for a cache, and a cache is the prerequisite for acceptable repeat-work time. The order is exactly this, and the first link cannot be skipped.

cards.heading: Small things that cost more than they seem
cards.text:
The progress-reporting function crosses the boundary between the worker thread and the page on every call. Call it once per file and once per major phase, never in a loop over rows: a loop of hundreds of thousands of iterations turns that boundary into a bottleneck.

Data types matter more than the algorithm. Categories instead of repeated strings, 32-bit numbers where the range suffices, no columns of generic object type in working structures. After aggregation, intermediate objects are deleted explicitly and no references to them are kept.

Output files are written in a streaming fashion. Assembling a giant byte array in memory in order to write it out in one piece is yet another materialization, just at the output instead of the input.

takeaways: The add_file/finish contract is the statement of the streaming discipline: after it returns, only aggregates remain of the file.
A file marked as a service file is kept by the engine until the outputs are assembled; all others are deleted immediately, so their paths must not be stored.
The naive version of the pilot generator on a year of data used 980 MB and growing, the disciplined one a flat 468 MB, against a tab wall of about 2.75 GB and a warning from 2.4 GiB.
The aggregate cache key includes a checksum of the generator's code, so a code edit resets the cache by itself; a warm run is 2.85–4.5 times faster than a cold one.
Streaming aggregation keeps memory at O(1) in the input, materialization at O(N); a browser tab has a harder ceiling than a server process, and there is no way around it.

sources.title: WebAssembly Concepts: memory and linear address space (MDN)

checks.q: In add_file a generator stores the file's path in a list self._paths, and in finish() it opens the files again to finish computing the detail. What will happen?
options: Files marked as parsed have already been deleted — opening them in finish() will fail
It will all work: the engine keeps every file passed to it until the outputs are assembled
It will fail only on a repeat run, when the files arrive recognized from the cache
It will work, but the outputs will stop being deterministic from run to run
checks.why: Until the outputs are assembled, the engine keeps only files marked as service files; all others are deleted immediately after add_file returns. So the failure will happen on the very first run, not only on a repeat one. Such a scheme also breaks the memory rule: detail assembled in finish() is a materialization of the entire input.

checks.q: The disciplined version of a generator holds a flat 468 MB on a year of data; the naive one — which piles frames into a list and concatenates them in finish() — holds 980 MB on the same data, against a tab memory wall of about 2.75 GB. The author picks the naive one: the list makes the code simpler, and there is still plenty of headroom. What is wrong with this reasoning?
options: Nothing is wrong: 980 MB is almost three times below the wall, both versions fit with room to spare
The error lies elsewhere: concatenating frames in finish() breaks output determinism, memory is beside the point
The headroom exists only for today's folder: the naive version's memory grows along with the data
The error is in estimating the wall: the engine warns from 2.4 GiB, so the real headroom is half as big
checks.why: 468 MB is a ceiling, while 980 MB is a snapshot at a particular volume: the naive version keeps everything it has read in memory, so its consumption is proportional to the folder, while the disciplined one does not depend on it at all. Double the folder and the “headroom” is gone — on someone else's machine and in the middle of the calculation. Determinism has nothing to do with it: concatenation by itself does not break it. The warning from 2.4 GiB is a signal, not a different wall: it does not change the fact that one quantity grows and the other does not.

checks.q: The engine's guidelines: on the order of 500 files in total, a total volume on the order of 500 MB, a single file on the order of 35 MB. An analyst connects a folder: 300 files of about 8 MB each. Which engine bound will they hit first?
options: The file-count guideline: 300 is already close to the recommended 500
The total-volume guideline: about 2.4 GB against roughly 500 MB
The single-file guideline: 8 MB is already close to the recommended 35 MB
None of them: all three engine guidelines are met here with room to spare
checks.why: 300 times 8 MB is about 2.4 GB, almost five times the 500 MB guideline, whereas 300 files fit within the guideline of 500, and 8 MB per file is far from 35 MB. All three are recommendations, not prohibitions: the engine will show a warning with the actual numbers and let you continue. The danger is that behind these figures stands a real wall — tab memory of about 2.75 GB.

checks.q: An analyst recomputes a report a second time in a row on the same data, but the run takes as long as a cold one. What is the most likely cause?
options: The aggregate cache only works for files under 35 MB; the rest are computed again
The cache directory does not survive a browser reload and is cleared on every start
A warm run is not supposed to be faster: the cache saves memory, not time
The cache was reset: the code changed between runs, and so did the key's schema version
checks.why: The cache key is a hash of the schema version, name, modification time and size, and the schema version is a checksum of the generator's code: any code edit resets the cache entirely, and that is intentional. The cache directory does survive a browser reload, and the cache's gain has been measured at 2.85–4.5 times in time. A missing cache because of the quota is also possible, but a code edit is a far more frequent cause.

checks.q: A report needs detail of hundreds of thousands of rows for a table and an export. Which solution follows the O(1)-per-file rule?
options: Keep the detail in the generator's memory until finish(), then sort and write it there
Send the detail upward in chunks through the progress-reporting function
Stream the detail into a slot file, and keep only aggregates in memory
Store the paths of all files and reread them in finish() as needed
checks.why: Detail is exactly what must go out to a slot file rather than live in the generator's memory until the end of the run; it is to be written in a streaming fashion, without assembling a giant byte array. The option of sorting in finish() is classic O(N) materialization. The progress function crosses the worker-thread boundary on every call and is not meant for data, and the paths of non-service files are no longer valid by the time of finish().

lessons.title: Where the calculation runs: browser, server, lake
lessons.summary: You will understand the three places where computation can live on the platform, what each of them trades off, and why the server rejects a manifest produced by a different engine.

cards.heading: Three places, not one
cards.text:
Computation on the platform can live in three different places, and choosing between them is choosing who pays and what travels where.

The first is the analyst's browser. The engine brings up Python in WebAssembly, reads the selected folder through the system file access API, and sends only the result upstream. The source workbooks never leave the machine.

The second is the server. After a successful publication, the calculation uploads the folder's columnar partitions and a manifest to the platform's storage, and the server runs queries over them.

The third is no calculation at all: the slot file is served as is, and all the work is done by the report's code in the reader's browser. That is what the two previous chapters were about.

cards.heading: Move the computation to the data, or the data to the computation
cards.text:
Underneath all three options lies one classic question of distributed systems: what is cheaper to move — the data or the code.

Data is almost always heavier. Calculation code is kilobytes; a folder of exports is hundreds of megabytes. So in the first case the code travels to the data: the generator bundle is downloaded to the analyst's machine, where the folder already is. In the second case the data moved to the server once, and now it is the query that travels to it, not the other way round.

The reason the second place appeared at all has been measured: indexing 34 weekly files in the browser took 38 s, and that was already from the cache. Users without access to the network folder could not ask a question at all. Data that has already been computed and published does not need to be parsed again in every browser.

Note the asymmetry that keeps these two places from collapsing into one. While the data sits in the analyst's folder, the server does not know about it and physically cannot compute it — the only option is to ship the code. As soon as the result is published, a copy of the data appears on the server, and now it is cheaper to ship questions. It is one and the same principle, simply applied to two different states of the world.

cards.heading: What exactly moved to the server, and within what bounds
cards.text: The decision on server-side partition storage is stated explicitly, together with which rule it lifts.
list: After publication the calculation uploads columnar partitions and a manifest to the server; only the latest run is kept.
Everyone with access to the report can read; those who can run the generator can write; external view links have no access.
Size limits: a single partition — 64 MB, the report's entire storage — 1024 MB.
The rule “cell values never go to the model” remains unchanged. The rule “cell values never go to the server” is lifted for exactly this cache: access to the primary data equals access to the report.
The folder mode stays local: that data is not on the server by definition.

cards.heading: Server-side execution as a transport
cards.text:
The second step was taken a year after the first, following the same logic. Even with the index on the server, every conversation in the browser began with loading the query engine: the WebAssembly runtime comes up anew after every window reset and every page reload, and that takes 5–10 s.

The solution: a separate route runs queries on the server. The platform brings up a fresh instance of the very same engine module — but on native libraries rather than in WebAssembly — with a catalog of references to the partitions and a snapshot of the catalog and semantics. Instances live in a registry with least-recently-used eviction: no more than two at a time, and an idle one is dropped after 30 minutes.

The most important thing here is not speed but form. The server's operations mirror those of the browser worker one to one, so for the page this is simply a transport: the same call goes either to the worker thread or as a request to the server, and the whole interface above it is unaware of the difference. The local download path has stayed as a fallback for when the server refuses.

The price is stated too: an instance's frames live in server memory, hence the two-instance limit and the idle reset. Plus a time guard: a timer races the query and aborts it when the limit expires, so a runaway query turns into an honest time-limit message rather than a hung response.

cards.note: The boundaries did not shift with the move to the server: cell values still never reach the model, trust in SQL remains the boundary of the engine itself, with its own protection and its ban on external access, and the SQL text is not written to the audit log — filter literals may quote data.

cards.heading: parser_version and a foreign manifest
cards.text:
The partition manifest carries a parser version field. Server-side execution compares it with its own version and, on a mismatch, answers with a conflict code and a request to recompute the report.

Why such strictness. The parser version versions the type coercions performed during indexing: how text turns into a date, when a numeric string stays a string, what counts as missing. Partitions parsed by one version and queries written with another in mind produce not an error but a quietly wrong answer. That is exactly why the refusal is loud.

This also explains a specific behavior: the server does not execute an index built by the experimental second engine — by design, not by oversight. The second engine builds its own version space and has its own set of type coercions; between the two engines a type divergence was measured in 7 columns out of 32, and every divergence traces back to a type-inference step that the second engine lacks. A saved query of the form “where week is greater than 7” will not fail on such a divergence; it will return something different.

For the same reason, converting a slot into a partition has its own version space: it never saw the Excel coercions and must not inherit their version.

cards.heading: WebAssembly as a runtime, and its limits
cards.text:
The browser engine is a real Python interpreter compiled to WebAssembly. The runtime provides a sandbox and near-native speed, but it has hard limits, and the generator contract names them explicitly: no I/O outside the directories and paths it is given, no network, no threads, no subprocesses — this environment simply does not have them.

From this follows a practical rule worth understanding as an engineering one, not a formality: the generator code must remain correct in ordinary Python on a developer's machine as well. That is how it is tested — with a thin harness, without a browser. The contract from the previous chapter is written precisely so that you need not know about the browser.

The runtime's cost has been measured honestly too: parsing an Excel workbook in WebAssembly is 1.14–1.25 times more expensive than natively. This is an important number, because it refutes the widespread expectation of a twofold penalty: optimize the algorithm instead of waiting for a move to a native agent.

A separate consequence concerns multithreading. Threads in WebAssembly require the page to be cross-origin isolated with special headers, and that cannot be enabled on the platform without risk: reports render in a sandbox and may pull in their own images and fonts, which under such isolation would simply stop loading. The decision is recorded as “stay non-isolated”: the measured gain from threads is not worth a broken fleet of reports.

takeaways: Three places of computation: the in-browser WebAssembly engine over a local folder, server-side execution over published partitions, and plain serving of a slot file.
Choosing between them is choosing what is cheaper to move: code to the data or data to the code; the folder stays local because the server does not have it.
Server-side execution mirrors the browser engine's operations one to one, so for the page it is a transport, not a different program.
A parser version mismatch is a loud refusal with a request to recompute: a divergence in type coercions yields not an error but a quietly different answer.
WebAssembly has no network, threads or subprocesses, so a generator must remain correct in ordinary Python; parsing in this runtime is 1.14–1.25 times more expensive than natively.

checks.q: What would become possible if server-side execution did not check the parser version in the partition manifest?
options: Queries would fail with an explicit error on the first type-incompatible column
The partitions simply couldn't be read: another parser version has another file format
Query execution time would grow, but the result would stay the same and correct
The query would run and quietly return a plausible but different answer
checks.why: The parser version versions the type coercions at the indexing stage, not the file structure: the partitions can physically be read by any version. That is exactly why the refusal must be loud — otherwise the error would show up as a silently changed number, not as a failure. The measured divergence between the platform's two engines is 7 columns out of 32, and all of them concern type inference.

checks.q: A report has been published, and an analyst asks a question about its data from the panel in the browser. Which placement of the calculation matches how the platform is built?
options: Download the partitions to the browser and bring up the WebAssembly query engine again
Run the query on the server over the published partitions — it is the same engine
Send the data rows to the model and ask it to compute the answer to the question
Recompute the report with the generator and take the number from the fresh outputs
checks.why: The data is already on the server, so there is no reason to move it back to the browser and pay 5–10 s for bringing up the WebAssembly runtime after every window reset — that is precisely why server-side execution was introduced. The rule “cell values never go to the model” is still in force, so the third option crosses the boundary. Recomputing with the generator is needed only if the data is stale, not to answer a question.

checks.q: A generator contains a line where a four-worker thread pool parses files in parallel, and a lookup table is pulled in via an http request. What is wrong here?
options: Nothing: the engine itself will provide threads and network access when the generator runs
Only the worker count is wrong: you should target the two cores of the device gate
The runtime has neither threads nor network: the lookup is declared a required input file
Network is allowed, threads are not — the parallel parsing is the mistake
checks.why: The contract explicitly forbids both: this environment has no network, no threads and no subprocesses, and the code must remain correct in ordinary Python, which is where it is tested. The reference to two cores is the device gate, not the reason for the refusal. A lookup table without which the calculation is incorrect is declared as a required file, and its absence stops the run with a diagnostic rather than quiet degradation.

checks.q: The report Q&A panel used to show “loading query engine” for 5–10 s after every page reload, and now it answers immediately. What changed, and what stayed the same?
options: Queries moved to the server over the partitions; the operation set stayed the same
The engine is now cached in the browser, and the panel's set of operations changed too
A model now runs the queries instead of the engine, hence the instant answer
The partitions got smaller, so the WebAssembly runtime comes up much faster
checks.why: The WebAssembly runtime came up anew after every window reset and every reload, and it cannot be cached in a way that avoids this cost. The server path removes both the runtime start-up and the partition download at once. The key detail is that the operations mirror the browser's one to one, so the interface above did not change; the model still does not run queries on this path.

checks.q: A calculation publishes 20 partitions of 70 MB each, about 1.4 GB in total. The ceiling for a single partition in server storage is 64 MB, the ceiling for one report's storage is 1024 MB. What happens on publication?
options: It hits both the single-partition limit (64 MB) and the storage limit (1024 MB)
Everything uploads: the limits apply only to source workbooks on the analyst's machine
It hits only the report storage limit; partition size is not restricted
It hits only the single-partition limit; the total volume is not restricted
checks.why: 70 MB per partition exceeds the 64 MB ceiling, and 20 times 70 MB is about 1.4 GB against a storage ceiling of 1024 MB: both limits are violated at once. The limits apply specifically to server-side partition storage, not to source workbooks, which never leave the analyst's machine at all. The right response is to split partitions finer or to reduce the volume of primary data being published.

lessons.title: Colors, themes and redrawing
lessons.summary: You will understand what on a report page can be recolored, what cannot and why, and how to write a report so that a theme change is a single operation rather than a list of exceptions.

cards.heading: What gets recolored
cards.text:
A report's owner can recolor it right in the browser — on the colors tab of the report page. Everything that lives in the declarative layer gets recolored: color values in stylesheet rules, colors in the style attribute of elements, and the fill and stroke attributes of vector graphics.

The mechanics are simple. The platform first collects a palette: it walks all rules of all stylesheets, all inline styles and the fill and stroke attributes, normalizes the colors it finds and counts their frequencies. Custom properties — variables declared with two hyphens — are collected separately. The owner sees the list and assigns replacements.

Application works through an “old color — new color” mapping: each declaration found is rewritten, and its original value is remembered so that the next application starts from a clean slate. Variables are set directly on the document's root element.

cards.note: A rule worth carrying over to any tool that rewrites someone else's styles: touch only the declarations that actually contain a color literal. Passing every declaration through the style object model loses data — a shorthand with a variable reference inside, such as a border given in a single line, simply gets zeroed out after such a pass.

cards.heading: What does not get recolored, and why
cards.text:
A chart drawn on a canvas is a raster. There are no nodes, no attributes, no rules there: there are pixels that have already been put in place. A selector cannot reach them by definition, and no walk over the styles will find them.

This is the chapter's central distinction: declarative styling versus imperative drawing. Vector graphics describe shapes as nodes with attributes — they can be rewritten, and the browser will repaint by itself. A canvas describes a sequence of drawing commands — once they have run, only the picture remains, and the commands that produced it live in the code and in the library's configuration.

So the platform comes at it from the other side: it recolors not the pixels but the chart library's configuration, through the library's own interface.

Remember the distinction in its general form; it carries far beyond colors. A declarative description persists after it is applied: it lives in the document tree, and it can be read, changed and reapplied as many times as you like. Imperative drawing does not keep the description: the commands ran, and a picture is left. Anything you want to change from outside must be expressed declaratively; otherwise it will have to be changed from inside.

cards.heading: How the platform reaches the charts
cards.text:
The platform finds live instances of popular chart libraries, walks their configuration and data in depth, and replaces values in fields that look like a color: the key ends in color, or it is a fill, a stroke or a background. Strings and arrays of strings are replaced using the same mapping as for CSS, after which a chart update is triggered.

The walk is deliberately bounded: it goes no deeper than six levels and remembers the objects already visited so as not to loop on a self-reference.

Before the first replacement, the original palette of each field is remembered. This is needed for idempotency: the second and third application of a theme compute the replacements from the original colors, not from already replaced ones; otherwise the chain of replacements would carry the palette further away with every preview.
list: Changed: plain color strings and arrays of such strings in the chart configuration.
Not changed: gradients, callback functions that return a color, color scales and baked-in images.
After the replacement the platform triggers a chart update through the library's own interface rather than repainting the canvas by hand.

cards.heading: The theme event: the technique that makes the problem disappear
cards.text:
The list of exceptions above is an honest boundary of what third-party code can do. It can be removed from inside the report, and there is exactly one technique: do not bake colors into the chart; keep them in one place and redraw on an event.

After a theme is applied, the platform dispatches an op:theme event into the report window, carrying both the assigned variables and the replacement mapping. Your code listens for this event and re-reads the colors from wherever you keep them.

Why this works and enumerating exceptions does not. The colors in the report become a value derived from a single source of truth: the root custom properties. The platform can change them reliably — it is the simplest and most robust layer. Everything else — fills, scales, gradients, labels — you recompute yourself, and you know exactly where to do it.

This is a general principle, not a technique for one platform: state in one place wins. As soon as the same color is written as a literal in four files, any theme change turns into a text search with inevitable misses. The report requirements checklist records this as a separate line: colors via root variables, the theme event redraws the charts.

cards.heading: Why recoloring works at all without editing the file
cards.text:
It is worth spelling out once where exactly recoloring happens, because that determines what is possible and what is not.

The published report file is not rewritten. The theme is stored next to the report as separate data and is applied on the already opened page: the platform goes over the live stylesheets and live elements and replaces the values. That is why a theme change costs nothing on the storage side and does not create a new version of the report.

This is also where the idempotency requirement mentioned above comes from. Since there may be many applications in a row — the owner tries palettes and looks at preview after preview — each of them must start from the original state. The mechanism stores what exactly it has touched and restores it before the next application, and it remembers the original chart palette as a separate snapshot. Without these two precautions, ten previews in a row would give ten different results, and none would match the chosen pair of colors.

The rule carries over: any mechanism that edits someone else's state on top of it must be able to roll back exactly its own edits and nothing beyond them. Otherwise it is not a tool but a one-way operation.

cards.heading: Raster and vector: how to choose
cards.text:
The choice between canvas and vector graphics is a trade-off, not a matter of taste.

Vector gives you nodes: every shape is accessible to selectors, styles, event handlers and screen readers, scales without losing sharpness and can be recolored from outside for free. It pays with the size of the document tree: tens of thousands of nodes make layout noticeably heavier.

Canvas gives a constant cost regardless of the number of points and wins on large volumes and animation. It pays in that from outside it is a single picture: no styles, no accessibility, no automatic recoloring, and pixels show when you zoom in.

A practical rule for a report. Up to a few thousand elements, use vector — you get recoloring for free. Beyond that, use canvas, but then be sure to handle the theme event: from that moment on your chart is recolored only by your code, and no platform will do it for you.

takeaways: The declarative layer gets recolored: style rules, inline styles and the fill and stroke attributes of vector graphics.
A canvas is a raster that selectors cannot reach; the platform changes plain color strings through the chart library's interface.
Gradients, callback functions, color scales and baked-in images stay as they were — this is an honest boundary, not a defect.
A tool that rewrites someone else's styles must touch only declarations with a color literal and remember the original values; otherwise it loses shorthands and loses idempotency.
The reliable technique: colors in root variables plus redrawing on the op:theme event — one source of truth instead of a list of exceptions.

checks.q: An owner recolored a report: the headings, the table and a vector diagram changed color, but the chart bars did not. The chart is drawn on a canvas, and its fill is defined as a gradient. Why did this happen?
options: The chart library isn't supported by the platform, so the walk can't see its configuration
The theme was applied before the chart was built, and the palette came out empty
A canvas is a raster, and a gradient is not a plain color string, so it is left alone
A canvas has no fill and stroke attributes, so it never made it into the color palette
checks.why: The platform reaches charts not through CSS but through the library's configuration, and there it replaces only plain color strings and arrays of strings. Gradients, callback functions and color scales are excluded on purpose: replacing them with a single color value would ruin the chart. A late chart is in fact handled: the platform rebuilds the base palette if it is empty.

checks.q: What would break if the recoloring mechanism rewrote every declaration in a row, rather than only those containing a color literal?
options: Nothing: the extra declarations would be written back with the very same values
Recoloring would get slower, but the result would still come out correct in the end
Custom properties set on the root element would stop being applied at all
Shorthands with a variable reference would be zeroed out when written back
checks.why: A round trip of a value through the style object model is not always reversible: a shorthand containing a variable reference gets lost on read and write-back and turns into an empty value. That is why the rule is phrased precisely as “touch only declarations with a color literal”. Speed is secondary here, and variables are set by a separate mechanism and would not have been affected.

checks.q: You are writing a report with several canvas charts and want it to recolor correctly. Which solution matches how the platform is built?
options: Set color literals in the chart config and have the owner assign replacements by hand
Keep the palette in root variables and redraw the charts on the theme event
Replace all charts with vector ones, whatever the number of points on them
Draw the charts in advance and insert them into the report as ready-made images
checks.why: One source of truth plus redrawing on an event removes the whole list of exceptions at once: the platform reliably changes the root variables, and everything else you recompute yourself. Literals in the configuration will be recolored only partially — exactly where they are plain strings. Switching to vector with tens of thousands of elements will weigh down the document tree, and an image is not recolored at all.

checks.q: In a report the accent color is written as a literal in four places: in a style rule, in a diagram's fill attribute, in the configuration of a canvas chart, and in a string the code builds for a label. What happens on a theme change?
options: The first three are recolored, but the label built in code keeps the old color
All four are recolored: the platform walks both the styles and the chart configuration
Nothing is recolored: the platform on principle never touches any color literals
Only the first two are recolored: the platform cannot reach the chart configuration
checks.why: The style rule and the fill attribute belong to the declarative layer, and a plain color string in the chart configuration is replaced through the library's interface — these three will be recolored. A string that the code builds by itself at run time does not exist at the moment of the walk and will keep the old color. This is the typical outcome of scattered state: almost everything was recolored, and that is exactly why the discrepancy catches the eye.

units.title: The generator: contract, cache, reproducibility
units.subtitle: How the code the platform runs on the analyst's machine is built, and what proves its numbers can be trusted

lessons.title: What a generator is and why it runs on the analyst's machine
lessons.summary: You understand why the code travels to the data rather than the data to the code, which steps a run consists of, and who declares a lost run lost.

cards.heading: Definition
cards.text:
A generator is a trusted Python package that the platform executes not on its own servers but on the analyst's machine: a browser engine built on Pyodide/WebAssembly brings up Python right inside the tab. The source Excel workbooks never leave the user's machine. Only the result goes up: a finished HTML dashboard and its data files.

Note that this is not “a script someone runs by hand”. The code lives on the platform as an immutable bundle version, while the platform delivers the runtime, keeps the run history and publishes the result. The person picks a folder and presses a button.

cards.heading: Why the code travels to the data
cards.text:
There is a general principle of distributed systems: move the computation to the data, not the data to the computation. Do the rough maths. If the sources weigh D and the result weighs R, network transfer costs roughly T ≈ D / B when you move the data and T ≈ R / B when you move the code, where B is the link bandwidth. In our case D is measured in gigabytes and R in megabytes: the ratio D / R here is three to four orders of magnitude.

On top of the arithmetic there is a legal side. Data that never travelled does not need to be stored, encrypted, deleted on schedule or explained to the security team. The platform is built so that the server simply has nothing to lose: it has never seen a single cell of the source workbooks.
The run lifecycle has five steps, and their order matters:
list: the analyst picks the data folder through the File System Access API; the browser asks for permission on an explicit user gesture
the engine checks the limits BEFORE starting — exceeding a limit yields a diagnostic card, not a crash halfway through
Pyodide comes up in a Worker, dependencies are installed, the bundle is unpacked and a begin(...) session is opened
files are streamed into the session one at a time with add_file calls — O(1) memory in the number of files
finish() collects the outputs; the platform publishes them atomically, and only then makes a best-effort write of the write-back files into the folder

cards.heading: Why publishing comes before writing to the folder
cards.text:
The order of the last two actions is not accidental. Writing to the user's folder can fail for reasons that have nothing to do with the calculation: the workbook is open in Excel, the folder is not writable, the network share has dropped. If the platform wrote to the folder first, that failure would wipe out a report that had already been computed.

So atomic publication on the platform comes first: every file is read and size-checked before the first write to disk, the whole version lands on disk, and only then does a single database commit move the pointer to the new version. The folder write comes afterwards and counts as an optional bonus: its failure shows up as a separate line, but the run remains successful.

cards.heading: What stays down below and what goes up

head: Stays on the analyst's machine
Goes to the platform
rows: the source Excel workbooks, in full
intermediate frames and aggregates in memory
slot files with the report's data
observation counts: sheet and column names, counters

cards.note: There is exactly one exception to the “cells never travel” rule, and it is declared openly: quality checks and column profiles send up to five sample values for review, each truncated to 64 characters. This is the first and only case where cell contents cross the browser boundary.

cards.heading: Trust and the sandbox
cards.text:
Generators are written only by the platform owner's team: no outside code gets in. But in this project trust is recorded as an organisational condition, while the boundary is enforced technically. Inside the wasm sandbox the code has no network, no threads and no subprocesses — they physically do not exist there — and file I/O is allowed in only three places: the output directory, the cache directory and the path the engine itself passed to add_file.

This is an important engineering technique: do not rely on discipline where you can rely on a property of the environment. Trusted code still makes mistakes, and the sandbox makes them less often.

cards.heading: The run lock
cards.text:
One report must not be computed by two people at once: two parallel runs would publish two versions back to back, and nobody could say which of them matches the folder. That is why a run has a lock. While a run is alive, an attempt to start a second one is refused with three fields: who holds the lock, when they started and how many seconds ago.

A run's liveness is confirmed by a heartbeat: the page periodically checks in with the server, at an interval of about one sixth of the lock lifetime, but no less than 15 seconds. The default is a 180-second lifetime, i.e. a check-in every 30 seconds.

cards.heading: A lost run is declared by the next request
cards.text:
The tab was closed, the laptop went to sleep, the network dropped — the run is dead, but its row in the database is still in the “running” state. Who will close it?

The obvious answer is a background janitor that walks the table once a minute and marks anything overdue. The platform answers differently: an overdue row is declared lost by the NEXT run request. The check lives on the read path, not in the background.

The reason is that a janitor is a separate process that has to be started, monitored, fixed when there are several workers and remembered during deploys. And it works where nobody is looking. A check on the read path costs nothing when nobody runs the report, and fires exactly when the answer is needed. The platform applies the same discipline to session lifetimes: anything expired is not deleted on a schedule; it simply stops being valid on the next access.

cards.heading: Why the browser, not the server or a separate program
cards.text:
The problem of “computing on the user's side” has three known solutions, and the platform chose not the most obvious one.

The first is a separate program on the machine: it is the fastest of all because it computes natively, but it has to be installed, updated and fixed on a hundred laptops, and its errors are seen only by the person whose machine it crashed on. This is exactly the pain that was abandoned: code was updated by hand, results were published by hand, and there was no run history anywhere.

The second is computing on the server: then code updates are free, but gigabytes of sources must first travel to the server and then live there, which contradicts both the arithmetic and the data handling rules.

The third, the one chosen, is the browser. The platform delivers the runtime on every run, so “update everyone” means uploading a new bundle version. The data stays down below. The price is the engine start-up and the tab's memory ceiling, and both constraints are stated as numbers, not promises.

This is an honest trade-off, not a victory: the browser engine is aimed at folders on the scale of hundreds of megabytes, and for genuinely large profiles the architecture provides a local agent with exactly the same contract.

cards.heading: The cost of start-up
cards.text:
The convenience of the browser engine is paid for with a fixed sum. Start-up on a corporate laptop with two cores and four gigabytes of memory costs 9.8 s cold and 7.0 s warm: downloading the runtime, compiling wasm, installing dependencies, unpacking the bundle.

This is not a design flaw but a deliberate price, and it has a consequence for authors: every new dependency lengthens the start-up of every run for every user. Before adding a package, check whether thirty lines of your own code would solve the problem.

takeaways: A generator is a trusted Python package executed in the analyst's browser; the source workbooks never go up.
Limits are checked before start-up: exceeding a limit becomes a card with numbers, not a crash in the middle of the calculation.
Atomic publication on the platform first, then a best-effort write to the folder — a failed write does not wipe out a finished calculation.
The run lock lives by a TTL, and an overdue run is declared lost by the next request: a check on the read path is cheaper than a background janitor.
Engine start-up is 9.8 s cold and 7.0 s warm — a fixed price that every unnecessary dependency makes longer.

checks.q: An analyst started a recalculation and closed the laptop halfway through. Four minutes later a colleague opens the same report and clicks “Run”. The lock lifetime is 180 s. What will the colleague see?
options: The run starts: this same request marks the overdue row as lost and takes the lock
A 409 refusal: the lock holds until a background janitor sweeps the table and clears overdue rows
The run starts, but the abandoned row stays in the “running” state forever
A 409 refusal: the heartbeat extends the lock until the tab is opened again
checks.why: The abandoned row is about 240 s old against a 180 s lock lifetime, so it is overdue. The platform has no background janitor at all: an overdue row is declared lost precisely by the next run request, which then takes the lock. The heartbeat marks a live page, and a closed laptop marks nothing, so a 409 refusal would come back only for a fresh check-in younger than 180 s.

checks.q: Imagine the limit check were moved from “before start-up” to “during the calculation”: the engine computes until it hits the tab's memory wall. What exactly would the analyst lose?
options: Only waiting time: the same message about exceeding the limit arrives, just a minute later
A diagnosis with numbers before start-up: instead, a tab crash after minutes with no limit named
The run lock: a tab that crashed on memory leaves the run row hanging until the 180-second TTL expires
The aggregate cache: it is filled only after the preliminary limit check succeeds
checks.why: Walking the folder and summing sizes costs milliseconds per file, while the calculation costs minutes, so checking before start-up turns an expensive failure into a cheap one. The option about a delayed message is wrong: when memory runs out the tab closes and there is nobody left to report — no numbers remain and no explanation of which limit was exceeded. A lock hanging until the TTL expires is true, but it happens on any tab crash and has nothing to do with moving the check.

checks.q: Someone asks to add an HTTP download of an exchange-rate reference table when the generator's calculation starts. Which solution respects the platform's invariants?
options: Make the request with requests right in begin(): the library is already in the bundle's dependencies, it is one line
Download the file in the Worker using JS and pass the generator the ready bytes as a separate argument
No network from the generator: declare the table as an input — a folder file, aux input or platform table
Allow network access only in finish(), when the main calculation is done and its failure wipes out nothing
checks.why: The network physically does not exist in the wasm sandbox, so the requests option and the finish() network option will not work either in the browser or in the native CPython used for acceptance. Passing bytes from the Worker is technically possible, but it breaks the contract's key property: the same code must work outside the browser, which means the input must be declared in the manifest and arrive through an ordinary add_file, wherever the platform got it from.

checks.q: A folder is recalculated five times a day. Each run pays a fixed engine start-up — 9.8 s cold and 7.0 s warm — and the calculation itself takes about 4 s with a warm cache. The analyst asks for “the maths itself” to be made twice as fast. What gain will they actually feel per day?
options: About half of the total daily time: the calculation is the main item of the budget here
About half the total time: the engine start-up fee is paid once per day
About 35 s per day: the 9.8 s cold start is paid again on each of the five runs
About 10 s out of roughly 55 s a day: the 7.0 s warm start outweighs the 4 s maths
checks.why: Over a day that is five times 7.0 + 4 ≈ 55 s, of which the maths itself accounts for 20 s, and a twofold speed-up saves about 10 s. Start-up is paid on every run, not once a day, and after the first run it is warm, i.e. 7.0 s rather than 9.8 s. It is the fixed start-up fee that dominates the budget — hence the rule to economise on dependencies, each of which lengthens it for every user.

checks.q: A run finished successfully and the report on the platform was updated, but the file the generator was supposed to write back into the folder did not appear — it is open in Excel. Which state does the platform consider correct?
options: The run is successful and published; the folder write failure is shown as a separate line
The run has failed: until the file is written to the folder, the result cannot be called complete
The whole run is rolled back so that the folder and the platform do not diverge in content
The platform retries the write in the background and marks the run successful once the file is free
checks.why: Publication comes before the folder write precisely for this case: the computed report already sits on the platform in a single commit, while the user's folder is an external environment where a workbook open in Excel or a vanished share must not wipe out minutes of computation. A rollback looks consistent, but it would trade a reliable result for the state of a system the platform does not control, and there are no background write retries here: write-back is declared best-effort, and its failure is simply visible as a separate line.

lessons.title: The engine contract
lessons.summary: You know the three contract methods by heart, understand the cost of every return value and every progress call, and can read someone else's generator for violations.

cards.heading: The whole contract
cards.text: The entire interface between the platform and your code is three signatures. The engine expects nothing from a generator beyond them, and guarantees nothing beyond them.

cards.heading: Inversion of control
cards.text:
Notice who calls whom. The generator does not open the folder, does not list the files, does not decide the reading order and does not publish the result. It provides an object whose methods the engine invokes. This is classic inversion of control: the framework owns the loop, the component owns the step.

This shape was not chosen for aesthetics. It lets you swap the executor without touching the generators: today the loop is driven by the browser engine, tomorrow by a local agent on the user's machine. The contract between them is the same, so write your code as if you knew nothing about the browser.

cards.heading: The contract as an interface between two implementations
cards.text:
Read the contract as a boundary between two worlds, not as a requirement of one of them. On one side of the boundary is the executor: today the browser engine, tomorrow a local agent that will compute natively and without the tab's ceiling. On the other side is the generator.

As long as the boundary is narrow, replacing the executor touches no generator at all. As soon as a detail of one of the worlds leaks into it — a reference to a browser object, reading an environment variable, an attempt to learn the folder's real path — the boundary stops being a boundary, and moving to a different executor turns into rewriting every report.

Hence a practical rule that is easiest to keep in mind: if your code contains a word that only makes sense in a browser, you are not writing a generator but a piece of the engine.

The narrowness of the boundary has a price too: anything that cannot be expressed through the three methods has to be added to the platform explicitly, as a separate decision. That is how input declarations in the manifest and declared calculation stages came about — instead of letting the generator do anything and then guessing what it did.

cards.heading: Three return values and what the engine does with the file
cards.text: The string add_file returns is not reporting but a command. The engine uses it to decide the fate of the file on the virtual file system's disk.

head: Return
Meaning
What the engine does right after
rows: file recognised from the cache, parsing skipped
keeps the file until finish() ends

cards.note: The rule that breaks the most generators on their first run: after “parsed” and “cached” you must not keep the path. It points to a file that no longer exists. Only code that honestly said “service” may hold on to it until finish().

cards.heading: Why “return a status string” rather than “put the file somewhere”
cards.text:
It could have been designed differently: let the generator copy the files it needs into its own folder, and have the engine delete nothing. That interface looks simpler and is worse in practice.

First, memory. The O(1)-in-the-number-of-files discipline rests precisely on the fact that after add_file only aggregates remain and the bytes go away. On the pilot report, a naive version that accumulated frames and concatenated them at the end hit the tab's ceiling — 980 MB and climbing — while the disciplined one holds a flat 468 MB on a full year of data.

Second, observability. From the returned string the platform knows how many files were parsed and how many were taken from the cache, without a single line of code in your generator. “Put it somewhere” tells the engine nothing, and the statistics would have to be requested through a separate call that the author would forget to make.

cards.heading: The cost of a message across the boundary
cards.text:
A progress(stage, done, total, msg) call looks free but costs a boundary crossing: the generator lives in a Worker, the progress bar lives on the page, and every message travels via postMessage. Between threads data is copied by structured cloning, not shared, so there are no cheap messages here — only rare ones.

There is also a converse consequence that is forgotten more often: silence is expensive too. A full-year calculation takes tens of seconds, and a person who stares at a motionless bar for two minutes closes the tab — losing both the calculation and the time until the run lock expires. A sensible frequency is one call per file: the boundaries are natural and the bar keeps moving.

The rule is simple: one call per file and one per major phase. Never inside a loop over rows. Estimate the order of magnitude yourself: with 300 thousand rows, a call per row gives 300 thousand messages, each with its own object and its own entry in the page's event queue; the progress bar will not get any more accurate, and the tab will start to stutter.

cards.heading: What O(1) in the number of files means
cards.text:
The phrase “O(1) memory” here means it literally: consumption does not depend on how many files the folder holds — ten or five hundred. The peak falls on a single file: the interpreter's baseline plus one parsed frame plus a small accumulated aggregate.

Compare this with the naive scheme: N frames in a list and a concatenation at the end, i.e. consumption on the order of N × frame size, doubled at the moment of concatenation because the copy exists alongside the original. With a large enough folder this arithmetic hits the tab's ceiling.

The practical conclusion is not about memory but about a way of thinking. Write add_file as if the file were the last one: read it, update the sums and counters, release the references. Everything you keep between calls must be small and must not grow linearly with the number of files. If the dashboard needs detail, its place is a slot file, not a list of frames in the generator's memory.

cards.heading: The same code in plain CPython
cards.text:
The contract does not mention the browser, and that is a requirement, not a coincidence. Accessing the JS environment, window, or objects passed from the engine other than through the arguments is forbidden. I/O is allowed only in out_dir, cache_dir and at the passed path; no network, no threads, no subprocesses.

The reason is practical. Generator acceptance runs in native CPython with a thin harness: create a session, feed it files, compare the outputs. Debugging in the browser is twenty times more expensive than debugging in a terminal, and the equivalence and determinism gates run a full year of data, which a tab might not survive. Code that “only works in the engine” simply cannot be verified.

cards.heading: Find the bug
cards.text: Below is a fragment of a generator that passes registration and crashes on its very first run. Read the line marked (1) carefully, along with what precedes it.

cards.heading: Two more invariants people forget
cards.text:
First: folders are invisible to the generator. An analyst can attach up to eight folders — the main one and seven additional ones, for example a network share with a reference table — and the engine passes a flat union into add_file. Classify files strictly by name. The engine rejects the same name in two folders before start-up, so ambiguity never arises.

Second: declare the service workbooks without which the calculation is incorrect in the manifest, as a separate list of required files. Then their absence stops the run with a diagnostic card instead of turning into a silent fallback inside your code that nobody will ever notice from the report's numbers.

takeaways: The contract is three signatures: begin, add_file, finish; the engine knows and guarantees nothing else.
The add_file return value is a command to the engine: after “parsed” and “cached” the file is deleted immediately, “service” lives until finish() ends.
The O(1)-in-the-number-of-files discipline holds because only aggregates remain after add_file: a flat 468 MB versus 980 MB and climbing for the naive version.
Every progress call crosses the Worker→page boundary via postMessage: one call per file and per major phase, never inside a loop over rows.
The contract is shared by the browser engine and the future local agent, so the same code must work in plain CPython — and that is how it is verified.
