checks.q: A generator classifies the regions.xlsx reference table in add_file, returns “parsed” for it and stores the path so it can read the file in finish(). What happens on the first run, and why?
options: Everything works as normal: the engine cleans the virtual file system only after finish()
finish() crashes: after “parsed” the engine deleted the file, so self.ref_path points nowhere
Registration rejects the bundle: returning “parsed” for a file on the required list is forbidden
The table is read, but with last run's data: the engine caches service workbooks between runs
checks.why: The return string is a command to the engine. “parsed” and “cached” mean “I need nothing more from this file”, and the engine deletes it immediately after add_file returns; only files declared as “service” survive until the end of finish(). The manifest does not catch this bug: it describes inputs and outputs, not code behaviour, so registration passes and the very first run crashes. The engine has no cache of service workbooks between runs either.

checks.q: A generator calls progress() inside a loop over a frame's rows. The folder contains 26 files of roughly 14 thousand rows each. What symptom will the analyst see?
options: A smooth and very precise progress bar: frequent calls have no effect on run speed
A wasm out-of-memory: unsent messages pile up in the generator's heap and grow linearly with rows
A stuttering page and a longer run: about 360 thousand messages across the Worker→page boundary
The run finishes in the usual time: postMessage is asynchronous, so sends go into the tab's idle gaps
checks.why: 26 files of 14 thousand rows give about 364 thousand calls, and each one is a structured clone of the arguments plus an entry in the page's event queue. Asynchrony does not make a call free: it merely moves the work into that very queue which is responsible for the tab's responsiveness. The generator's memory does not grow, because the arguments are copied to the page side — the symptom is exactly the stuttering interface and the overall run time.

checks.q: A generator needs a reference table that lives in a separate network folder rather than next to the weekly files. Which solution fits the contract?
options: Read the file by its network path straight from Python: the generator's author knows the path in advance
Identify the right file by the folder number that the engine passes to add_file along with the name
Copy the table into the main folder before every run: the engine does not walk additional folders
Ask the analyst to attach a second folder and classify the file by name, returning “service”
checks.why: An analyst can attach up to eight folders, and the engine walks them all, but they are invisible to the generator: add_file receives a flat union of names, with no folder number at all. Classifying strictly by name is safe because the engine rejects identical names in two folders before start-up. Reading directly by network path is impossible in the sandbox and would break the requirement to work in plain CPython, and manual copying brings back exactly the manual labour the platform was meant to remove.

checks.q: Suppose the contract changed: add_file returns nothing, and the engine never deletes files until the run ends. What breaks first?
options: Memory: consumption stops being O(1) in the file count, and a full year hits the tab's ceiling
The “parsed/from cache” stats: the platform no longer knows how many files came from the cache
Determinism: without a returned string the engine cannot guarantee the same reading order
The aggregate cache: without a status string the engine cannot compute the next run's cache key
checks.why: The return value is how the engine decides the fate of the bytes: without it, copies of every workbook stay on the virtual file system's disk and in the tab's memory at the same time. That is exactly what the pilot's naive version looked like, going from 468 MB to 980 MB and climbing. Losing the “parsed/from cache” counters is true, but that is observability, not what breaks first. The reading order and the cache key do not depend on the return value: they are set by the engine and by the file's own parameters.

checks.q: An author proposes reading xlsx with openpyxl because “the library is already in the dependencies for writing”. What is the right objection?
options: There is nothing to object to: saving a dependency beats read speed, as every package lengthens start-up
xlsx is read with python-calamine, openpyxl stays for writing, and xlrd for legacy .xls
Keep openpyxl for both reading and writing; the local agent will erase the difference anyway
Better to write your own xlsx parser: any extra dependency lengthens every start-up
checks.why: The division of roles here is measured, not a matter of taste: the Rust parser reads a workbook noticeably faster, while wasm overhead compared with native execution is only ×1.14–1.25, so the gain comes from choosing the parser, not from waiting for a future local agent. Nor is a dependency saved: openpyxl legitimately stays in the bundle because it is needed for writing xlsx, so calamine is added alongside it, not instead of it.

lessons.title: manifest.json: the contract the platform checks
lessons.summary: You understand exactly what the manifest declares, which of it is checked at registration, and why an unknown top-level key is an error rather than a trifle.

cards.heading: Why a separate file
cards.text:
The generator's code describes HOW to compute. The manifest describes WHAT the generator reads, what it produces and within which limits it works. This separation lets the platform reason about a generator without ever running it: check the dependencies for suitability, build a data lineage map, tell the analyst in advance which files are missing.

The manifest sits at the root of the zip bundle next to your package. It is declarative: there are no conditions or branches in it, only statements.

It helps to keep the division of responsibility in mind. The platform reads the generator's name and entry point to find your module. The engine reads the inputs to decide which files to show the generator at all. Publication reads the outputs to lay the result out into slots. The pre-start check reads the limits. No field exists “just for tidiness”: each has a consumer, and that is precisely why the list of fields is closed.

cards.heading: Example
cards.text: A sample manifest for a weekly sales report. The names here are made up; the structure is real.

cards.heading: The fields that matter

head: Field
What it declares and what is checked
rows: up to 32 entries: a glob over file names, the data or reference role, sheets and columns. When inputs is non-empty, the engine reads exactly the matching files and skips the rest
indices are unique and non-negative; write_back: true means the file is additionally written back into the folder
top-level flag: the engine needs write access to the folder
up to 8 exact names of service workbooks; their absence stops the run before start-up
up to 3 entries: a file the analyst brings themselves, the label of the second run button and a reference to the write-back output it is downloaded from
exact name-version pins; the server decides the fate of each one at registration
recommendations for the number of files, total volume and single-file size
a row-level access declaration: which column of each slot file restricts its rows

cards.heading: What is checked at registration
cards.text:
Registration is the moment a manifest stops being text and becomes a commitment. The server checks the shape of every field, the cross-references between fields and the outside world.

Cross-checks are more interesting than formal ones. A name given in aux_inputs as a download source must refer to an existing slot with write_back: true. A quality check must name a column declared in inputs for a matching sheet, otherwise it would be checking something the generator does not read. Every slot in outputs.slots must be covered by the row-level access policy — either by a column or by an explicit list of pass-through slots: an uncovered slot would mean denying access to every viewer without full rights.

The outside world means dependencies. The server checks each pin against the vendored lock of the Pyodide 314.0.2 distribution and against live PyPI, determines whether a wasm build exists, and freezes the verdict into the immutable version. If the engine is declared as browser and a dependency is unsuitable, registration returns 422: a bad manifest stops the administrator, not an analyst in the middle of the working day.

cards.note: All manifest errors come back as a single list in a single response, in readable text. This too is a design decision: fix the manifest in one go instead of discovering errors one at a time over ten uploads.

cards.heading: Why an unknown top-level key is an error
cards.text:
The tempting alternative is “ignore whatever is extra”. It feels friendly and over the long run costs the most.

Imagine a typo: instead of required_files the author wrote requiered_files. Under an “ignore” policy the manifest registers, the report is computed, the service workbook is not checked before start-up, the generator silently takes the “without reference table” branch, and for weeks the report's numbers differ from what was expected — without a single error in the log. With a strict schema the author gets an “unknown field” response that same minute.

This is a general principle known as fail fast: detect an error where its cause is still visible. The manifest is a contract, and a typo in a contract must be visible. Note the symmetry: the same strictness applies to unknown keys inside inputs, inside sheets and inside columns, not only at the top level.

cards.heading: How declared inputs turn into mechanics
cards.text:
A declaration in inputs works in three places at once, and that is the main reason to fill it in thoroughly.

First, the read filter. While inputs is empty, the engine works in the old mode and hands the generator everything it found. As soon as inputs appears, the mode switches to an allow-list: a file outside the patterns is not read at all and is visible only as unmatched. Hence a practical warning: an overly narrow glob silently loses files. A pattern like Sales_2026_w??.xlsx will not catch Sales_2026_w37 (2).xlsx, and the report will be computed from an incomplete folder.

Second, the lineage map. The engine records which sheets and columns the generator actually opened and compares them with the declaration. Discrepancies of the “declared but not read” and “read but not declared” kind are visible in the data lineage graph.

Third, checks. A content check may refer only to a declared column, and a column profile is computed only for declared columns.

cards.heading: Declarativeness: what a declaration gives beyond the code
cards.text:
Everything declared in the manifest could in principle be deduced from the generator's code: it knows which files it opens. But “in principle” is expensive here.

To learn intent from code you have to execute the code — that is, wait for a run, on a real folder, by a specific person. A declaration, by contrast, is read instantly and without data. From it the platform builds the sources page before the first run, tells the analyst in advance which files are missing, and shows the author the discrepancy between what was promised and what was done.

Declarativeness has a flip side worth remembering: a declaration can drift away from the code. That is exactly why the platform does not take the manifest at its word but compares it with observation — what the generator actually opened. Here the declaration does not replace the check; it gives the check a reference point: without a declared intent, the observation would just be a list of facts with nothing to compare against.

cards.heading: An input the analyst brings themselves
cards.text:
Aux inputs have a role of their own. These are files that do not live in the data folder but come from a person: a template exported by the report, annotated by hand and brought back.

The mechanism is closed entirely by the manifest. A slot with the write-back flag yields a file the analyst downloads; the aux_inputs entry names the exact name under which it will return, the label of the second run button and a reference to that very slot. The platform checks that the reference points to an existing write-back output — otherwise the loop would not close, and this would be discovered only by the user.

Such a file reaches the generator through the same add_file and is classified as a service file. There are at most three entries, the name is exact and the size is limited. These restrictions are not stinginess but a way to preserve the “input is declared” property: a file a person brings in still remains part of the contract rather than a surprise.

cards.heading: Honest blind spots of observation
cards.text:
Observation has two limitations, and the platform names them plainly. A file recognised from the cache and not reopened by the generator is not caught by the hooks: there is nothing to observe, so the structure is taken from a previous observation, marked with exactly which run it came from. The agent engine with frozen SQL has no hooks at all, and its lineage map is only what is declared in the manifest.

This is a useful example of engineering honesty: a limitation named in the interface costs less than a limitation the user has to infer from mismatching numbers.

cards.heading: Freezing a version
cards.text:
Versions on the platform are immutable. Every upload is a new version; the pointer to the current one moves, and old bytes are never rewritten. Frozen together with the bundle are the dependency verdicts, the wheel name for PyPI packages, the report's semantics and the row-level access declaration.

This dictates the shape of a rollback: it is not “restore a version” but “upload the previous code as a new version”. Such a rollback does not rewrite history and does not break the runs' references to what they were computed with.

takeaways: The manifest is declarative: it says what the generator reads and produces, and lets the platform reason about the generator without running it.
An unknown top-level key is a registration error by design: a typo in the contract must be visible at once, not after weeks of mismatching numbers.
A non-empty inputs switches the engine to allow-list mode: a file outside the patterns is not read and is visible only as unmatched.
Dependencies are checked for wasm suitability at registration and frozen into the version; browser with an unsuitable dependency means a 422 for the administrator.
Versions are immutable; a rollback is uploading the previous code as a new version.

checks.q: An author added a top-level field "description": "weekly sales report" to the manifest and had registration rejected. What happened here?
options: The description string exceeds the limit: manifest text fields have a 64-character ceiling
Registration failed not because of the description but because the required top-level params field is missing
An unknown top-level key is rejected by design: the schema is closed so that a typo is visible
A description is allowed only inside entrypoint, next to the name of the generator's entry module
checks.why: The list of allowed top-level keys is closed, and anything not in it comes back as an “unknown field” error. It is not about the word description but about the policy: under “ignore whatever is extra”, a typo like requiered_files would register silently and turn into a quiet degradation of the calculation. There is no params field in the schema at all, and the 64-character ceiling for a description is invented: the schema simply does not know such a key.

checks.q: A generator declared inputs with the pattern Sales_2026_w??.xlsx. The folder contains files named like Sales_2026_w37.xlsx and Sales_2026_w37 (2).xlsx. What will the analyst see?
options: The run stops with an error: a file in the folder matched none of the manifest's declared inputs
The file is read: the glob is also matched against the base name, dropping the copy number in brackets
The file is read, but its rows never reach the slot file: only declared sheets go into a slot
The report covers an incomplete folder: the unmatched file is not read and only shows as unmatched
checks.why: A non-empty inputs switches the engine from “read everything you find” mode to allow-list mode, and a file outside the patterns is simply not read — with no error, because from the manifest's point of view nothing has been violated. The ? sign in a glob matches exactly one character, so “ (2)” does not fit into the name, and the option about matching the base name is wrong. This is the most expensive kind of error: the report looks successful but was computed from incomplete data.

checks.q: A report with row-level access publishes four slot files, but the rls policy describes a column for only three of them. What should happen at registration, and why?
options: Registration is rejected: every slot must be covered by a column or an explicit pass-through list
Registration passes: an uncovered slot counts as pass-through and is served to all viewers unfiltered
Registration passes, but the report won't publish: uncovered slots are weeded out at the publish step
Registration is rejected for another reason: outputs.slots may not declare more than three slot files
checks.why: The check cross-matches every index in outputs.slots against the row-level access policy: silence about a slot is not consent but ambiguity, and in production it would turn into denying access to every viewer without full rights. So the option about “pass-through by default” is wrong: an explicit decision by the author is required — either a column restricting the rows or an entry in the list of pass-through slots. There is no three-slot limit, and things never get as far as publication.

checks.q: In the data lineage graph, one file says its structure was taken from a previous run. The run succeeded and the generator works correctly. What is the reason?
options: This file's sheets and columns are not declared in inputs, so it was not observed at all
The file was recognised from the cache and not reopened: the hooks had nothing to observe
The engine exceeded its observation budget and dropped this file's schema, keeping the old record
The file came in as an aux input classified as a service file, and hooks don't observe service files
checks.why: Observation works by intercepting real read calls, and nobody opened a file with the “from cache” status — so there was nothing to observe, and the platform honestly marks which run the structure was taken from. The option about the observation budget describes a separate situation with its own truncation mark, and undeclared sheets would produce a “read but not declared” discrepancy, not a reference to a previous run.

checks.q: A team wants to update the pandas pin in the manifest and expects all already-published reports to start computing on the new library version. How accurate is that?
options: Accurate: pins are read from the generator's current manifest every time any run starts
Accurate, but only after a server restart: until then the engine takes dependencies from the old lock
Inaccurate: the dependency verdict is frozen into the generator version; the new upload becomes current
Inaccurate: pins have no effect on installation at all; the engine always takes the latest PyPI versions
checks.why: Versions are immutable: the server determined each dependency's suitability at registration and froze the result together with the bundle, so runs already computed keep referring to what they were computed with. The new upload becomes current and is picked up on the next run — a server restart has nothing to do with it. The “pins have no effect” option is also inaccurate: for PyPI packages a specific wheel name is frozen.

lessons.title: The aggregate cache and determinism
lessons.summary: You understand what the cache key is made of, why the bundle checksum must be part of it, and where non-determinism creeps into a calculation.

cards.heading: What is cached
cards.text:
The cache directory the engine passes into begin() is mounted in the origin private file system — the one the browser keeps for the page separately from the user's folders. It survives a browser restart, so the cache lives between runs.

What you should cache is the file's finished aggregates in a compact binary form: arrays, not raw rows and not half-processed data. The point is not saving parsing as such, but making sure the warm path does not rebuild in memory exactly what the O(1) discipline deliberately got rid of. On the pilot, a warm run is 2.85–4.5 times faster than a cold one — a difference the user feels on every repeat recalculation, so the cache is mandatory, not optional.

Note the word “aggregates”. What gets cached is not whatever is convenient to save, but what is expensive to compute and cheap to store. Intermediate state — a parsed frame, a half-cleaned table — meets neither condition: it is quick to compute relative to the whole pipeline, and it takes as much space as the source data.

cards.heading: The key
cards.text: The key is defined by the platform and is not open to invention.
cards.code_text:
# the aggregate cache key — exactly this, nothing more
key = sha256(f"{schema_version}|{name}|{mtime_ms}|{size}".encode()).hexdigest()

# schema_version arrives in begin() and equals the bundle checksum:
#   edit one line of code → new bundle sha256 → new schema_version
#   → no old key will ever match again → full invalidation

cards.heading: A hash as a name
cards.text:
This applies a general technique: content addressing. An object's name is a function of everything that affects it. If something had an effect but did not go into the name, you get the right name for the wrong content, and the cache starts lying.

Let us go through the components. The file name and its size are obvious. The modification time is a cheap “same file” signal that costs one stat call instead of reading megabytes. And schema_version is the SHA-256 checksum of the whole bundle, i.e. of your code.

It is the last one that keeps the cache honest. You changed a formula — a byte in the bundle changed — the sha256 changed — schema_version changed — no old key matched — every user recomputed from scratch. Invalidation here is not a delete operation but a key rotation: old entries simply stop being found. The platform applies the same technique to its report rendering cache.

cards.note: The cache may be absent: quota exhausted, private mode, a write error. Your code must work without it, losing only speed. Write to the cache best-effort, read from it with validation — the cache is not a source of truth but an accelerator.

cards.heading: Determinism as a prerequisite
cards.text:
The contract's requirement sounds strict: identical inputs produce byte-identical outputs. This is not aesthetics; two constructions rest on determinism at once.

The first is the cache. A cache substitutes a stored result for a computation, which is legitimate exactly when the computation would be a function of the same arguments. A non-deterministic calculation with a cache yields a report that depends on which files happened to be warm, and that is the worst kind of error: an irreproducible one.

The second is the equivalence gate. You can verify that a new generator version computes the same as the old one only if each of them computes the same thing twice. Otherwise comparing old and new degenerates into an argument about noise.

cards.heading: Reproducible builds
cards.text:
The idea is not ours. The Reproducible Builds movement defines its goal like this: “Reproducible builds are a set of software development practices that create an independently-verifiable path from source to binary code”.

Replace “binary code” with “dashboard” and you get our problem word for word. A report is a build artefact made from the generator's code and the data folder, and we want exactly the same property: an independently verifiable path. The reproducible builds community also has our list of usual suspects — build time, file system traversal order, locale, paths.

cards.heading: Where non-determinism comes from

head: Source
How it shows up
What to do
rows: the generation date is written into the data or the name
do not bake time into the data; if you need a timestamp, put it in a separate field excluded from comparison
columns and rows come out in a different order from run to run
sort everything that comes from sets and from file system traversal; fix the column order explicitly
decimal separator, string sort order, month names
format numbers and dates explicitly, sort by a given key rather than by locale
identifiers derived from id() or an object's hash
a timestamp is written into the container
check byte-identity on the finished file, not on the unpacked contents

cards.heading: Cache invalidation: why it is a hard problem
cards.text:
The joke goes that cache invalidation is one of the two hard problems in programming. The difficulty is not in deleting but in knowing exactly what has gone stale.

The platform sidesteps the difficulty with a technique worth remembering: it invalidates nothing. Instead of deleting stale entries, it changes the key they are looked up by. Old entries stay where they are, but nobody asks for them any more, and they leave when eviction needs the space.

The advantage here is not speed but the absence of a whole class of errors. Deletion can be partial: something was deleted, something was missed, and the system runs on a mix of old and new. With key rotation a partial state does not exist: either the key matched entirely or it did not. The server-side report rendering cache and slot file addresses work the same way — it is one discipline applied in three places.

The price of the technique is space: old entries live until they are evicted. For the aggregate cache this is acceptable, because quota eviction is routine and losing an entry costs only speed.

cards.heading: Serialisation practice
cards.text:
A simple rule: any serialised output must have a canonical form. Python's standard library has ready-made levers for this. json.dump's sort_keys=True parameter outputs dictionaries sorted by key, and the documentation names its purpose outright: so that serialisations can be compared between runs.

For checksums use hashlib: a file's sha256 and a hexdigest comparison is the cheapest and most honest determinism test you can write. Two runs on the same data, two sets of hashes, a character-by-character comparison. If they match, you have the property; if not, look through the five sources of non-determinism: time, order of sets and dicts, locale, object addresses, a timestamp inside the archive.

cards.heading: Determinism and performance are not opponents
cards.text:
Determinism is sometimes seen as a tax on speed: sorting costs time, the argument goes. Work out the orders of magnitude before agreeing.

Sorting a list of column names is tens of elements, microseconds. Sorting an aggregate before output is thousands or tens of thousands of rows, i.e. on the order of N log N over a quantity that has already been aggregated and become small. Compare that with parsing a workbook: hundreds of thousands of cells, each through a parser. Determinism is paid for in the part of the pipeline where there is already little data.

What is more, determinism saves time elsewhere. Without it the cache cannot be trusted, and the cache makes a warm run 2.85–4.5 times faster than a cold one. So the property that looks like a tax actually pays for the biggest optimisation in the pipeline.

cards.heading: What invalidates what
cards.text:
It helps to keep a dependency map in mind. Editing the generator's code changes the bundle checksum and thereby wipes the aggregate cache for every user — a price worth remembering when you publish a version for a cosmetic change to a chart caption.

Changing a file in the folder changes its size or modification time, and only that file is recomputed: the rest come from the cache and return “cached”. That is what makes warm incremental recalculation fast.

But a change to the data INSIDE a file without a change in size and modification time goes unnoticed by the cache — and that is a deliberate limitation, not a defect: checking the content would require reading the whole file, which is exactly what the cache avoids.

takeaways: The cache key is the sha256 of schema_version, name, modification time and size; there is nothing to invent beyond that.
schema_version is the bundle checksum, so editing the code automatically invalidates the cache for every user.
Invalidation here is a key rotation, not a deletion: old entries simply stop being found.
Determinism is a prerequisite for both the cache and the equivalence gate: versions can be compared only when each one is repeatable.
The usual suspects of non-determinism are time, set order and locale; the cure is explicit sorting, explicit formatting and canonical serialisation.

checks.q: Imagine the bundle checksum were removed from the cache key, leaving the name, modification time and size. What error would become possible?
options: The cache stops working altogether: keys start colliding across files and entries overwrite each other
The cache takes noticeably more space: old entries stop being evicted by the private FS quota
Invalidation becomes manual: an administrator has to clear the cache on every version publish
The report becomes a mix: unchanged files return aggregates computed by the old code, with no error
checks.why: The cache stores the result of a computation, and the computation is defined by code, so the code must be part of the entry's name. Without it, after a formula change, files unchanged on disk would return “cached” with aggregates under the old logic, and changed ones under the new; the report would become a mix of two versions without a single error message. The keys would still tell files apart by name, size and time, and the cache would take less space, not more: there would be fewer entries.

checks.q: Two runs on the same folder produce reports with identical numbers but different sha256 hashes of the output files. Where should you look first?
options: At non-determinism of order or time: set traversal, column order, a date inside the file
At the cache: a warm run serves aggregates from an entry and so writes different bytes than a cold one
At compression: gzip puts a timestamp into the container that is bound to differ between runs
At the data itself: the workbook changes on opening, so its size and modification time drift
checks.why: Identical numbers with different bytes mean the calculation is correct and the representation differs: the order of elements from a set or dict, or a baked-in timestamp. A warm run must produce a result byte-identical to a cold one — that is a separate acceptance requirement, so the cache is no excuse. A timestamp in the compression container is a special case of the same time disease, not a property of the algorithm.

checks.q: A folder holds 26 weekly files. The analyst added one new file and started a recalculation. How many files will be parsed again, and why?
options: All 27: adding a file changes the folder's contents, and the cache key is computed per folder, not per file
One: the rest match on schema_version, name, time and size, so add_file returns “cached” for them
None: the new file enters the cache only on the second run; the first uses the previous aggregates
About half: the cache evicts old entries as the private file system's quota fills up
checks.why: The key is computed for each file separately, so adding a new file does not change the keys of the others: their name, size and modification time are unchanged, and the bundle checksum is the same. Exactly the new file is parsed again — that is what the 2.85–4.5× warm-run gain rests on. Only a change to the generator's code wipes the whole cache, and quota eviction does not work “by halves” but as space runs short.

checks.q: To speed up the warm path, an author proposes caching the entire parsed frame and doing the aggregation in finish(). What is wrong here?
options: Nothing is wrong: parsing is skipped, and finish() aggregates frames more cheaply than add_file one by one
The problem is the key: the frame would have to be hashed in full, but the key is built from file metadata
The warm path would rebuild the frames in memory, bringing back the problem the O(1) discipline exists for
The error lies elsewhere: aggregating in finish() breaks determinism, since file order is not fixed
checks.why: Parsing is indeed skipped, but a frame read from the cache has to be put somewhere — and it takes the same tens of megabytes per file in memory as a fresh parse. The warm path would then hit the tab's ceiling exactly where the cold one does; that is why the rule requires caching compact aggregates. The cache key does not change either way: it is already built from the file's metadata and the bundle checksum, not from the entry's contents.

checks.q: An analyst corrected one number inside a workbook, saved it so that the file size matched the old one, and immediately started a recalculation. The report did not change. Is this a defect?
options: Yes, a defect: the cache must notice any change to a workbook's content and recompute it
Yes, a defect: schema_version broke, otherwise a data edit would yield a new key just like a code edit
No: after a manual edit the first recalculation is always cold; the cache kicks in only on the second
No, it is a declared limit: the key is metadata, and comparing content requires reading the file
checks.why: The key is a cheap identity signal, and it is cheap because metadata is read with a single file system call instead of megabytes of content. Full certainty would cost reading every file on every run, i.e. abolishing the cache itself. schema_version is fine here: it accounts for the generator's code, not the data, and saving usually does change the modification time, so the case is rare.

lessons.title: Checks before hand-over
lessons.summary: You know the three gates before a bundle is handed over, can line up the repository's tools in the right order, and understand why the engine shows diagnostic cards before start-up.

cards.heading: Why gates at all
cards.text:
A report differs from an ordinary program in that its errors do not crash — they compute. A wrong number looks like a number. So before a bundle is handed over to the platform owner, it is checked not by eye but by gates: a set of conditions, each either green or not, none of which requires judgement.

Anthropic's playbook on the AI-native SDLC states the same idea about developing with a model: “Every session checks its own work before a human sees it, whether tests, a build, or a screenshot diff”. The point is not bureaucracy but that feedback must be deterministic: for it to be useful to both a person and a model, a “matches / doesn't match” answer must come out without discussion.

cards.heading: Gate one: a run in plain Python on a real folder
cards.text:
The contract does not depend on the browser, so the generator is checked in native CPython with a thin harness: create a session, feed it files one by one, compare the outputs. This gate gives several answers at once.

Are the dispositions right: reference tables return “service”, data returns “parsed”. A repeat run with the same cache returns “cached” for every file. The outputs of a warm run are byte-identical to those of a cold one. The peak memory of a native run on a FULL year of data is used as a proxy for the browser.

That last word matters: the run is done on a full year, not on a sample. The engine's limits are checked against the real maximum the user will see; otherwise the first live run becomes the first real test.

cards.heading: Gate two: equivalence of the old and new version
cards.text:
When an existing report is rewritten to fit the contract or its internals are changed, you need to prove the numbers have not drifted. The comparison works differently for different kinds of output: aggregates are compared element by element, detail rows as multisets, i.e. respecting multiplicity but ignoring order.

This is a well-known technique — a characterisation test: the reference here is not “what is right” but “what it used to be”. It says nothing about the correctness of the old version, and that is precisely why it applies to legacy code where nobody remembers why the formula is the way it is.

In the repository this gate has a tool for reports with declared semantics — tools/semantics_gate.py. It loads the declared tables, runs each metric's SQL FROM THE semantics FILE and compares every cell of the totals with the reference calculation. The verdict is the share of matching cells, with a threshold of 0.8; below the threshold the tool exits with code 1. In the same pass it times each metric against a default budget of 2000 ms and also returns 1 if the budget is exceeded: a slow metric is a problem of the report layer, not a reason for the platform to raise the timeout.

cards.heading: Gate three: a byte-identical repeat
cards.text:
The cheapest and most merciless gate. Two runs on the same data, sha256 of all outputs, a character-by-character comparison. If they match, you have the property.

Put this gate first in execution order: it runs in minutes and cuts off a whole class of defects that would otherwise make the second gate raise false alarms. Order in the chain matters in general: cheap and broad first, then expensive and narrow — that is the whole point of the test pyramid.

cards.heading: The repository's tools and their order

head: Step
Tool
What it answers
rows: reproducibility of the numbers against the reference (threshold 0.8) and a per-metric time budget of 2000 ms
quality of answers to questions over the semantics: deterministic metric matching separately from the model (--no-llm) and, optionally, running the found query over a real folder
a live browser via the debugging protocol: the same scenario end to end, checking that the console has no errors

cards.text: The third step deserves a word of its own: it measures not “whether the answer is liked” but the share of questions on which the chain chose the correct metric. On a pilot set of 20 questions with the model switched off, the tool showed 18 out of 20: 14 matched deterministically with 100 % accuracy, 4 correctly rejected, 2 left to the model, 0 SQL errors. The value of the number is that it was obtained with no model in the loop: the deterministic part is verifiable, the probabilistic part is not.

cards.heading: The pyramid and its foundation
cards.text:
The classic test pyramid arranges checks by cost and coverage: many cheap, narrowly focused ones at the bottom, a few expensive, all-encompassing ones at the top. For a generator the pyramid looks like this: at the bottom, repeat and contract on a small folder; in the middle, equivalence and reproducibility of the numbers at full volume; at the top, the live browser.

The pyramid's foundation is not tests but a property without which no level works: determinism. If a calculation is not repeatable, cheap checks give false positives and expensive ones give false reassurance, because “it matched once” stops meaning anything.

That is why determinism appears twice in this course: as a contract requirement and as the first thing checked before hand-over. This is not a repeated topic — it is one and the same invariant seen from two sides.

cards.heading: Why the browser comes last
cards.text:
The browser run is the most expensive of all: it brings up a real Chrome, a real engine, real assets, and debugging it is several times slower than in a terminal. But it alone sees a class of defects invisible anywhere else — errors that exist only in the combination of page, worker and wasm.

Hence the ordering rule. Each next step is more expensive than the previous one and narrower in coverage. If a cheap step is red, there is no point running an expensive one: it will confirm the same thing, only twenty minutes later.

cards.heading: Diagnostic cards before start-up
cards.text:
Gates live with the author and cards live with the analyst, and they share a goal: turn silent degradation into an understandable error.

The engine distinguishes two kinds of findings. A blocking one is when there is physically nothing to run: the selected folder contains not a single matching file. An advisory one is when the folder is larger than the measured comfort zone; then the card shows the actual numbers alongside the recommended ones, adds a warning about a possible shortage of tab memory and a “Calculate anyway” button. The decision is made by a person, not the engine.

Identical file names in two attached folders and a missing declared required file come as separate cards. The second case is especially telling: without the card, the generator would simply take the “without reference table” branch, and the report would come out plausible and wrong.

cards.note: An engine memory warning during acceptance counts as a failure: the engine warns from 2.4 GiB, while the tab's wall is around 2.75 GB. There is too little room between the warning and the crash to treat it as headroom.

cards.heading: Hand-over checklist
cards.text: Before the bundle is handed to the platform owner, everything listed must hold. The list is short on purpose: anything that cannot be checked unambiguously is left out.
list: the manifest is valid — registration on the staging stand passes without a 422
all gates are green, and the acceptance report contains numbers, not words
dependencies have been agreed with the platform owner in advance
the report's HTML contains no external URLs — the corporate network will not open them
write-back and aux file names match between the manifest and the code
the HTML is under 1.5 MB, slot files are compressed, the bundle is no larger than 20 MB

takeaways: Three gates: a run in native CPython on a full folder, equivalence of the old and new version, a byte-identical repeat.
The chain goes from cheap and broad to expensive and narrow: harness, then the reproducibility gate, then answer evaluation, and only then the live browser.
semantics_gate compares the numbers with the reference at a 0.8 threshold and at the same time holds a 2000 ms budget per metric, returning code 1 if either is violated.
Equivalence is a characterisation test: the reference here is “what it used to be”, and that is exactly why it applies to a legacy calculation.
Diagnostic cards before start-up exist for one reason: silent degradation must become an understandable error before the report is published.

checks.q: You have an hour before hand-over and four check steps. The byte-identical repeat gate takes minutes, the browser scenario takes twenty. In what order do you run them, and why?
options: Cheap and broad gates first (repeat, contract), then the numbers gate, and only then the browser
The browser first: it is closest to reality and alone sees defects in the page–worker–wasm combination
Only the reproducibility gate: it computes the numbers, so it covers both contract and determinism
All four steps at once in parallel: total time then equals the time of the longest one
checks.why: The test pyramid is about the cost of feedback: a cheap step reports a defect in minutes, an expensive one confirms the same in twenty, so a red cheap step makes running the expensive one pointless. The browser is irreplaceable, but it sees its own class of defects and does not replace checking the contract; the reproducibility gate computes the numbers but says nothing about dispositions and memory.

checks.q: The reproducibility gate checks two things: the share of cells matching the reference at a 0.8 threshold and each metric's time against a 2000 ms budget. On a run it showed a matching share of 0.94 and exited with code 1, yet the report computes correctly. What happened?
options: The cell-match threshold is not 0.8 but 0.95, and a share of 0.94 fell just below the required level
A metric exceeded the 2000 ms budget: the gate returns 1 on time, not on a mismatch in the numbers
The gate returns 1 on any cell mismatch, and the matching share is only printed in the report
The tool did not find the declared tables in the folder and exited with a source data loading error
checks.why: The gate checks two things at once and fails on either of them: 0.94 is above the 0.8 threshold, so the numbers passed, and the non-zero code came from the time check with its default budget of 2000 ms per metric. This combination is deliberate: a slow metric is a defect of the report layer, and it is better seen in the same gate as a mismatch in the numbers.

checks.q: A required reference table was removed from the manifest, while the code keeps a branch “if there is no reference table, compute without it”. What changes in the report's life?
options: The run starts failing: the engine still requires every file declared in the bundle's manifest
The engine shows an advisory card with recommended numbers and a “Calculate anyway” button
The pre-start card disappears: the run succeeds and the report is published with wrong numbers
The report stops being published until the reference table appears in an attached folder
checks.why: The list of required files exists precisely so that the engine checks their presence before start-up and stops the run with a diagnostic. An internal fallback handles the same situation, but its decision is invisible from outside: the report looks successful, and the difference in the numbers is discovered weeks later. The advisory card is about the folder's size relative to the comfort zone; it has nothing to do with a missing declared file.

checks.q: During acceptance, the first browser run on a full year showed an engine memory warning. The engine warns from 2.4 GiB, and the tab's memory wall is around 2.75 GB. How should this be interpreted?
options: As normal: a warning is not yet an error, and there is more than a gigabyte left before the tab's wall
As a reason to raise the limit in data_scale: it describes the generator's memory use during a run
As a signal to compute on a sample instead of a full year so that the run fits in the tab's memory
As an acceptance failure: the warning starts at 2.4 GiB with the wall at about 2.75 GB — no headroom
checks.why: Between the 2.4 GiB warning threshold and the wall at around 2.75 GB there is roughly 0.3 GB — less than one large file or one unfortunate intermediate frame costs. data_scale describes the folder, not the generator's memory use, and editing it cures nothing; switching to a sample merely hides the limit that the run must find before the user does.

checks.q: The answer evaluation tool showed 18 out of 20 with the model switched off. Why is this number considered more valuable than the same one with the model switched on?
options: It measures the deterministic part of the chain: reproducible, so it guards against regressions
Without the model the tool runs in minutes, so such a gate can be placed first in time order
The model is not used in this chain at all; metric matching is always fully deterministic
Without the model data never leaves the machine, so the number was obtained in a proper security perimeter
checks.why: A gate makes sense when red and green do not depend on the run: only then can the number be pinned down and a regression noticed. The model takes part in the chain as a fallback for questions not matched deterministically — of the same 20 questions, two reached it — so the claim that it is absent altogether is false. Speed and the data perimeter are true in themselves, but it is reproducibility, not they, that explains the number's value.

units.title: Meaning: report semantics and asking in plain language
units.subtitle: How the platform tells a number from its meaning: definitions as data, three answer tiers, the boundary between data and the model, clarifying instead of guessing

lessons.title: Why a number needs meaning, not just a value
lessons.summary: After this chapter you understand how meaning differs from data and from schema, what exactly lives in semantics.json, and why a typo in a column name must be the author's error at registration rather than the user's empty answer a month later.

cards.heading: Data, schema, meaning — three different layers
cards.text:
Take a cell containing the number 0.87. On its own it means nothing: it could be a share, a coefficient, a price in some currency or a fraction of the plan. For a number to become a statement about the world you need three layers, and they work differently.

The first layer is data: rows and cells in the workbook the operator dropped in. It changes every week. The second layer is schema: which columns exist, what type they are, what the key is. Schema changes rarely and lives with the file. The third layer is meaning: what the “Shipped” column means in business terms, which rows are excluded from the calculation, which formula turns two columns into a metric, and what that metric is called in plain language.

The third layer is usually written down nowhere. It lives in the generator author's head, in code comments and in email threads. That is exactly why two reports on the same thing disagree in the third decimal place and nobody can say which one is right: a formula is not an object; it cannot be shown, checked or compared.

cards.heading: The platform's solution: meaning is data
cards.text: In OnePage, meaning is moved into a semantics.json file at the root of the generator bundle (ADR-13). The file is optional: a bundle without it registers exactly as before. But if it is present, it is frozen together with the generator version and becomes the single source of the metric's definition.
list: tables — canonical tables: which file (a glob over the workbook name), which sheet and which header row the columns come from, and how the source header maps to a snake_case name with a type (text, number, datetime, date, bool) and a role (key, dim, measure, time, attr)
views — DuckDB SQL views on top of these tables, created in order
kpis — metrics: name, a human-readable definition, question phrasings, unit and, most importantly, cell_sql — SQL that returns the dimensions plus either n and d (for a ratio) or value
rules — calculation rules in prose plus named values in curly braces that are substituted into the SQL during normalisation
glossary — the report's terms: what a “week” is, what counts as a fulfilled order
aggregations, periods, output_tables, uncertainties, known_findings, questions — auxiliary blocks of the same file

cards.heading: What it looks like
What is checked at registration
cards.text:
The file is not taken on trust. app/services/semantics.py checks it when a generator version is registered, in four passes.

Shape: are the top-level keys known, are the ceilings respected — at most 64 tables, 256 columns per table, 64 views, 128 metrics, 400 glossary terms, 20,000 characters per SQL statement, 2000 rows of inline data, 16 question phrasings; the whole file no longer than 512 KB.

Identifiers: every column name must fit a pattern of lowercase Latin letters, digits and underscores, up to 64 characters long; a double-underscore prefix is reserved for the engine's service columns. Two different source headers that coincide after normalisation are one column, and the platform requires them to be told apart by an explicit occurrence field rather than by hope.

Read-only: every SQL statement is run through the guard_sql protective filter. And the filter is not rewritten a second time on the server: the server loads the very same static/py/_explore.py module that will later run in the browser. One filter, one test suite, and whatever passed registration the engine will accept.

cards.heading: A dry run over empty tables
cards.text:
The fourth pass is the most interesting. The platform creates, in an isolated DuckDB (no external access, a 512 MB memory ceiling, single-threaded, with every statement interrupted after a 5 s timeout), empty tables of exactly the shape the engine will build: the declared columns of the right types plus two service columns. It then runs all the views and all the cell_sql statements against them.

There is not a single row of data — and none is needed. An empty typed table already answers whether a column exists, whether a name resolves, whether the result fits the required shape: dimensions plus n and d, or dimensions plus value. From the shape of the result the platform also derives the metric's dims and measure fields — the author does not write them, so they cannot drift out of sync with the formula.
cards.note: The check is separated from the data on purpose. A check “against a real folder” would pass only on whatever folder happens to be at hand and would fail for an operator a month later. An empty typed table gives the same verdict on typos and shape but depends on nobody's files.

cards.heading: Why a typo must be the author's error
cards.text:
Imagine the author wrote shiped instead of shipped. Without a dry run this typo has three lives. First: registration passes. Second: the report is published and the metrics panel shows a button. Third: an operator asks a question and gets either a DuckDB error in a language they do not speak or — worse — an empty result that reads as “no short shipments”.

The platform cuts this chain at the first point: the dry run returns an error, registration responds with a 400, and the error text is seen by the person who knows what shipped is. This is a general principle that reaches far beyond OnePage: the cost of a defect grows by an order of magnitude with each step down the pipeline, and shifting the check to the author (shift left) costs exactly one run over empty tables.

There is a second reason too, not about convenience but about honesty. An empty answer and an answer of “zero” look the same on screen but mean opposite things. A system that lets a typo turn into an empty answer systematically produces statements it has not verified.

cards.heading: A single source of definition
cards.text:
The normalised file is frozen into the generator version's semantics_json field and served by a separate route with the same access rights as the manifest. It is then bound to the catalogue tables of the attached folder (matched by file and sheet, with each column name mapped to the normalised header) and goes into the snapshot of the Explore page for every generator the user is allowed to run.

In the worker the bindings become views in a separate sem schema: columns are renamed and cast to the declared types, and files split into partitions are unioned by column name. Then the declared views are created. Readiness is computed for each metric separately: a metric is ready only if its tables were actually found in this folder.

An important consequence: the formula exists in exactly one copy. The metrics panel, the deterministic answer to a question, the reproducibility check — all of them take the same cell_sql. A metric stops being an agreement between people and becomes an object that can be versioned, diffed and presented.

cards.heading: Where others keep meaning

head: Where the metric definition lives
What happens when they disagree
rows: two reports compute differently; the difference is visible only by reading two codebases
In the author's head and email threads
the definition is lost along with the author; there is nothing to check
In a prompt to the model
the wording drifts from call to call; the answer is irreproducible
In semantics.json, frozen with the version
the difference is a diff of two bundle versions, and the dry run catches a typo before publication

cards.heading: Reproducibility as a gate
cards.text:
A declaration has value only if it matches what the report actually prints. There is a separate tool for this, tools/semantics_gate.py: it runs the definitions from the JSON over real exports and compares them with the authors' reference calculation. On the first generator, where the gate was set up as a pre-registered experiment, 482 out of 482 Grand Total cells matched (312 of them numeric), and the merge checkpoints matched row by row. On the second generator the experiment was run blind: an independent agent received only the bundle, one data workbook and a description of the JSON's shape — no reference output and no hints; the independent gate passed 12 out of 12 checks.

This is a gate, not a one-off win: every new version must pass it. A declarative layer that nobody reconciles with the calculation is just more prose documentation, only in curly braces.

takeaways: Data, schema and meaning are different layers that change at different rates; in OnePage the third layer lives in semantics.json and is frozen together with the generator version.
semantics.json describes tables, views, metrics with a cell_sql formula, rules and a glossary; dims and measure are not written by the author but derived from the shape of the SQL result.
Registration checks shape, identifiers, read-only status and a dry run over empty typed tables in an isolated DuckDB — not a single row of data is on this path.
A typo in a column name must become a 400 error for the author: otherwise it survives until it reaches the operator and turns into an empty answer indistinguishable from an honest zero.
One cell_sql feeds the metrics panel, the answer to a question and the reproducibility gate — the metric becomes an object, not an agreement.

checks.q: The dry run over empty tables was removed from registration, leaving the shape check, the identifier check and the read-only filter. Which defect will now reach the operator?
options: A metric referencing a non-existent column yields an empty result or an error in the browser
The semantics file exceeds the 512 KB ceiling and no longer fits into the Explore page snapshot
Views start being created in arbitrary order and stop being able to reference one another
Two headers with the same normalisation merge into one column without requiring occurrence
checks.why: The shape check looks at keys and ceilings, the identifier check at how names are spelled and at clashes between normalised headers, and the protective filter at whether this is a single SELECT. None of them knows whether the orders table has a shipped column: that can be found out only by executing the SQL, even over an empty table. The file size is covered by its ceiling, and the order of views by the rule that they are created in order.

checks.q: An author proposes validating semantics.json by running the formulas over a real data folder on their laptop instead of over empty typed tables. What does this violate?
options: Only the time budget: a run over the full folder won't fit in the 5 s timeout per SQL statement
The check becomes dependent on a particular folder, while the verdict on typos would be the same
dims and measure would be derived from real rows and drift away from the metric's declared formula
Data from the folder would land in the model's prompt and breach the boundary between data and context
checks.why: A typo in a column name and a wrong result shape (no n and d, no value) are visible on an empty typed table — no rows are needed for that. A run over a particular folder, however, passes or fails depending on what happened to be in that folder today, so registration stops being reproducible. The model is not involved at all: the dry run does not call it, and dims and measure are derived from the shape of the result, not from the data.

checks.q: An author declared two different source headers that coincide after normalisation and did not give the occurrence field different values. Registration returned 400. Why didn't the platform resolve this silently by taking the first match?
options: DuckDB does not allow two columns with the same name in one table and would abort the dry run
From coinciding headers the platform cannot derive the column's type and its role in the dimensions
Column order in a workbook isn't guaranteed, so a silent choice would differ from file to file
Header normalisation runs in the browser, and the server cannot see its result at registration
checks.why: The engine resolves a source header into a catalogue key and adds a suffix by occurrence number; if the author has not said which occurrence they need, the binding depends on the column order in a particular workbook. The same frozen declaration would then give different numbers on two exports — exactly the irreproducibility semantics was introduced to eliminate. The type has nothing to do with it: it is declared explicitly, and the server performs normalisation itself.

checks.q: In semantics.json an author changed the fill_rate metric's measure field from ratio to value but left cell_sql as it was: it returns the dimensions plus columns n and d. What happens when the version is registered?
options: The metric is computed with the old formula: the engine derives the shape from cell_sql, not measure
Registration passes, and the discrepancy surfaces later at the reproducibility gate's comparison
The metric disappears from the metrics panel but remains available to deterministic matching
The dry run fails: the result has no value column, which the declared shape requires
checks.why: The dry run checks not only that the SQL executes but also the shape of the result: a ratio needs columns n and d, an ordinary metric needs value. The formula returns n and d, so declaring value makes the result incompatible with the stated shape, and registration responds with an error. The tempting idea that measure is just a label is doubly wrong: it is exactly what the engine uses to decide whether to roll the ratio up as SUM(n)/SUM(d) or as an aggregate over value.

checks.q: A generator has 40 metrics, each with a formula of about 600 characters, 12 tables of 30 columns and a glossary of 120 terms. The semantics ceilings: the whole file no longer than 512 KB, at most 128 metrics, 256 columns per table and 20,000 characters per SQL statement. Which ceiling will you hit first?
options: The 512 KB whole-file ceiling: the sizes of all declared blocks add up together
The 128-metric ceiling: the declared 40 are already almost a third of the limit
The 256-columns-per-table ceiling: 12 tables of 30 columns add up to 360 in total
The 20,000-character SQL ceiling: formulas of 600 characters grow faster than that
checks.why: A rough estimate: 40 × 600 ≈ 24 KB of formulas alone, plus 360 column descriptions and 120 terms with descriptions — together that is tens of kilobytes, and the total grows with every description added. The other ceilings are far away: 40 of 128 metrics, 30 of 256 columns per table (the limit is per table, not per bundle), 600 of 20,000 characters per SQL statement. Only the file ceiling adds everything up at once, which is why it is reached first.

lessons.title: Three tiers of answering a question
lessons.summary: After this chapter you understand which of the three tiers answers a question, why auto-execution is safe only where the engine writes the SQL, and why constrained decoding does not replace the validator.

cards.heading: A problem everyone solves equally badly
cards.text:
Translating a natural-language question into SQL (NL2SQL) is a classic semantic parsing problem. The Spider benchmark contains 10,181 questions and 5,693 unique complex queries over 200 databases from 138 domains, and the databases in training and in testing are different: a system must generalise not only to new queries but to new schemas.

Crucially, even a good result on such a benchmark is a share of correct queries, not a guarantee. A model that is right nine times out of ten is more dangerous in analytics than one that is right half the time and says so: the tenth error is indistinguishable from the nine correct answers, because it looks exactly the same — like a number.

Hence OnePage's design: do not improve the probability; narrow the set of questions for which the model decides anything at all.

cards.heading: Three tiers, top to bottom
cards.text: A question passes through the tiers from top to bottom and stops at the first one that can answer.

head: Tier
What happens
Who writes the SQL
Is it executed
rows: the question is matched against the metrics' phrasings; the engine builds SQL from the frozen cell_sql
no metric fitted: the model writes a single SELECT from the description of tables and views
the folder has no ready semantics: a query over the catalogue's raw tables

cards.heading: Tier 1: matching on question phrasings
cards.text:
The first tier starts not with a model but with the match_forms function. Each metric is scored against the question using its own phrasings, its short name and its full name. The score for one phrasing is the number of shared content word stems (stop words are dropped on both sides, two-letter tokens are kept), plus 2 per stem if the whole phrasing appears verbatim in the question: the author's phrase quoted back to us is the strongest signal available.

The confidence rule: the best metric must score at least FORM_MIN_SCORE and be at least FORM_LEAD times better than the runner-up. Today these are 4 and 2. The threshold was raised: at a threshold of 2 a single shared word read as a confident match, and a question from another area latched onto a random metric; on the authors' held-out set, raising it cut false matches from 6 to 1 with no losses on the main question bank.

With a confident match the metric is chosen without a model. An intent is built: the metric; a dimension — only if the question literally names the dimension; a period — the one the question actually named (the same extraction procedure applied to the model's answer; nothing is invented); sorting by value, descending; a limit of 10 rows.

cards.heading: Phrasings live in the bundle, not in the code
cards.text:
Phrase matching is platform code, but the phrasings themselves come only from the semantics.json of the generator being asked about. The platform knows not a single word of the domain and should not: adding a synonym means releasing a new bundle version, not changing the platform.

This is the course's architectural seam: the mechanism is universal, the knowledge is specific and versioned. You saw the same seam in the first chapter — calculation rules are data, not code.

cards.heading: When the model is called after all, it is clamped
cards.text:
If the phrasings gave no confident match, the model is called — but not for SQL; for a filled-in form: {kpi, dims, filters, order, limit}. The metric shortlist is capped at six, and build_intent_schema turns it into a JSON schema where the metric keys, their dimensions and the allowed operations are enums. The schema goes to the provider as the response format (constrained decoding), behind a flag that is on by default.

Anthropic's documentation describes the point of this mode directly: structured outputs constrain the response to a given schema, guaranteeing a valid, parseable result. An invented metric name becomes unrepresentable rather than rejected after the fact.

And yet parse_intent remains the validator. Constrained decoding is an optimisation, not a trust boundary: the provider may be a different one, the version may be old (an old server answers the format field with a 4xx error — this is logged once, the request is retried without the format, and the format is never sent again), and the answer may come from the user's browser. Text from the browser is just as much “the model's speech” as the server's answer and goes through the same parsing.

cards.heading: With a confident match, the model is asked only about the dimension
cards.text:
There is an intermediate case that combines both properties. The question confidently matched a phrasing, so the metric was chosen deterministically, but the question also contains a dimension and a period. Then the model is called once more — with the metric pinned: the enum keeps one key with no null option, the prompt names one metric and no other, and the answer parser sets that key itself, whatever the model wrote.

A model that drifted off or refused to answer cannot cancel a deterministic match. If there is no model at all — neither on the server nor in the browser — the page computes the total for the whole metric without a dimension and opens the metric form pre-filled with the period: there is an answer right away, and the dimension is refined with a single click.

cards.heading: Tier 2: the model writes a single SELECT
cards.text:
When the intent route honestly answers that there is no suitable metric, and the folder's semantics are ready, the second tier kicks in. The prompt describes the report's own relations to it: the name, description and granularity of each table or view, the column names, their types and the author's descriptions, the text of the rules and the glossary. Only the relations that were actually built on the attached folder are described.

The model writes a single SELECT over the views of the sem schema. There are two checks, both fail-closed: is_select_only (one statement, nothing after a semicolon, no DDL, DML or file reads) and the worker's very own guard_sql, imported rather than rewritten. In the browser guard_sql runs once more, this time in front of a read-only DuckDB.

This SQL is executed, but the page shows it with the label “SQL was written by the model from the report's semantics — check it”. The wording is precise: safety rests on the protective filter, not on the user having pressed a button.

cards.heading: Tier 3, and why it is not executed
cards.text:
The third tier — a query over the catalogue's raw tables — is reachable only when the folder has no ready semantics at all. The result is placed in the editor and does not run on its own.

The reason is that the model has nothing to stand on here: only table names, column names, types and partition keys, taken from the export's headers. Guessing from raw headers is worse than honestly admitting that the first two tiers did not answer. Auto-execution on this tier would mean showing a number whose formula nobody stands behind.
cards.note: The invariant that makes auto-execution safe on the first tier: only deterministic SQL assembled by the engine from the frozen cell_sql is executed automatically. The second tier is executed because two independent protective filters let it through and it is shown with a label; the third is not executed at all.

cards.heading: What it costs in accuracy
cards.text:
A measurement on one of the generators (20 operator questions, four of which are deliberately not about metrics) with no model at all: 18 out of 20 = 90 %, of which 14 matched on phrasings with 100 % accuracy, 4 were correctly rejected, 2 were left to the model, 0 SQL failures. An earlier version of the same generator's semantics scored 16 out of 20.

What is remarkable is not so much the share as its nature: the difference between 16 and 18 was obtained not by changing the model but by adding question phrasings to the bundle. That is data, not code, and the report's author can improve it.

takeaways: The three tiers differ in who writes the SQL: the engine from a frozen formula, the model from the report's semantics, the model from the raw catalogue.
Only first-tier deterministic SQL runs automatically; the second tier runs under the protection of two filters and with a visible label; the third does not run at all.
A confident phrasing match (a threshold of 4 and a twofold lead over the runner-up) answers with no model at all, and with a pinned metric the model cannot swap the metric.
Constrained decoding makes an invented name unrepresentable, but the answer parser remains the validator: the schema is an optimisation, not a trust boundary.
First-tier quality is improved by the bundle's data (question phrasings), not by swapping the model.
