checks.q: Someone proposes running third-tier SQL automatically — “the user presses the button anyway, let's save a click”. Which invariant does this break?
options: The data minimisation invariant: on the third tier the schema of raw catalogue tables goes outside
The auto-execution invariant: only SQL the engine assembled from cell_sql runs on its own
The protection invariant: since the SQL passed guard_sql, auto-execution is safe on any of the three tiers
The fail-closed invariant: third-tier SQL passes neither is_select_only nor the worker's guard_sql
checks.why: The protective filter answers the question “can this SQL damage anything”, but not the question “does its result mean what was asked”. On the third tier the model has neither a formula nor descriptions — only raw headers, so nobody stands behind the meaning of the number. The option about guard_sql being sufficient conflates these two questions, and it is exactly this conflation that makes a wrong answer look like a real one.

checks.q: Constrained decoding was made mandatory and the validator of the model's answer was removed: since the schema guarantees the shape, there is nothing to parse. What becomes possible?
options: The shortlist stops being capped at six metrics, and the generator's whole semantics goes into the tier-1 prompt
The model starts returning SQL instead of an intent form, and nobody is left to check it with the protective filter
An answer from the browser or a schema-less provider arrives unconstrained, with an invented metric
The schema keeps guaranteeing both metric names and their dimensions: it goes to the provider as the response format
checks.why: The schema works only where it has been accepted: an old server answers the format field with an error and the request is retried without it, and on the production path the answer comes from the user's browser altogether and enjoys no trust. The validator is the only place where names are checked against the frozen semantics regardless of who answered and how. The option about returning SQL describes a different tier: on the first, the model fills in an intent form rather than writing a query.

checks.q: A phrasing match counts as confident when the best metric has scored at least 4 points and beats the runner-up at least twofold. A question scored: best metric 4, runner-up 2. Is the match confident? And if the best is 5 and the runner-up 3?
options: Both confident: in both cases the best metric scored at least the 4-point threshold
Both not confident: the lead over the runner-up must be at least threefold
The first not confident, the second confident: the absolute lead matters, not the ratio
The first confident, the second not: 5 is less than twice the runner-up's score
checks.why: The rule consists of two conditions at once: at least 4 points and at least a twofold lead over the runner-up. 4 against 2 passes both conditions (4 ≥ 4 and 4 ≥ 2 × 2). 5 against 3 passes the first but not the second: 2 × 3 = 6 is greater than 5, i.e. the runner-up is too close, and the difference between them could have arisen from one random shared word.

checks.q: A question confidently matched a metric's phrasing, but names the dimension indirectly. The model is called with the metric pinned. Why does the answer parser still set the metric key itself?
options: So that a model that drifts off or stays silent cannot cancel the deterministic choice
So that the shortlist stays at six metrics and the prompt need not be rebuilt for one key
So that the metric key gets into the audit record: after parsing there is nowhere else to take it from
To save tokens: the model then returns only the dimension and period, without the key
checks.why: A schema with one key and a prompt naming one metric are two layers of pressure on the model, but neither is a guarantee: the answer may come back empty, corrupted or via an untrusted path. Forcing the key moves the deterministic decision from the “highly likely” category into the “by construction” category. With a pinned metric the shortlist actually collapses to a single metric, so the option about six metrics describes the opposite of what happens.

checks.q: On a set of 20 questions with no model, 18 correct outcomes were obtained: 14 phrasing matches, 4 correct rejections. Three of the remaining questions concern metrics that have no question phrasings in the bundle at all. Which gives the bigger gain — switching to a stronger model or editing the bundle?
options: Switching the model: these three questions would go to the model tier and be solved correctly there, no bundle edit
Editing the bundle: phrasings move these questions onto the deterministic tier with 100 % accuracy
Neither: 18 out of 20 is already the ceiling of phrasing matching; it cannot go higher
Switching the model: the confidence threshold would reject the new phrasings as unconfident anyway
checks.why: A rough estimate: 14 out of 20 are already solved deterministically with 100 % accuracy, and the three problem questions have no phrasings — that is a defect in the bundle's data, not in the code or the model. Adding phrasings raises the share of deterministic answers, which depend neither on the provider nor on its availability. A stronger model would improve only the remaining tail, at the cost of a trip outside for every question.

lessons.title: The boundary between data and the model
lessons.summary: After this chapter you can say precisely what goes to the model, what never does, where the call physically happens in production, and what secures that boundary beyond a promise in the documentation.

cards.heading: A rule that holds on every path
cards.text:
Cell values never go to the model. This is formulated not as a promise in prose but as a property of the code: prompts are built from definitions, and tests fail if even a single value from the data gets into the prompt or into the preparation route's response.

Two kinds of statement need to be told apart here. “We do not send data” is a policy: it can be broken by one line of code and nobody will notice. “The function that builds the prompt has no access to rows, and a test checks this” is a property: to break it you have to change both the function and the test, and that shows up in the diff.

cards.heading: What goes out on each tier
cards.text: What leaves the company when an external provider is called is fixed per tier.
list: Always — the user's question, as they wrote it

Tier 1 — names, definitions, question phrasings and dimensions of metrics from the semantics of the generator being asked about, and only of the metrics left on the shortlist (up to 6; with a pinned metric, exactly one)

Tier 2 — names and descriptions of tables and views: the relation's name, its description and granularity, column names, types and the author's descriptions, the text of the rules; only relations actually built on the attached folder are described
Glossary terms — from the platform and the bundle, up to 24 of them at 160 characters each

Tier 3 — the schema of the catalogue's raw tables: table names, column names, types, partition keys; sample values only if the operator has explicitly raised a separate flag — by default there are zero
The verifier — the question, the chosen metric's name and definition, dimension names, filters (their values come from the question text), the output format

cards.heading: What never goes out
cards.text:
Data rows, cell contents, query results, the metrics' own SQL (the frozen cell_sql stays on the server and in the browser), user names, files.

The second tier is especially telling. The model needs the list of a view's columns, but a view is SQL, and in the general case its columns are known only after execution. The platform obtains them by executing the view's SQL over empty typed tables in an isolated DuckDB — that is, not a single row of data exists on this path, in principle. A test even pins down separately that values sitting directly in semantics.json as inline rows do not get into the second tier.
cards.note: The boundary is drawn not by “secrecy” but by nature: a column name is the author's declaration, versioned together with the bundle. A cell value is a fact from the user's folder. The first describes the shape of the question; the second is the answer.

cards.heading: Why this is called data minimisation
cards.text:
The data minimisation principle is known as a legal one: the data processed must be adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary for the purposes of processing. The engineering reading of the same principle: the boundary is drawn not by what is scary to hand over but by what is necessary for the task. Everything else is not sent — not because it is forbidden, but because it is not needed.

To choose a metric, a name and a definition are enough. To write a SELECT, column names and their types are enough. Data is needed in neither case. So the minimal boundary coincides with the sufficient one — a rare and convenient case, and it is used.

This echoes how Anthropic describes context engineering: find the smallest possible set of high-signal tokens that maximise the likelihood of the desired outcome; the model's attention is a limited resource and should be spent only on material that actually leads to the result. Two arguments that usually conflict coincide here: sending less is both safer and more accurate. Data rows in the metric-selection prompt would not only be a leak, they would also get in the way — they say nothing about which metric is meant.

cards.heading: Where the call happens in production
cards.text:
The platform container in production has no outbound access: measured on 2026-08-22, a call to an external provider ends in a connection timeout. So the historical “browser → server → provider” path is not used in production; it remains for a local model and for running the evaluation tool from a laptop that does have outbound access.

The production path is the reverse: the server prepares, the browser calls, the server verifies.
cards.code_text:
browser → POST /api/explore/intent/prepare  → server (prompt and schema, no model)
browser → POST {endpoint}/chat/completions  → provider (the key is sent from here)
browser → POST /api/explore/intent/validate → server (answer validation)

cards.heading: Who remains responsible
cards.text:
The server does everything except the network call itself: it checks the rights to the generator, assembles the semantics, runs the phrasing match, builds the prompt and the schema and — most importantly — verifies what the model returned. Text that arrived from the browser enjoys no trust: it is just as much the model's speech as a local service's answer and goes through the same parsing.

The second tier mirrors this: it has the same trio of routes, and the prompt preparation function and the SQL checking function are shared between the browser path and the server path so that they cannot diverge.

This scheme has a separate consequence for debugging: everything that can break after the server part breaks in the browser — the provider call through the corporate proxy, SQL execution in the browser's DuckDB, the page's own JavaScript. So the page sends one record per failure to the audit log, with the stage and the reason, but without cells and without the key.

cards.heading: The deterministic tier works without a model
cards.text:
If the question confidently matched a metric's phrasing, the preparation route answers with a ready intent, and the page calls nobody at all: nothing goes out, including the question itself.

This is the answer to “what happens if the provider is unavailable”. Not “nothing works” but “the first tier works in full”. The metrics panel, where every ready metric is a button with a form (dimensions as checkboxes, time dimensions as a period picker, sorting, a row limit), does not even know models exist: the form becomes an intent, the intent becomes SQL, the SQL is shown and executed.

A general design conclusion: it pays to build a system so that the model is an accelerator, not a load-bearing wall. Anthropic states a similar rule for agents: start simple and add multi-step systems only when a simpler solution stops being enough.

cards.heading: Keys and audit
cards.text:
The provider key lives in three possible places, each with its own scope: the server key for the server's own calls goes to nobody except the header of the outgoing request; the key handed out to the page goes to a signed-in user who can run at least one generator; the user's own key lives in their browser's local storage and never reaches the platform server.

The key is not logged: the prompt log records the prompt, not the headers, and the provider's error text is additionally scrubbed. The fact that a key was handed to the page is written to the audit log once per session — without the key itself, only the provider, the model and the endpoint. Every validation of a model answer is written to the audit log marked as originating in the browser: you can see who asked and what the model chose.

cards.heading: What secures the boundary
cards.text:
The promise is checked by tests, and it is useful to know which ones, because this is a behaviour pattern worth carrying into your own systems.

There is a test that puts an inline row with a deliberately recognisable value into the semantics and requires that it be absent from the first-tier prompt. There is a test requiring that the text of a metric's formula does not get into the prompt. There is a test of the verifier's prompt: the question, the metric and the filters are in it; cells are not. There is a test of the line about the previous answer in the chat: it carries dimension names but neither the month number, nor the year, nor a filter value — because the month number was read from the user's folder and does not cross the data boundary.

Note the form of these tests: they check for absence. Such a test is cheap, reads like a specification and breaks exactly when someone carelessly widens the prompt.

takeaways: Names, descriptions, phrasings and rules go to the model; rows, cells, results and the text of metric formulas do not go on any tier.
The columns of views for the second-tier prompt are obtained by running their SQL over empty typed tables — there is no data on this path.
In production the server has no outbound access, so the provider is called by the user's browser; the server prepares the prompt and verifies the answer, and text from the browser enjoys no trust.
The minimal boundary here coincides with the sufficient one: data is needed neither to choose a metric nor to write a SELECT, so sending less is both safer and more accurate.
The boundary is secured by absence tests: a recognisable value from the semantics must not appear in the prompt — such a test reads like a specification.

sources.title: Anthropic — Effective context engineering for AI agents
GDPR Art. 5 — principles of processing, including data minimisation

checks.q: A developer adds “three sample values per column — it'll be clearer for the model” to the second-tier prompt. What exactly breaks?
options: Only context economy breaks: samples are allowed by an operator flag, just as on the third tier
The glossary limit breaks: samples would crowd out some of the 24 terms of 160 characters each
The empty-tables property breaks: it stops being true that there are no data rows on this path
The test on inline rows in semantics.json breaks, which already forbids values on the first tier
checks.why: Right now the second tier has a stronger claim than “we do not put values in”: there is nowhere to take values from, because the schema is determined by executing SQL over empty tables. Adding samples requires reading data, i.e. it changes the construction itself, not just the prompt's content. The flag from the third-tier option relates to the raw catalogue, where there are no semantics, and by default yields zero samples; the glossary limit has nothing to do with it.

checks.q: On the production path it was decided to trust the browser: since the server built the prompt and the schema, the browser's answer can be accepted without parsing. What becomes possible?
options: The constrained-decoding schema remains the guarantee: it fixes both the shape and the list of valid names
The provider key starts getting into the audit log along with the record of it being handed to the page
The second tier stops differing from the first: both become model-based and both run immediately
An arbitrary intent arrives from the browser, and a metric or dimension outside the semantics hits SQL
checks.why: On the production path the browser sits between the server and the provider, i.e. an environment the platform does not control; so the text that arrives is treated as the model's speech and must go through the same parsing against the frozen semantics. The schema works on the provider's side and carries no guarantees through to the server. The key does not get into the audit log for a separate reason: the record stores only the fact of hand-out, not the key itself.

checks.q: A user got an answer with a metric for July, then asked “and by week?”. One line about the previous answer goes into the prompt for this follow-up. Why does it contain no month number?
options: The month was read from the user's folder, so it is data; the platform carries the period itself
The line about the previous answer is capped at 160 characters, and the month number does not fit
The period is always asked of the user again, because a follow-up starts a new parse from scratch
The month number is already in the user's question itself, which goes out in full and unchanged
checks.why: The line about the previous answer carries the names of the metric and dimensions, plus the names of the time dimensions the period was set on — i.e. declarations. The specific period value was obtained by parsing the folder's data, so it stays inside and is carried into the new intent by the grounding procedure on our side. This is exactly the boundary a separate test checks: there is no month number, no year and no filter value in that line.

checks.q: The model provider is unreachable from the corporate browser. Which statement about the page's functionality is correct?
options: Answers to questions stop completely: only the manual SQL editor on the page remains
The metrics panel and confident phrasing matches work: they need no network call
The second tier works: its SELECT is written by the server, which has its own provider key
Everything works: the server picks up the call itself via the historical browser → server → provider path
checks.why: The metrics panel builds the intent from a form, and a confident phrasing match is returned by the preparation route already finished — in both cases the page opens not a single outbound connection. The second tier, by contrast, is entirely model-based, and the server path is unavailable in production: the container has no outbound access, as measured by a connection timeout. The manual editor does remain, but it is not the only thing that works.

checks.q: Estimate which weighs more in the first-tier prompt: the fragment about one metric or the menu of six metrics, if by measurement one fragment is about 480–510 tokens and the six-metric menu is about 310.
options: The menu is bigger: six metrics cannot weigh less than a detailed description of one
They are roughly equal: 310 tokens must be multiplied by the menu's six metrics, about 1900
The fragment: one metric's full description outweighs a menu line for each of the six
The comparison is invalid: the whole semantics file, about 5000 tokens, goes into the prompt
checks.why: The numbers refer to different things: 480–510 tokens is the detailed fragment for one metric, while 310 is a compact menu of six lines, one per metric, i.e. about 50 tokens per metric. The menu is compressed on purpose, because its job is only to choose a key, not to explain the calculation. The option about sending the whole semantics file is factually wrong: the file in full (about 5000 tokens on the measured generator) is never sent.

lessons.title: Clarifying instead of guessing
lessons.summary: After this chapter you understand how the residue of a question turns into a probe over the data, why there is only ever one clarification, and why an advisory check that never blocks the answer runs before a number is shown.

cards.heading: The defect the solution grew out of
cards.text:
A question like “which sites in XYZ were behind schedule” broke silently. The word XYZ is a column value, not a metric name and not a dimension name. The model does not know values by construction: they are not shown to it. The engine does know the values — they sit in the indexed folder — but nobody asked it. As a result the word was silently dropped, and the user got an answer across all sites that looked flawless.

This is the worst class of error: not a failure but a silent narrowing or widening of the question. The user cannot notice that their word was ignored, because the number looks like an answer.

cards.heading: Layer 1: the residue of the question
cards.text:
The residue_words function collects the meaningful words of the question that nothing has consumed: not the metric's vocabulary (name, short name, definition, question phrasings), not the names of its dimensions, not table and column names, not glossary terms, not the values of filters already in the intent.

The selection is deliberately conservative. Only a code-like word made of Latin letters and digits, or a phrase the user put in quotes, becomes a candidate. The free prose of the question never becomes a candidate: ordinary words are the question's own speech, and a false clarification is worse than a missing one. The residue is capped at four words.

The residue travels in the intent routes' responses as a separate field, and the page passes it to the engine as words to probe. Note: these residue words are not sent outside, to the model, on their own — their addressee is the engine, not the provider.

cards.heading: Layer 2: a probe over the data
cards.text:
The engine takes each residue word and checks whether it exists as a VALUE of some non-time dimension of this metric. The check is an exact, case-insensitive match, performed by a query on top of the metric's formula with a one-row limit.

An implementation detail matters here that looks like a trifle at first sight. One could take the list of a dimension's distinct values and search in it. But the list has to be capped, and on a high-cardinality dimension (an item code, for instance) the value sought simply will not fall into the slice. A point query asking “is there such a row” works at any cardinality and is equally cheap.

cards.heading: Three outcomes, and they must be different
list: The word was found in exactly one dimension — that is the filter the person meant. The engine adds the condition and writes a note: “interpreted XYZ as site = XYZ”. The answer comes at once, but with an explicit trace of how the question was understood.

The word was found in two or more dimensions — the engine returns not SQL but a clarification request. The page shows chips with the options INSTEAD of a number. A click on a chip gives an instant answer: the word is consumed, the filter is added.

The word was found nowhere — there is no silence here either: the engine writes a note that the word was searched for and not found in any of the metric's dimensions, and answers the rest of the question.

cards.heading: Why there are never two clarifications in a row
cards.text:
The stopping rule for clarifications is an invariant, not a policy. A clarification exists only while there is an unconsumed word. A click on a chip consumes the word and adds a filter, so re-entering the same procedure yields an empty residue. The loop “did you mean… or perhaps… could you clarify once more” is impossible by construction, not because someone set a counter.

This is an important distinction in design. A limit expressed as a counter (“no more than two clarifications”) is a policy: it can be bypassed, forgotten to reset, applied in the wrong branch. A limit expressed as a monotonically decreasing quantity (the number of unconsumed words) can be proved on your fingers and has no edge cases.
cards.note: The same mechanism fixes a neighbouring defect: a value hung on the wrong dimension, or a value with a typo. If a filter that came from the model is not found in the named dimension but is unambiguously found in another non-time dimension, the filter is moved there with a note. If the value differs only in case or spelling and the match is unique, it is corrected with a note. If it is found nowhere, the engine honestly says that this dimension has no such value and lists a few known ones.

cards.heading: What the engine says instead of staying silent
cards.text:
Let us state the general principle applied consistently here: any change the system makes to the question must be visible. A dimension declared in the semantics but missing from a particular folder does not lead to an empty grouping — it is dropped with a note that the attached files have no such column, and the total is shown without it. A filter on a dimension the metric does not have at all does not turn into an error and is not applied silently — it is skipped with a note listing the available dimensions.

Behind each of these rules is a specific case where silence was read as an answer. A question about short shipments for a specific code over a folder without that column gave the overall top list; a question with a weekly period against a monthly ratio gave a dead end instead of a number.

The general rule goes like this: a system that interprets a question must show its interpretation before the result.

cards.heading: Layer 3: the verifier
cards.text:
After the intent is assembled and before the number is shown, the page may make one advisory call to the model. The question it is asked is narrow: does the assembled query answer the user's question, and is the answer format right.

The verifier's prompt receives: the question itself, the chosen metric's name and definition, the dimension names, the filters with values taken from the question text, and the expected format (a number, a number with a unit, a ratio). Plus a separate line: these words will be automatically checked against data values — do not count them as missed. Cells do not go out, the result does not go out, the SQL does not go out.

The answer is required strictly as JSON: either an acknowledgement that the query answers the question, or a denial with a short description of the problem and ONE clarifying question in plain language. The model is explicitly asked not to write SQL, not to ask for data and not to suggest metrics that were not on the list.

cards.heading: Fail-open, and why exactly so
cards.text:
Parsing the verdict is as lenient as possible: the first JSON object in the text is taken; anything that fails to parse counts as agreement. A provider error, a timeout (20 s), no model at all — the answer is shown as usual.

This is fail-open, and it is appropriate here precisely because the verifier is advisory. Compare two constructions. The SQL protective filter is fail-closed: what does not pass the check is not executed, because the cost of letting a harmful query through is high and the cost of a false rejection is one answer not shown. The verifier is fail-open: it does not protect against harm, it catches a mismatch of meaning, and its unavailability must not turn the whole page into a broken one.

Choosing the direction of failure is not a matter of taste but a consequence of what the mechanism guards. A mechanism guarding safety fails closed. A mechanism improving quality fails open.
cards.note: If the verdict is negative, the number is held back and the verifier's own clarifying question is shown along with a “Calculate anyway” button. The last word stays with the person: the model advises, it does not decide.

cards.heading: First show what you understood
cards.text:
Let us bring the three layers together into one idea. A cheap clarification beats an expensive error, but only if the clarification really is cheap: a single one, finite, with options instead of free input and an instant answer on click.

The order of the layers is not accidental either: a deterministic residue, then a deterministic probe over the data, and only then the advisory model. Each next layer is more expensive, less predictable and kicks in only on what the previous ones did not resolve. The answer tiers themselves are built exactly the same way — it is one and the same discipline applied twice.

takeaways: The residue of a question is the meaningful words nothing consumed; only Latin letters with digits and quoted phrases become candidates, and a false clarification counts as worse than a missing one.
The probe over the data is done by the engine, not the model: a point query asking “is there such a value” works at any dimension cardinality.
The three outcomes differ by construction: one dimension — a filter with a note; two — chips instead of a number; none — an honest note and an answer to the rest of the question.
There is never a second clarification by construction: a click consumes the word and the residue shrinks; this is an invariant, not a counter.
The verifier is an advisory, fail-open layer: safety fails closed, quality fails open, and the last word stays with the person.

sources.title: Anthropic — Effective context engineering for AI agents

checks.q: Someone proposes extending the residue to ordinary prose words: “users mostly write in plain words, so we'll catch more values”. What outweighs what?
options: We win: plain-word dimension values occur in data no less often than Latin codes and item numbers
We lose: values are compared case-insensitively, and for non-Latin scripts that comparison is unreliable
We win: the residue is capped at four words anyway, and the cap itself cuts off excess candidates
We lose: the question's free prose will accidentally match some cell and silently become a filter
checks.why: The probe decides on a match between a word and a real value, and the wider the stream of candidates, the higher the chance that an ordinary word of the question matches some cell and quietly narrows the answer. That is exactly why the selection is kept conservative: Latin letters with digits and explicit quotes — the forms in which a person writes a code or a name. The option about the four-word cap is true in itself, but the cap reduces volume, not the probability of a false match for an individual word; and the probe compares case the same way for any alphabet.

checks.q: The “found in two dimensions” outcome was removed from the probe, leaving the rule “take the first matching dimension and write a note”. What gets worse?
options: The system silently picks one of two incompatible readings; a note under the number won't save it
The answer gets slower: the engine has to go through every dimension instead of stopping at the first
The clarification stopping rule breaks: the word is not consumed, and the residue stops shrinking
The data boundary is breached: dimension values start going into the prompt along with the question text
checks.why: Two dimensions containing the same value are two different questions, and only the person who asked can choose between them. Chips instead of a number cost one click, while a number on screen closes the topic: a reader rarely double-checks a note under a plausible figure. The speed option gets the mechanics wrong — dimensions are walked in both variants; when the first dimension is chosen the word is in fact consumed, and the probe runs inside the engine, so it does not touch the data boundary.

checks.q: The verifier did not answer: the provider returned an error at the 21st second with a 20 s timeout. What will the user see?
options: An error message instead of a number: without the verifier's verdict the answer must not be shown
The usual answer: the verifier is advisory, and an error or timeout is treated as agreement
A default clarifying question from the verifier with a “Calculate anyway” button next to it
An answer recomputed by the second tier: the model will write its SQL from the semantics
checks.why: Parsing the verdict is lenient: anything unparsed counts as agreement, and a provider error, a 20-second timeout and the absence of a model are explicitly listed as fail-open cases. Otherwise the unavailability of an optional adviser would turn a ready deterministic answer into a refusal. The option with a clarifying question describes the behaviour on an explicit negative verdict, and the verifier's silence does not trigger a switch to the second tier.

checks.q: Why is the SQL protective filter fail-closed while the verifier is fail-open, even though both stand between the question and the number?
options: The filter is faster and cheaper, so it can afford strictness without hurting responsiveness
The filter is deterministic, and a deterministic mechanism must fail closed for reproducibility
The filter guards execution safety, where a miss is costly; the verifier guards answer quality
The verifier calls an external provider, and by convention any network call fails open
checks.why: The direction of failure is chosen by the asymmetry of costs. A harmful SQL statement that slips through may execute and change something, while a false rejection by the filter costs one answer not shown — hence fail-closed. For the verifier it is the other way round: a missed mismatch of meaning costs one debatable number with the SQL visible next to it, while a false rejection would devalue the whole deterministic path, which needs no model. Neither speed, nor determinism, nor the way the call is made decides anything here.

checks.q: It was decided that a click on a clarification chip should not count as consuming the word: the filter is added, but the word stays in the residue. What happens?
options: The second pass sees the filter already added, counts the word as consumed and returns the same number
The word goes into the model's prompt and breaches the data boundary: values must not be sent outside
The engine applies both candidate dimensions at once and returns an empty result from conflicting conditions
The probe finds the word in two dimensions again and again shows chips instead of a number — a loop
checks.why: A clarification is finite because the number of unconsumed words strictly decreases with every click. If the word stays, re-entry produces exactly the same picture — two candidate dimensions — and the page again shows chips instead of a number. The option about the filter already added describes what one would want, but it does not follow from the mechanics: the probe looks at the residue, not at the set of filters; the engine does not combine conditions from different dimensions at once, and a residue word does not go into the prompt.

lessons.title: How to read the SQL you are shown
lessons.summary: After this chapter you can read a displayed query as a verifiable statement: what it is assembled from, what in it should raise a flag, and which signs tell a deterministic answer from one written by the model.

cards.heading: Why the SQL is shown before the number
cards.text:
On the Explore page the query is visible before the result. This is not decoration for engineers, nor a debug mode someone forgot to switch off.

A number is a statement with no form of its own: 0.87 looks the same whether it was computed correctly or whether an extra month slipped into the calculation. SQL has a form. It shows which rows were taken, what they were grouped by, what they were filtered by and in what order they were sorted. A statement can be checked only when it is presented in full.

This is a property of the interface, not of the model: verifiability is built into the screen. And it works both ways — not only to “catch an error” but also to “make sure everything is above board” in five seconds of reading.

There is an organisational side too. While the calculation is invisible, an argument about a number turns into an argument about trust in the system, and nothing but authority can settle it. As soon as the calculation is presented, the argument becomes concrete: the parties look at the same text and disagree on a specific line — the period, the dimension or the filter. A displayed query moves a disagreement out of the realm of opinion into one where it can be settled in a minute.

cards.heading: What a first-tier query is assembled from
cards.text:
Deterministic SQL is assembled to an unchanging pattern of four parts. The metric's frozen formula goes in whole into a common table expression. The dimensions become the list of selected columns and the grouping. Filters — on the period, from the question and from the data probe — become WHERE conditions. Sorting and the limit come from the intent.

Measures are added according to the metric's declared type. For a ratio it is always the sum of numerators, the sum of denominators and their rounded quotient: a ratio of sums, not an average of ratios. For an ordinary metric it is the aggregation the author declared, because an average rolled up with a sum is a wrong number behind plausible SQL.

Every name in the query is wrapped in double quotes and checked against the metric's list of dimensions. Every value is a literal: strings are escaped by doubling the apostrophe, non-numeric floating-point values become NULL. The model does not write a single character here.

cards.heading: This is what a first-tier answer looks like
cards.code_text:
WITH c AS (
SELECT region, client_code, week,
       SUM(LEAST(shipped, ordered)) AS n,
       SUM(ordered) AS d
  FROM orders
 GROUP BY 1, 2, 3
)
SELECT "region",
       SUM("n") AS "n",
       SUM("d") AS "d",
       ROUND(SUM("n") / NULLIF(SUM("d"), 0), 4) AS "value"
  FROM c
 WHERE "week" = 37 AND "client_code" = 'C-100'
 GROUP BY "region"
 ORDER BY "value" DESC
 LIMIT 10

cards.heading: Read it like this
cards.text:
Start with the common table expression. It is the metric's formula from the semantics, verbatim — the very same one that passed the dry run at registration and the reproducibility gate. It is not rewritten to fit the question: the question affects what surrounds it, not the formula itself.

Then look at four places. The column list and GROUP BY are your dimension, and they must match what you asked. The WHERE condition holds the period and the filters; check every literal against your question, including the one the probe added (it always comes with a note like “interpreted X as Y = Z”). ORDER BY with LIMIT is the answer to “which are the most”, and without sorting a 10-row limit means an arbitrary ten, not the top ten. And the measures: for a ratio it must be exactly the sum of numerators divided by the sum of denominators.

cards.heading: What should raise a flag
cards.text: Here is a query that looks plausible but answers the wrong question.
cards.code_text:
WITH c AS (
SELECT region, week,
       SUM(LEAST(shipped, ordered)) AS n,
       SUM(ordered) AS d
  FROM orders
 GROUP BY 1, 2
)
SELECT "region",
       ROUND(AVG("n" / NULLIF("d", 0)), 4) AS "value"
  FROM c
 WHERE "week" = 37
 GROUP BY "region"
 LIMIT 10

cards.heading: A short list of suspicions
cards.text: When reading a displayed query, look for these signs. Each of them is a real class of error, not a theoretical one.
list: An average of ratios instead of a ratio of sums: AVG(n/d) instead of SUM(n)/SUM(d) — with unequal denominators it gives a different number, usually inflated on small groups
LIMIT without ORDER BY: ten arbitrary rows presented as the “top 10”
A filter that is not in your question, with no accompanying note on where it came from
A period you did not name: trust what is written in WHERE, not the caption above the table
A dimension in GROUP BY that you did not ask for: the answer will be more granular than the question, and the overall total undercounted
A formula in the expression body that differs from the metric formula you know: on the first tier it never changes

cards.heading: How to tell the first tier from the second
cards.text:
The difference is visible both in the interface and in the query text itself.

In the interface: second-tier SQL always carries the explicit label “SQL was written by the model from the report's semantics — check it”. The label is not an optional design detail: it is the very boundary of responsibility between the formula's author and the model.

In the text: the first tier has a stereotyped form — a common table expression named c, the verbatim cell_sql inside, and outside only the measures, WHERE, GROUP BY, ORDER BY and LIMIT. It always quotes a single formula and never joins relations together. The second tier writes a free-form SELECT over the report schema's views: it may contain joins, subqueries, window functions — anything DuckDB allows and the protective filter lets through.

The reading rule is simple: if the query contains anything that never occurs in the first-tier template, you are looking at the model's text, and its formula must be read in full rather than trusted as frozen.

cards.heading: What the protective filter checks and what it does not
cards.text:
It helps to understand the limits of its competence. The filter requires a single statement beginning with SELECT or WITH, nothing after a semicolon, and rejects constructs that change data or state as well as file-reading functions. It works in two layers: language keywords are searched for with identifiers masked (a column genuinely named “set” must remain accessible), and function names with identifiers readable, because DuckDB lets you call a function written in quotes exactly like an ordinary one.

But the filter does not and cannot know whether the query answers your question. A query with an average of ratios passes it without a single remark: it is syntactically impeccable and perfectly safe. That is exactly why the label on the SQL's origin and the habit of reading the four key places cannot be replaced by any automation.
cards.note: To put it in one sentence: the protective filter is responsible for the query breaking nothing, and showing the SQL is responsible for you being able to check what it means. These are two different questions, and neither answers for the other.

cards.heading: Explainability without magic
cards.text:
It is tempting to build the explanation of an answer as yet another text from the model: “I computed the fill rate for week 37 by region”. Such an explanation reads more pleasantly than SQL and guarantees nothing — it is a second statement about the first, and it can be wrong regardless of whether the calculation is right.

Displayed SQL is different: it is not a story about the computation but the computation itself. When you check it, you are checking exactly what will execute — a property engineering usually calls the absence of a gap between description and execution.

Hence a practical tip for reading any analytical interface, not just this one. Do not ask “explain how you calculated it”; ask “show me exactly what will run”. The first is a genre. The second is a verifiable statement.

takeaways: The SQL is shown before the number because a number has no form and a query does: only a statement presented in full can be checked.
A deterministic query is assembled from the frozen formula in a common table expression plus the dimension, period, filters, sorting and limit — every name checked, every value a literal.
Red flags: an average of ratios instead of a ratio of sums, LIMIT without ORDER BY, unnamed filters and periods, an extra dimension and a changed formula.

The first tier is recognised by its stereotyped form and the absence of a label; the second by the label “SQL was written by the model from the report's semantics — check it” and the query's free form.
The protective filter guarantees harmlessness, not meaningfulness: showing the SQL is needed precisely because no automation can do the second check.

sources.title: DuckDB — SELECT statement (WITH, GROUP BY, ORDER BY, LIMIT)
Spider: Yale Semantic Parsing and Text-to-SQL Challenge

checks.q: You are shown a query: the inner expression computes, by region and week, the numerator n = SUM(LEAST(shipped, ordered)) and the denominator d = SUM(ordered), and outside it reads SELECT "region", ROUND(AVG("n" / NULLIF("d", 0)), 4) AS "value" ... WHERE "week" = 37 GROUP BY "region" LIMIT 10. The metric is declared as a ratio, and the week column as a number. Where does the query produce a wrong number, and why?
options: In AVG(n/d): a ratio must be rolled up as SUM(n)/SUM(d), otherwise small denominators weigh the same
In ROUND to four places: with large denominators the rounding eats the ratio's significant digits
In GROUP BY 1, 2 inside the expression: grouping by column numbers breaks the link to the n and d aliases
In WHERE "week" = 37: the week came from the intent as a string, and comparing it to a number drops every row
checks.why: An example: two weeks with n/d = 1/1 and 0/99. The ratio of sums is 1/100 = 0.01, while the average of ratios is (1 + 0) / 2 = 0.5 — a fiftyfold discrepancy on the very same rows. That is why for a metric declared as a ratio the engine always prints the sum of numerators divided by the sum of denominators. Rounding to four places and grouping by column numbers are correct here, and the week is declared as a number and compared with a number.

checks.q: A displayed query for a ratio metric has GROUP BY "region" and LIMIT 10, but no ORDER BY at all. The user asked “which regions are the worst”. What will they see?
options: The ten worst regions: without ORDER BY rows come back in ascending order of the measure
Ten arbitrary regions, and the “top 10” caption above them will be false
An execution error: next to LIMIT the engine requires an explicit ORDER BY
All the regions: LIMIT takes effect only after the rows are explicitly sorted
checks.why: LIMIT caps the number of rows returned but does not specify which ones: without ORDER BY the order is determined by the execution plan and may change between runs on the same data. No error occurs and the rows are not returned sorted by the measure — which is exactly what makes the defect dangerous: the result looks like a finished ranking. In a deterministic first-tier query the sorting comes from the intent.

checks.q: You are shown a query that joins two views and uses a window function, with no label of any kind about its origin. Which conclusion is correct?
options: This is the first tier: the engine joins views when the metric's formula relies on several tables
This is the third tier: it runs automatically when the previous two were not enough to answer
Not the first tier: a free SELECT with joins is the second tier, and the label is mandatory
This is the user's manual query, and hand-written queries get no label about their origin
checks.why: The first-tier query form is stereotyped: one common table expression with the metric's verbatim formula, surrounded only by measures, WHERE, GROUP BY, ORDER BY and LIMIT — the engine adds no joins or window functions there and does not link relations together. A free SELECT over the report's views is the second tier, and the label about its model origin is mandatory for it, because that label is the boundary of responsibility.

checks.q: Displaying the SQL was replaced by a text explanation from the model: “computed the fill rate for week 37 broken down by region”. What is lost?
options: An engineers' habit is lost: for the report's reader the text describes exactly the same calculation
Safety is lost: the protective filter checks precisely the text that is displayed on the screen
Speed is lost: generating an explanation with the model costs more than running the query itself
Verifiability is lost: the explanation is a separate claim, true even if the calculation is wrong
checks.why: Displayed SQL is the object of execution itself; there is no gap between description and execution. A text explanation is generated separately and can diverge from the actual query in any direction: an extra filter will go unmentioned, and a dimension that is mentioned may be absent from the query. The protective filter would keep working without the display — it checks the statement being executed, not a picture on the screen — and that is precisely why it does not replace showing the SQL.

checks.q: Under the answer there is a note “interpreted ABC as customer code = ABC”, and a matching condition the user did not write explicitly has appeared in WHERE. How should this be read?
options: As the result of a data probe: the residue word was found in exactly one dimension and became a filter
As an error: WHERE must not contain conditions the user did not name in the question text
As the model's guess: it inferred the filter from the question's context and wrote it into the intent itself
As a trace of a reference table substituted during the generator run along with other dimension values
checks.why: Dimension values are never shown to the model, so it cannot meaningfully set a filter on a specific value — the engine does that, checking the residue word with a point query over the data. The note is mandatory precisely because the filter was not named explicitly: any change the system makes to the question must be visible before the result. The error would be the opposite — adding the condition silently.

units.title: Trust: provenance, quality, row-level access
units.subtitle: Where the numbers came from, what is wrong with them, who has the right to see a row, and what of all this remains in the audit log

lessons.title: Provenance: a graph instead of faith
lessons.summary: You will understand exactly what the platform records about every run, how those records assemble into the "folder → report" graph, how "declared" differs from "observed", and why observation is always incomplete.

cards.heading: Why provenance at all
cards.text:
Nobody asks "where does this number come from" out of curiosity. They ask when the number disagrees with someone else's number, and the cost of the answer is hours of back-and-forth between whoever built the report and whoever owns the source files. The answer "I read the exports folder" cannot be verified: the folder changes, a file may have been renamed, a sheet may have been added.

In general theory this is called provenance — information about the entities, activities and people involved in producing data; W3C PROV describes it precisely as the triple "entity — activity — agent", and OpenLineage builds the same model around job, run and dataset. The idea is the same everywhere: provenance is not a document someone maintains, but a by-product of execution, recorded by the executor itself.

OnePage works the same way. Nobody fills in a source card by hand. Every generator run leaves behind a record of which folders it saw, which files it listed, which ones it opened and which columns it read from them.

cards.heading: Declared: the inputs field in the manifest
cards.text:
The first half of the truth is what the generator's author declared. In the manifest this is the `inputs` field: up to 32 patterns, with exactly the same glob syntax as the in-browser engine (one matching implementation for the whole platform, `app/services/globmatch.py`, which also validates the pattern at registration).

A declaration is not a description but a constraint. When `inputs` is present, the engine lists only the matching files and skips the rest with an honest reason, "not declared in inputs". So the manifest turns from a document into an allow-list: a file the author did not name will not be seen by the generator, even if the analyst put it in the same folder.

Old generators without `inputs` keep working under the previous rule, "every workbook in the selected folders". In the graph such a generator gets a single synthetic pattern node `*` marked "legacy" — because "reads everything" is also a pattern, not the absence of one, and it should be drawn rather than hidden.

cards.heading: Observed: hooks on reads
cards.text:
The second half is what actually happened. Before the generator code is imported, a platform module installs hooks: the workbook-reading library is proxied down to the sheet level (the first row is taken while iterating rows), and pandas table-read calls are tracked down to the column level — both through an explicit column list and through access by name.

Separately there is "sniffing": the file's headers are read before the file reaches the generator. This matters because the header must be known even for a file the generator never opens in this run.

The engine then sends observations to the server in batches: each batch has a monotonic sequence number, a duplicate number gets a 409, and the last batch is flagged and commits the source fingerprint plus an audit log entry. Incrementality here is not an optimisation but a requirement: a run over hundreds of files must not accumulate everything in browser memory until the end.
What remains in the database after one run:
list: an observation row per (run, source) pair: number of files, total size, a fingerprint of the set of names, skip reasons
a row per file with its role: listed, parsed, taken from cache, system, unreadable, excluded, legacy
each file has a "schema" (what the sniffer saw) and "consumed" (what was actually opened), plus the pattern the file matched
exclusion rules are set on the (generator, source) pair, not on the folder: someone else's report reading the same folder is not affected by your decision

cards.heading: A six-layer graph
cards.text:
These rows assemble into a directed graph: folder (or external source) → pattern → sheet → generator → output → report. Columns are not separate nodes; they are shown inside the sheet node as chips in three colours: declared, observed, and both.

There is also an intermediate band — run stages: if the generator code itself took snapshots of its intermediate tables, read edges end not at the generator but at the stage that read those files. A generator that declares no stages simply keeps the direct edge.

One edge runs backwards, from an output to a source: a generator that writes a workbook back into the analyst's folder makes that folder both an input and an output. The cycle is drawn on purpose — it is exactly what you need to see before deleting a file.

The graph is bounded by construction: the node ceiling is 5000, and on overflow sheet nodes are dropped first (the only unbounded axis — a single workbook declares up to 32 sheets), while a truncation flag is raised in the metadata.

The graph is not a picture but data: it can be exported to JSON, Markdown or diagram text, and the export keeps the same scope as the page, including narrowing to the selected node. The graph deliberately has no cache: the page is opened by hand, and a graph lagging behind a run that just finished is worse than one that cost an extra second. Finally, you see in the graph exactly the reports you can run yourself: this is not a company-wide map but a map of your reach.

cards.note: A column's state is ternary, not boolean. "Declared" and "observed" are yes/no, but "consumed" may be empty: that marks the case where there was nothing to observe with. "Declared and never touched" and "declared, but nobody could have touched it" are different statements, and they must not be confused.

cards.heading: Three honest limits
cards.text: Observation is always incomplete, and the platform says so out loud rather than pretending the graph is the truth.
list: A cached file: if the file's modification time has not changed, the generator does not open it at all — the hooks are blind. The header is known (the sniffer read it), the list of columns read is not.
The agent engine: it executes SQL in a separate process with no hooks. A source read only by it yields no observations — and that is silence, not "all is well".

Budget: up to 2 MB of schema per run. Exceeding it does not fail the run but raises a truncation flag — an incomplete schema with an honest mark is better than a full schema at the cost of a failed run.

cards.heading: The report provenance page
cards.text:
The graph answers the question "who reads this folder". The reverse question — "where do the numbers in this particular report come from" — is answered by a separate provenance page: the report version, the run that produced it, the frozen generator version and its dependencies, the semantics, the reference tables applied, the row-level access policy, the index and the observed source folders.

An important detail: every field there is a counter, a hash, a timestamp or an identifier, but never a data value. And access to it is deliberately narrower than access to the report itself: the block on the run, generator, dependencies and sources requires the right to refresh the report's data, and the index block additionally requires full row access. Someone who was simply given the report to read sees the version record, but not who runs it and on which dependencies.

takeaways: Provenance in OnePage is a by-product of a run, not a document someone maintains by hand.
"Declared" (manifest inputs) and "observed" (read hooks) are two different facts, and the graph shows the difference between them.
Declaring inputs does not describe behaviour, it constrains it: the engine skips an undeclared file.
The three limits of observation — cached file, agent engine, schema budget — are named explicitly; silence in the graph does not mean "everything was read".
The report provenance page returns only counters, hashes and identifiers, and its gate is narrower than the right to open the report.

checks.q: The folder holds 40 workbooks. The run has finished; in the graph one file has headers but an empty list of columns read, and the file is marked as taken from cache. What does this mean?
options: The file matched none of the inputs patterns and was skipped with the reason "not declared in inputs"
The 2 MB schema budget was exceeded, and this file's column list was cut off by the truncation flag
This source was read by the agent engine: it executes SQL in a separate process with no hooks
The file hasn't changed since the last run and wasn't opened: the sniffer gave the header, hooks saw nothing
checks.why: The "from cache" role is set exactly when the file's modification time has not changed and the generator does not open it. The headers are still known because a separate sniffer reads them before the file is handed to the generator, while the read hooks stay silent because there was no read. Exceeding the budget would raise a truncation flag, not change the file's role; failing to match a pattern would give the role "excluded"; the agent engine leaves no headers either.

checks.q: What breaks if you remove the inputs field from the manifest of a generator that declares it today?
options: Observations stop being written: without declared patterns the hooks have nothing to match, the graph empties
Read behaviour won't change: inputs is documentation, and exclusion rules on the source limit what is read
The manifest becomes invalid, and the generator stops running until the inputs field is restored
The engine reads every workbook in the folder again, a "*" node appears, and checks have nothing to bind to
checks.why: The presence of inputs switches the manifest into allow-list mode, so removing the field changes the engine's behaviour, not just the look of a document: every workbook in the folder is listed again. The graph does not disappear — observations are still written — but the declared side is gone, and instead of patterns a single synthetic "*" node marked legacy is drawn. Content checks and thresholds are keyed by the declared pattern and sheet, so they go away along with the declaration.

checks.q: A generator reads a workbook with 30 sheets of 40 columns each, and the folder holds 20 such workbooks. Which limit will you hit first when building the graph?
options: The graph node ceiling: sheet nodes come to about 600, and on overflow they are the first to be dropped
The 2 MB per-run schema budget: 20 workbooks of 30 sheets give a schema noticeably larger than the limit
The 32-sheets-per-workbook ceiling: thirty declared sheets come very close to this limit
The graph node ceiling: 20×30×40 is 24,000 column nodes, which immediately exceeds the 5000 limit
checks.why: Estimate: 20 workbooks × 30 sheets ≈ 600 sheet nodes, plus pattern, generator, output and report nodes — still far from the 5000 ceiling, but sheets grow fastest and are dropped first when the ceiling is near. Columns do not become separate nodes; they are shown as chips inside the sheet node, and there are one or two declared patterns here, not 32.

checks.q: You want to exclude temporary files that someone keeps dropping into a shared folder from being read. Which solution matches how the platform works?
options: Create an exclusion rule on the folder: all reports over it stop seeing these files at once
Set the exclusion on the report: it travels with the frozen generator version and dependencies
Create a rule on the (generator, source) pair: one owner's decision doesn't change others' reports
Mark such files as system files: the "system" role excludes them from reading for all generators
checks.why: Exclusion rules in OnePage are set precisely on the (generator, source) pair, not on the folder. A folder is a shared resource: a rule on it would mean the owner of one report silently changes the input data of someone else's. The "system" role is not a setting but the result of parsing the file during a run, and the report with its frozen version is a different layer altogether, on which exclusions are not keyed.

checks.q: An author writes a conclusion in the graph: "the 'Region' column is declared, but 'consumed' is empty, so the generator doesn't use it — it can be removed from the export". What is wrong here?
options: Something else is wrong: columns aren't graph nodes, they are three-colour chips inside the sheet node
Wrong: inputs is an allow-list, and the generator won't see an undeclared column even if it exists
The conclusion is right: an empty "consumed" is exactly the case "declared but never touched"
An empty "consumed" means "nothing to observe with": the file was cached or read by the agent engine
checks.why: A column's state is ternary: "declared" and "observed" are boolean, while "consumed" is empty exactly when observation was impossible: a cached file, the agent engine, a reader without hooks. That is a different statement from "declared and never touched", and the third state was introduced for the sake of this distinction. Deciding to delete a column on an empty value treats absence of evidence as evidence of absence.

lessons.title: Data quality as a computation on read
lessons.summary: You will understand which findings the platform computes, why they are not stored, what a stable finding identifier gives you, how acknowledgement works, and why a "sample" mark is worth more than a tidy zero.

cards.heading: Findings are not stored
cards.text:
The usual path for a subsystem like this is to compute checks during the run and store the result in a findings table. OnePage does not do that. A finding is a statement about the CURRENT state of a source, seen through the CURRENT manifest. Storing it means invalidating the record on every manifest edit, every accepted value baseline, every threshold change — three write paths, and each one must remember to do it.

So evaluation happens on read: when a person opens the page, the platform joins afresh what the author declared, what the engine observed and what a person accepted. Nothing is written at all.

The window is bounded: the last 10 runs per report. For a daily report that is two weeks, for a weekly one a quarter: enough for a trend line and small enough to keep the page's queries small.

cards.heading: Five families of findings
cards.text: The classic data-quality dimensions — completeness, timeliness, schema conformance, validity, consistency — are laid out here by where the evidence comes from.
list: Schema: a declared pattern found no files, a sheet disappeared, a column disappeared or appeared, a file is undeclared, a file is unreadable, the header row shifted
Freshness: a source has not been updated for a long time; a required file vanished; a report was published on a reference table version older than the current one
Volume: the number of files dropped, the number of rows dropped (default threshold — a fall by half), rows went to zero
Content checks: not-null, uniqueness, range, regular expression, enumeration, set of known values, membership in a reference table
Drift: a column gained values that were not in the baseline set from past runs, or values that have no row in the reference table

cards.heading: A stable finding identifier
cards.text:
A finding identifier is a sha1 prefix of WHAT is wrong and WHERE: the kind of finding, the source, the generator, the file or pattern, the sheet, the column. There is no run and no time in it. The parts are normalised before hashing the same way columns are compared, so "Date " and "date" give one finding, not two.

Everything else follows from this. A problem that came back after the run that fixed it is the very same finding with the same identifier, not a new one. Acknowledgements rest on this (a person acknowledges an identifier), so does the question "since which run has this been going on", and so does history.

There is a subtlety: two different checks on the same (file, sheet, column) triple are two different problems, so for a "check failed" finding the check identifier is added to the hash, while for every other kind this part is empty — and their identifiers coincide with what a six-part hash would give.
cards.code_text:
finding_id = sha1("kind|source|generator|file|sheet|column")[:16]
# for check_fail, "|check_id" is appended

cards.heading: Acknowledgement: "I know"
cards.text:
Acknowledgement does not hide a finding. It stays in the list but stops counting as open — and a red source stops being red because of it.

There are two bounds, and both must hold at once: the date until which the acknowledgement is valid, and the run from which the finding reproduces. As soon as a newer run shows the problem again, or as soon as the date passes, the finding is open again.

An acknowledgement is tied to a single source. This is not a formality: sixteen hex characters is a short hash, and identifiers colliding across different sources is theoretically possible. Without the source check, a person with access to source B could acknowledge a finding observed on source A and silently extinguish it for everyone.

An honest limit: for schema findings, "since which run" points to the oldest run of continuous reproduction, and while the problem is alive that mark does not move. So acknowledging a schema finding "until the next run" is in practice forever. For such findings you should offer a date, not an "until the next run" button.

cards.heading: A sample matters more than a pretty zero
cards.text:
Content checks run in the analyst's browser before the file reaches the generator, and they have ceilings: up to 200,000 rows per sheet, up to 500 distinct values in a known-values set, up to 5 examples per check, each example truncated to 64 characters.

A 900,000-row sheet will be checked on the first 200,000 — and the result gets a "sample" flag that reaches the page as a badge. This is not a shortcoming but a mandatory element of honesty: "zero violations on a sample" and "zero violations" are different statements, and the person making the decision must see which of the two is in front of them.

The same principle applies to the known-values set: if there are more distinct values than the ceiling, the check does not return a plausible but wrong answer — it reports that it was not performed, with a reason.

cards.note: False positives are a tax on attention. When there are too many alerts, people start scrolling past them without reading and miss the real one. That is why every finding is tied to a (generator, source) pair, that is, to whoever can fix it: a folder read by two reports gives two "source is stale" findings — noisier than one counter per folder, but every row is addressed to a specific owner.

cards.heading: Value baselines and reference tables
cards.text:
The "set of known values" check starts with a baseline: the first run seeds the set of expected values on the server, and subsequent runs report only NEW ones. The analyst can accept new values into the baseline — and then they stop counting as drift.

The neighbouring kind of drift is values that have no row in a platform reference table. Its peculiarity is that it closes without a run: importing the missing keys into the reference table extinguishes the finding by itself, because it is computed on read as "what the engine brought minus the keys of the current version".

And two more honest limits. A generator without declared inputs gets only freshness, completeness and the row trend — there is nothing to diff, no checks, nothing to bind a baseline to. The agent engine observes nothing, so a source read only by it gives no findings at all. That is silence, not "all is well", and the page says so plainly.

cards.heading: The data boundary
cards.text:
There is a price the platform pays for content checks, and you need to know it. Up to 5 raw examples per check and up to 5 most frequent values of a column on the first run are sent to the server — meaning real cell contents cross the network boundary. The documentation records this as requiring a separate decision before deployment, not as a minor detail.

On the other hand, the "who else does this affect" field never guesses beyond the evidence: every answer is marked with where it is known from — "consumed in run N" is evidence, "declared" is the author's claim, "sheet level" is the reading library's ceiling, "unobservable" is the agent engine.

takeaways: Findings are not stored but computed on read over a window of the last 10 runs — so a manifest edit or an accepted baseline needs no invalidation.
A finding identifier depends only on "what and where", with no run and no time, so a returning problem is the same finding.
Acknowledgement does not hide a finding but removes it from the open count, and it is held by both bounds at once — date and run.
"Zero violations on a sample" and "zero violations" are different statements; the "sample" mark is mandatory.
Silence where there was nothing to observe with (agent engine, generator without inputs) does not mean "the data is fine".
