checks.q: A sheet holds 900,000 rows, and the content-check ceiling is 200,000 rows per sheet. The "not-null" check returned zero violations and a "sample" flag. What can correctly be claimed?
options: The sample is random, so most likely there are no nulls in the remaining 700,000 rows either
The first 200,000 rows have no nulls; the check says nothing about the other 700,000
The check wasn't performed and there is no result: above the ceiling the platform reports a reason
There are no nulls in the whole sheet: the 200,000-row ceiling applies only to the examples
checks.why: The content-check ceiling is 200,000 rows per sheet, and exceeding it is marked with the "sample" flag. This is neither a random sample nor an estimate over the whole sheet: a bounded prefix is taken, so no probabilistic conclusion about the full set follows from it. The result is still meaningful — it speaks about 200,000 rows, not 900,000; refusing with a reason is how a different check, the known-values set, responds.

checks.q: What would become possible if the finding identifier included the run number?
options: Findings would have to be stored in a table: computing them on read with the run in the hash would be impossible
Identifiers would coincide across different sources, and an acknowledgement would extinguish the finding for all
Nothing: the identifier is unique anyway, and acknowledgement is held by the date and the run bound
The same problem would get a new identifier every run, and an acknowledgement would live for one run
checks.why: The identifier is built only from "what is wrong and where" precisely so that a returning problem remains the same finding. With the run number inside the hash, every new observation would give a new identifier, an acknowledgement by identifier would stop matching on the very next run, and the "oldest run of continuous reproduction" calculation would have nothing to anchor to. Computation on read would survive: it does not depend on the shape of the identifier.

checks.q: New values regularly appear in the "Client code" column that are missing from the platform reference table. Which way of closing the finding matches how the platform works?
options: Accept the new values into the baseline: then they stop counting as drift on the next run
Import the missing keys into the reference table: the finding is computed on read and closes without a run
Run the generator again: the finding is recomputed only at the moment content checks are run
Acknowledge the finding with no end date, so it stops counting as open and doesn't colour the source
checks.why: Evaluation happens on read, so misses are recomputed as what the last run brought minus the keys of the CURRENT reference table version — importing the keys extinguishes the finding immediately, without a run. A value baseline closes the neighbouring kind of drift, new column values, not a missing row in a reference table. Acknowledgement removes the finding from the open count but does not fix the data.

checks.q: The interface offers an "acknowledge until the next run" button on the schema finding "column disappeared". What is wrong with this?
options: For schema findings the "since run" mark doesn't move while the problem lives — the acknowledgement is eternal
The button removes the finding from the list, and the missing column will only show up as a drop in row count
Schema findings can't be acknowledged at all: acknowledgement only works on content-check findings
Nothing: the next run will reproduce the finding, and the acknowledgement will expire on the run bound
checks.why: An acknowledgement holds while both bounds are true at once, including "the run from which the finding reproduces is not newer than the one given". For schema kinds this mark is pinned to the start of the continuous series, so a new run does not move it and the acknowledgement never expires — contrary to the promise on the label. A finding never disappears from the list, it only stops counting as open, so the correct remedy is to offer a date.

checks.q: A folder is read by two reports. The source hasn't been updated for two weeks, and the quality page shows two findings with the same meaning, "source is stale". Is this a defect?
options: No: findings are computed per (generator, source) pair — checks, thresholds and baselines are tied to it
Yes, the counter is doubled: "source is stale" findings should be collapsed into one row per folder
No: the reports have different freshness thresholds, which is why one folder gives two dissimilar findings
Yes: it follows from computing on read, as the 10-run window is taken for each report separately
checks.why: The unit of everything else in the subsystem is the (generator, source) pair: declared inputs, checks, aliases, baselines and thresholds are tied to it. So a folder read by two generators gives two findings, and this is a deliberate choice in favour of addressability: every row belongs to the owner of its report, who can fix it. A single counter per folder would be quieter but would not name who is responsible.

lessons.title: Reference tables: one truth on the platform
lessons.summary: You will understand why the mapping is moved out of generator code, how versions and ownership work, and why there must be exactly one key-normalisation rule for the whole platform.

cards.heading: Why the mapping moves out of code
cards.text:
A typical story: the generator code holds a "code → name" dictionary, assembled by hand at some point, with a quiet fallback of "if not found, show it as is". Codes arrive regularly, they are labelled not by the generator's author, and the same mapping is needed by two more reports. As a result, "a new value arrived that nobody labelled" is already happening — invisibly.

This is a classic master-data management problem: an entity must have one definition, and that definition must have an owner, a version and consumers. OnePage states the decision firmly: one truth per platform. One reference table — one row per key, no overrides "for this report".

A miss does not stay silent: it becomes a quality finding naming the reference table, the values themselves and the owner. How the report shows unlabelled rows — as an "other" bucket or as the raw code — is up to the generator's author; it is their convention, not a platform rule.

cards.heading: Versions, immutability, owner
cards.text:
A version is created on every import, always. A version has a number, a row count, a sha256 of its contents, an "added / changed / removed" summary and a note; the (reference table, version number) pair is unique. A version's rows are never edited retroactively — a correction is a new version.

A separate flag allows pinning a version at run time: by default the generator takes the current one, and with the flag the analyst can choose a specific one. The run records which reference table at which version it applied, and whether it applied one at all — so later you can see exactly what stood behind the numbers.

A reference table has an owner. If the field is empty, the miss notification goes to everyone who can refresh the data of any consuming report: a problem must always have an addressee.

Consumers are counted by declarations, not by rows: a generator that has no reports yet still appears in the list. And a claim to read a reference table in the chat semantics is an "in chat" badge, but NOT access: the line `sources: [{reference: …}]` can be written by anyone allowed to register a generator, and if it granted rights, publishing a report that merely mentions someone else's reference table would hand its rows to every reader of that report.

cards.heading: The key-normalisation rule
cards.text: A key is stored as entered and compared normalised. There is one rule for the whole platform, and it looks like this:
list: empty and not-a-number (NaN) give an empty string
an integral floating-point number becomes "7", not "7.0" — that is how Excel returns an integer cell
the string is converted to normal form NFC
the whole family of Unicode dashes and the minus sign are reduced to an ASCII hyphen
any whitespace characters, including the non-breaking space, collapse into one ordinary space
the ends are trimmed, and the result is casefolded (more aggressive than "to lower case")
leading zeros are NOT touched: "007" stays "007", because they are part of the value, not whitespace or punctuation
key length is limited to 64 characters — otherwise a long key would produce a permanent false "miss"

cards.text: The same rule gives rise to a schema requirement: the first column of a reference table is the key, and its type must be text. A numeric or date key would reopen exactly the problems normalisation exists to solve: leading zeros, locale formats, "7" versus "7,0".
cards.note: The normalisation function is written twice — on the server and in the generator's browser runtime — and must give byte-for-byte identical results. So it contains nothing that could diverge between the two execution environments: only standard regular expressions and Unicode tables, no locale and no third-party libraries. The match is pinned by a dedicated test.

cards.heading: Why there must be one normalisation
cards.text:
Imagine the server and the browser normalise differently in even one character. The "membership in a reference table" check runs in the browser: the engine takes normalised keys from the server and compares them with the column's normalised values. If the rules diverge, a value that is found perfectly well on the server will give a "miss" in the browser — or the other way round, the analyst sees a clean check while the report still shows an unlabelled row.

The problem runs deeper than neatness. Unicode allows several representations of the same text, and the normalisation standard exists precisely so that equivalent strings have one binary form. Casefold, in turn, is designed for caseless comparison and does more than lower-casing: the German "ß" becomes "ss", which "to lower case" does not do.

So the normalisation rule is not an implementation detail of reference tables but a platform invariant. Create a second, "slightly more convenient" copy of it — and you get two sets of keys that match almost always.

cards.heading: Import: rejection instead of silent coercion
cards.text:
Import from Excel validates rows against the frozen schema and REJECTS them rather than silently coercing them. You can request a dry run first: the response is the "added / changed / removed" diff and per-row errors; if there are errors, writing is impossible.

Writing uses optimistic locking: you send the version number you saw, and if someone managed to import theirs in the meantime, you get a 409 instead of a silent overwrite. Deleting missing rows happens only with an explicit flag, not by default.

Re-registering a generator never recreates or empties an existing reference table: the key and the types of existing columns are frozen (a mismatch is a rejection with a diff), a new column is added on top, and a column that disappeared from the declaration does not count as a change. A generator that stops declaring a reference table does not delete it: deletion is only a human action.

An empty reference table gives a single informational row, "upload Excel", not a "100% misses" warning — these are different situations, and alarming people with the second instead of the first is dishonest.

cards.heading: The data boundary
cards.text:
Reference table rows and examples of missed values live on the server by design — a deliberate decision, aligned with the decision on the report's server-side index. But they never get into the model's prompt: the chat receives only the declaration of the table and its columns, not the contents.

Sizes are limited separately: up to 20,000 rows and up to 2 MB per version, up to 32 columns, types only text, number or date. These are not arbitrary numbers but the boundary beyond which a reference table stops being a reference table and becomes a data mart — the platform has other mechanisms for that.

And one last point about interface honesty. A reference table declared in the manifest but not yet set up is created by itself when the generator is registered: empty, with the schema from the declaration, without an owner and at version zero. This is done so that the declaration does not diverge from reality: the list of consumers and the "upload Excel" finding appear immediately, not after the first run, which would otherwise quietly complete with an empty mapping.

takeaways: One truth per platform: one reference table, one row per key, no overrides "for this report".
A version is created on every import and is immutable; the run records which version it applied and whether it applied one at all.
A key is stored as entered and compared normalised; leading zeros are not stripped, and key length is limited to 64 characters.
There must be one normalisation rule per platform, because comparison happens both on the server and in the browser — a divergence gives false misses.
Import rejects failing rows instead of silently coercing them, and re-registering a generator never empties an existing reference table.

checks.q: In the analyst's file the client code is written as "007", in the reference table as "7". What happens during the reference-table membership check?
options: They match: the server compares raw values, and only the browser runtime applies normalisation
They match: an integral float gives "7", and the same rule strips leading zeros from the code
No match: normalisation doesn't touch leading zeros, so "007" and "7" stay different keys
They match: before comparison the key is cast to a number, and leading zeros are dropped
checks.why: Normalisation removes differences that are known to carry no meaning: case, the kind of space, the kind of dash, the Unicode form. A leading zero is not classified that way — it is part of the value, and the rule says so explicitly. The "7.0" rule concerns integral floats from Excel, not stripping zeros, and both sides of the comparison are normalised identically. That is exactly why the key column must be text: casting the key to a number would erase "007".

checks.q: What becomes possible if the generator's browser runtime gets its own, "slightly more convenient" version of key normalisation?
options: Nothing: the comparison is finally done on the server, and the browser just draws the finished result
The membership check slows down noticeably: keys have to be normalised twice, on both sides
Divergence both ways: false misses and missed real ones, rarely and unnoticed
Reference table import starts rejecting valid rows that fail the new key form
checks.why: The membership check runs in the browser: the engine fetches normalised keys and compares them with the column's normalised values, so the two sides of the comparison are normalised by different code. Any divergence in the rules produces errors of both kinds — a false miss and a missed real one — and not always but occasionally, which is the worst thing for trust. Import validates rows against the schema on the server and is unaffected. For byte-for-byte identity the function is restricted to standard tools and pinned by a test.

checks.q: Two reports want different names for the same code. How is this solved in the platform reference-table model?
options: Not in the reference table: one row per key is an invariant, different views are made in the reports
Create a second version of the reference table and pin it with the flag for one of the two consumers
Add a name override in the reference table at the consuming-report level, keeping the key shared
Add a column per report to the reference table and read different names of the same code from them
checks.why: The model deliberately has no per-report overrides: as soon as a second truth appears for one key, the question "which name is correct" stops having an answer on the platform. Version pinning solves a different problem — run reproducibility, not a difference of opinion — and keeping a report on an old version forever means not updating the mapping. A separate column is formally possible, but that is a different attribute, not a second value of the same one.

checks.q: A reference table import loads a file where three rows have text in a column of type "number". What should the platform do?
options: Create a version with all rows and mark it in the summary as partially valid, with a note
Change the column type to text: the reference table schema adapts to the fresh import file
Reject these rows with per-row errors: a dry run will show them in advance
Coerce values to numbers where possible, write the rest as empty and create a version
checks.why: The reference table schema is frozen by its consumers and does not adapt to each new file: changing a type retroactively would break everyone who already reads that column as a number. Silent coercion is worse than rejection, because a lost value surfaces later and without a trace, and the model has no "partially valid" version — a version is either created in full or not created. That is why import works as a dry run with a diff and per-row errors.

checks.q: The semantics of someone else's report say that it reads your reference table. What does this give that report's author?
options: The right to update the reference table's rows on a par with the owner, since the report declared reading it
Access to the reference table's rows for everyone who can open that report, even as a reader
Only an "in chat" badge in the consumer list: rights follow manifest consumers
The reference table's rows get into the model's prompt for questions asked over that report
checks.why: A declaration in the semantics can be written by anyone allowed to register a generator, and it names someone else's reference table identifier. If such a line granted access, publishing a report that merely mentions the reference table would hand its contents to all readers. So rights follow only manifest consumers plus the owner, creator and administrator, and a reader without rights receives the table unbound. Contents never reach the model's prompt: the chat receives the declaration of the table and columns.

lessons.title: Row-level access
lessons.summary: You will understand why filtering inside a report is an illusion, where the server actually filters, how a scope column is declared, and why "nothing is visible by default" is the only safe rule.

cards.heading: A filter in the report is not protection
cards.text:
An interactive OnePage report contains no data in its HTML: it all lives in slot files that the page loads. So any "territory filter" written in the report's JavaScript hides rows only visually — the whole file is already in the browser, and it is visible in the network panel of the developer tools.

This is a general principle, not a platform quirk: access checks run on the server, on every request, and client-side checks cannot be relied upon. Sending everything and hiding the excess in JS is exactly what we are moving away from.

So in OnePage rows are filtered ON THE SERVER, every time a slot file is served, not once at publication. One and the same generator run serves all viewers; the only difference is which bytes each one receives.

cards.heading: Who sees: the subject
cards.text:
The "who" side is separated from the "what" side. "Who" is a scope record tied to the person's identifier in the corporate directory: a set of keys (for example, position or territory names) or a "sees everything" flag.

The default rule is deny. No record for the viewer — they get an EMPTY but format-valid slot file: zero rows. Not the full contents and not a 403: the report opens and honestly shows nothing. A missing record is never read as "no restrictions".

This is exactly the same decision as in PostgreSQL: when row-level security is enabled and there is no policy, a default-deny policy applies — not a single row is visible. The opposite rule ("not in the rights table → everything is allowed") turns every import failure, every new employee and every typo in an identifier into a leak, and a silent one at that.

"Sees everything" is an explicit exemption, not a side effect of a role: a platform administrator, the report owner or an explicitly set flag. Only for such a viewer does the server not run the filter at all and serve the file byte for byte.

cards.heading: What is filtered: the policy
cards.text:
The "what" side is a policy declared by slot index. For each data slot you specify either the column by which rows are matched against the viewer's keys, or an indirect binding: "take from the neighbouring slot the key values of the rows whose scope column fell within my keys, and filter by those".

An indirect binding has a depth of exactly one: the slot being referenced must itself be filtered by a column. Otherwise a chain of references would turn a single response into a traversal of every slot in the report.

Non-data (for example, a library file) is listed separately as passthrough. A slot described NOWHERE is a refusal: a file was added to the version and the policy was forgotten, meaning nobody adopted a rule for this data, so it must not be served.

The validator is deliberately stricter than necessary: an unknown field is an error. A typo in the name of the "column" field would otherwise produce a slot without a filter — a leak that looks like a successful validation.
Three refusals that look rude but are in fact the only safe behaviour:
list: the declared column is missing from the file (the column was renamed in the generator) — a refusal, not serving without a filter: there is nothing to filter by
an undecipherable policy — a refusal: a report with an unreadable policy serves no data at all
an unknown file extension in a data slot — a refusal on serving: a format the filter cannot read safely must not be served "as is"
cards.note: Zero rows in a published file is not a refusal. If the run honestly produced an empty table, the viewer receives an empty but valid table: the report must show emptiness, not break.

cards.heading: Leakage through metadata
cards.text:
There is a trap that is easy to miss. In a columnar format with dictionaries, the column dictionary itself is a list of all distinct values: all territories, all clients. If you cut the rows but keep the dictionary, the file still carries the full list, and the leak happens through metadata rather than data.

So on every filtering pass the dictionaries are rebuilt from the surviving rows.

The same class of error exists in indirect binding: an empty key in the source slot (NULL in the export, an empty cell) does not enter the allowed set. Otherwise one such row would open every row of the target slot with an empty key.

cards.heading: The bypass perimeter is closed entirely
cards.text:
A filter on the main slot-serving route is useless if even one path to the same bytes remains nearby. So all of them are closed: external access links (both new and already issued tokens stop working as soon as the report has a policy enabled), downloading the source HTML, writing and deleting a slot, serving a file by its original name bypassing the slot number, the server-side index and the chat endpoints where a question is asked over this report.

The reason for chat and links is the same: a query over the index would return aggregates over other people's rows, and an external link has no subject at all — in OnePage the unit of access is a viewer with a session and their scope, and an anonymous token has no such unit. So links for such a report are closed completely rather than filtered.

The whole generator surface belongs here too: a run's auxiliary file is the entire source workbook, and the run card returns the input manifest. The right to "refresh data" for such a report does not substitute for the right to "see everything".

One more thing: the report's shared saved-state block is one per report and used to be embedded in everyone's HTML. Under a policy it is not embedded at all — otherwise HTML that is promised to "contain no data" would carry other people's selections.

cards.heading: The cache must tell viewers apart
cards.text:
Filtered bytes are cached, and the cache key includes the report identifier, version, slot number, file time and size, the policy fingerprint and the fingerprint of the viewer's keys. A change of file version, policy or viewer rights misses the cache by itself — invalidation by key rotation, not by deletion.

The policy fingerprint in the key is essential with several worker processes: cache clearing lives in one process, and without the fingerprint the processes that did not handle the policy change would keep serving bytes under the old, broader policy.

The same goes for headers. Slot files of such a report are served as private and requiring revalidation — always, including to viewers with full access. The reason was found on the test stand: the URL is the same for all viewers, and the browser serves an "immutable" response from its disk cache without contacting the server — on a shared computer the next user received the previous user's full file. Passthrough slots (libraries) remain immutable: they contain no viewer-dependent rows.

cards.heading: What this mechanism does not do
cards.text:
This is worth saying plainly. The policy here is a filter by a column value in the file, not a projection of rights from the corporate directory: the platform does not read security groups itself, and viewer keys arrive by manual import. Reports that existed before the mechanism was introduced do not get a filter automatically: a silent manifest means "as before", and the policy is switched on by an explicit action.

A rights-table row for which no account had been found at import time is stored without an identifier and matched up on the person's first sign-in — so that a new employee gets their scope immediately, without waiting for the next import.

And separately: the report type and the policy do not diverge. A policy cannot be set on a report whose data lives inside the HTML, and a report with a policy cannot be turned back into one — otherwise rows would move inside the HTML while the badge promises the opposite.

takeaways: An interactive report's data lives in slot files, so a filter in the report's JS hides rows only visually; the server filters on every response.
No scope record — an empty valid file, not the full one and not an error; a missing record never means "no restrictions".
A policy declares a scope column by slot index or an indirect binding of depth one; a slot described nowhere is a refusal.
The bypass perimeter is closed entirely: external links, source HTML, index, chat, generator surface — otherwise the filter becomes theatre.
The cache key and ETag must carry the fingerprint of both the policy and the viewer's keys, otherwise one viewer's bytes will go to another.
