checks.q: A report author proposes: the generator will add a "visible to" column to the file, and the page will hide other people's rows. Why doesn't this match how the platform works?
options: The file still goes to the viewer in full, and the rights hierarchy moves into every generator
The generator doesn't read the corporate directory, so it has nothing to fill "visible to" with
The report's saved state is embedded in the HTML, and others' selections would leak with it
Such a column would noticeably enlarge the slot file and slow the report page down for viewers
checks.why: Two independent reasons. First, client-side filtering is pointless: the entire slot file is visible in the network panel, so other people's rows have already left the server. Second, such a scheme shifts keeping rights up to date onto the report author, who would have to know the entire territory hierarchy and keep it in sync with the directory. File size and the saved-state block are true facts from the chapter, but they do not answer the question asked.

checks.q: What would become possible if the fingerprint of the viewer's keys were not part of the ETag and the cache key?
options: Passthrough slots would stop being served as immutable and would reload on every visit
A cache, server or browser, would give one viewer bytes filtered for another
The cache would become less effective: any rights change would evict entries for every viewer
Nothing: the slot file URL contains the viewer's identifier, so cache entries simply don't overlap
checks.why: The slot file URL is the same for all viewers — only the bytes after filtering differ, so the only thing that separates the responses is the cache key and the validator. Without the key fingerprint, two people with different territories would land in the same cache entry. The policy fingerprint is needed for a symmetric reason: without it, processes that did not handle the policy change would keep serving bytes under the old, broader one.

checks.q: A report's policy describes slots 0 and 1, and slot 2 is passthrough. In a new version the generator started publishing a slot 3 with a fact table as well. What happens, and why is that right?
options: Slot 3 is filtered by the scope column of the first described slot as the closest in meaning
Slot 3 is served unfiltered: since there is no rule for it, there are no restrictions on it either
Slot 3 gets a refusal: neither its own rule nor a passthrough one was adopted for this data
Slot 3 is served as passthrough: every slot not listed in the rules counts as passthrough
checks.why: An uncovered slot is treated as a hole by definition: no person adopted a rule for these rows, so a refusal applies — the same "deny by default" principle as for a viewer without a scope record. Passthrough slots are listed explicitly, and guessing a rule from a neighbouring slot would be the worst option of all: it would look like working filtering. The report still opens; the refusal goes to that specific slot.

checks.q: A viewer opens a report and all tables are empty, while the serving log shows rows_in greater than zero and rows_out zero. What does this tell you?
options: The file was published empty in this run, and the viewer honestly sees empty but valid tables
The file has rows, but not a single scope-column value matched the viewer's keys
The filter is broken: with non-zero input the output can't be zero, it's a defect in serving
The viewer has no scope record, so the server returned a refusal instead of the file's rows
checks.why: The log counters distinguish exactly these cases: rows_in is how many rows were in the file, rows_out how many survived the filter. Non-zero input with zero output means comparing the column values with the viewer's keys produced no matches — a normal result for someone else's territory and the first sign of a mismatch in how keys are spelled. An empty publication would correspond to zero input, and a viewer without a scope record gets an empty valid file, not a refusal.

checks.q: An owner asks for an external link to a report with row-level access, "read-only, filtered by the recipient's territory". What matches the platform model?
options: Issue the link: the server filters the response by the recipient's scope just like a normal session
External links for such a report are closed entirely: an anonymous token has no subject
Issue the link, opening only passthrough slots through it and keeping data slots behind a session
Issue the link and lift the policy temporarily, restoring it right after the recipient views the report
checks.why: The filter works from a subject: the key set is taken by the identifier of the signed-in person. An anonymous token has no subject, and building a separate key circuit for it for the sake of one scenario was judged unjustified — so links are closed entirely, and previously issued tokens stop working too. Disabling the policy "temporarily" contradicts the point of the mechanism, and partially serving passthrough slots does not bring the link to life anyway.

lessons.title: Audit, perimeter and honest limits
lessons.summary: You will understand what goes into the platform's audit log and why, what never goes into it, why a client-side error log appeared, and which threats the organisational perimeter closes — and which it does not.

cards.heading: One table for everything
cards.text:
The platform's audit log is a single table: who acted, what action, on which resource, details as JSON, address, time. There are indexes on time and on the (actor, time) pair — otherwise the check "what has this person done over the last month" would be a full table scan.

Every subsystem discussed so far writes to it: folder operations, completion of a run's observation upload, generator registration, actions on reference tables, scope matching on first sign-in, chat questions, serving a filtered slot file.

An important subtlety of slot serving: an entry is made only on a cache miss, that is, on actual filtering, not on every access. The log must not grow linearly with the number of page refreshes — otherwise it turns into a traffic log in which an event can no longer be found.

cards.heading: What is never in the log
cards.text: The boundary here is drawn deliberately and identically in every subsystem.
list: Data values. An entry about serving a slot file carries the slot number, how many rows went in, how many came out and how many keys the viewer has — and not a single cell
SQL text. An entry about a chat answer stores it only as a sha256: a literal in a filter may quote real data
Query results. There is not a single row of an answer in the log, by construction
Full tokens. An entry about a link keeps a short token prefix by which the event can be identified, but which is not an access key
Translations. Entry details are not localised: the log is not an interface, and the same entry must read the same for everyone

cards.text: This is not a platform quirk but standard discipline: logging guidelines explicitly list what must not be written to logs — session identifiers, access tokens, passwords, keys, payment and sensitive commercial data — and at the same time require writing what incident investigation is impossible without: authorisation failures, input validation failures, administrative actions, data exports.
cards.note: The point of the restriction is simple: the log lives longer and is copied more often than the data. A log export goes outside for incident investigation, sits in an archive, ends up in someone else's mailbox. Whatever you wrote into it, you wrote forever and in many copies.

cards.heading: The client-side error log
cards.text:
Why it was needed at all. For the report chat, the server side ends early: the call to the model through the corporate proxy, SQL execution by the in-browser engine, the page's own work — all of this happens on the user's machine, and the server never learned about these failures. Meanwhile the container output is empty by design: the access log is switched off, and the application writes to its own table, not to the output stream.

So the page sends one entry per failure, without waiting for a response: stage, reason, question, status code, node, tier, a "from browser" flag. The stages are named in advance and form a closed list — the provider call (network, empty response, HTTP error), intent parsing, SQL preparation and validation, query execution, building a trend, no model available, and the umbrella case "sent — got no answer".

The fields are length-limited, and SQL text gets in here in one single case: SQL that the model composed and that the engine REFUSED to execute — that is, text that was never run against data.

After that these are ordinary log rows, and the question "what breaks for people in the chat" becomes one query by action name.

cards.heading: Log export
cards.text:
The log is visible on the admin page, but the page is no good for external investigation. So there is an export to JSONL — one line per entry: the actor (their directory identifier, or empty for system entries), action, resource, already unpacked details, time, address.

The same code is available both as a command (for a regular scheduled archive) and as a route for the administrator. What matters is that there is nothing to redact during export: the details contain no query results anyway, so the export carries no more than the page already shows.

That is the practical criterion of a well-designed log: you can hand it over in full without scrubbing.

cards.heading: The perimeter: what it closes
cards.text:
The server is isolated, and access to it is only through the corporate VPN with the same directory account as single sign-on. Several things follow from this that would otherwise have to be built separately.

Revoking an account in a single action closes both the VPN and sign-in to the platform. So the offboarding process, signing out of all sessions and external access via links coincide with one and the same organisational lever that IT already controls. That is precisely why sign-in rate limiting and a separate single-sign-out circuit were deliberately postponed: without a valid account, a request never reaches the sign-in form.

It is important to understand the shape of this argument. Revoking access here is a property of the system, not a procedure someone must perform on time in three places. Any scheme where revoking rights requires manual actions in several independent systems fails exactly where one of them was forgotten.

cards.heading: What the perimeter does not close
cards.text:
Listing this is as important as listing what is closed.

The model key in "bring your own key" mode lives in the user's browser and is deliberately outside the perimeter — this is a separate decision, not an oversight.

The platform does not read directory security groups itself: scopes arrive by manual import, and this is recorded as an open question for the directory administrators, not as an implemented capability.

The server is offline by design, so dependency checks for known vulnerabilities are run from a machine that has network access, not by the server itself.

And finally, the perimeter says nothing at all about what a person who was legitimately granted access does. Exactly three things from this unit answer that question: provenance (where the numbers come from), row-level access (which rows they could see) and the audit log (what they actually did). None of them replaces the other two.

It is useful to state this as a rule for reading any system, not just this one. Every protective mechanism has a boundary, and it is either named by the author or found by whoever runs into it at an unfortunate moment. "We don't read directory groups", "the model key is outside the perimeter", "the agent engine observes nothing", "the check was performed on a sample" — none of these phrases is in the documentation out of modesty. A system that lists its limits lets you build on top of it; a system that promises completeness forces every user to discover the boundaries on their own and at different times.

takeaways: The audit log is one "who, what, on what, when" table, and the slot-serving entry is made on filtering, not on every access.
The log never holds data values, results, SQL text or full tokens — only counters, hashes, prefixes and identifiers.
The client-side error log appeared because after the chat's server side everything breaks in the browser, and the container output is empty by design.
A well-designed log can be exported in full without scrubbing anything; that is exactly what the JSONL export does.
The perimeter closes sign-in and access revocation with a single organisational lever, but does not answer what a person with legitimate access did.

sources.title: OWASP Logging Cheat Sheet (what to log and what to exclude)
NIST SP 800-92: Guide to Computer Security Log Management

checks.q: A developer proposes adding to the slot-serving log entry the list of scope-column values that matched, "to make incidents easier to investigate". What is wrong?
options: The entry is made only on a cache miss, so some accesses will never get into it
The list of matched values is exactly what's missing when investigating an incident
The entry details would have to be localised, but the log must read the same for all
Data values would enter the log, which lives longer and is copied more often
checks.why: The boundary "counters, hashes and identifiers go into the log, but not values" is drawn identically in every subsystem precisely because the log export goes outside and lives in archives. The diagnostic need is met without values: the number of rows in and out and the number of viewer keys already answer the question "did anything match at all". Details are deliberately never localised, and logging on a cache miss is a separate decision about volume, not about values.

checks.q: A user complains that the report chat "doesn't answer anything". The server log for this report has no errors at all, and the container output is empty. Where should you look?
options: In the client-side error log: after the server side, the failure happens in the browser
In the slot-serving entries: they show the cache miss and the number of viewer keys
In the container output: switch on the access log, and page failures will become visible
In the chat answer entry: it stores the query text, which shows what failed
checks.why: Empty container output is not a symptom but a decision: the access log is switched off, and the application writes to its own table. Failures after the server side happen on the user's machine (the provider via the proxy, SQL execution in the browser, the page itself), and the client-side log was introduced precisely for this blind spot: the page sends an entry with a stage and a reason, which lands in the shared table under its own action name. Slot serving is a different subsystem, and the query in the answer entry is stored only as a sha256.

checks.q: What would change if the entry for serving a filtered slot file were made on every access rather than only on a cache miss?
options: The table would grow, but the indexes on time and on the actor would compensate for it
The log would grow with page refreshes and become a traffic log with no events
The cache of filtered bytes would stop paying off: requests would bypass it
The JSONL export would have to be scrubbed before handing it over in full
checks.why: The event worth recording is the fact of filtering: for whom and by which keys the bytes were assembled. Serving the same bytes again from cache asserts nothing new, yet it happens on every page refresh, and such entries would crowd out meaningful ones — the same logic by which noisy alerts crowd out real ones. Indexes speed up search but do not save you from noise; this has no effect at all on how the cache works or on what the export details contain.

checks.q: A draft change proposes writing to the client-side error log the SQL text that the engine executed and that failed on the data. Why does this cross the boundary?
options: An executed query quotes values in literals; only a rejected one is logged
Client entry fields are length-limited, and the query text doesn't fit into them
The client log's stages are a closed list, and there is no stage for query execution
SQL text never enters the log in any form: the answer entry stores a sha256
checks.why: The boundary is drawn not by "SQL in general" but by whether the text quotes data: a literal in a filter condition is a real value from the user's folder, which is why the answer entry stores the query only as a sha256. The exception is made exactly for text the engine rejected: it was never executed against data and is needed to understand what the model composed. Field length limits and the closed list of stages exist, but they are not the reason for the ban.

checks.q: There is a discussion about whether a separate mechanism is needed to force-terminate all sessions of a departed employee. Which argument matches the decision taken?
options: Needed: the model key in "bring your own key" mode lives in the browser, outside the perimeter
Needed: until the session expires, the departed employee keeps access, and VPN won't help
Not needed: scopes arrive by manual import, so the departed person's rights will reset
Not needed separately: VPN and sign-in use one account, revoking it closes both
checks.why: The decision rests on the levers coinciding: the server is reachable only from the VPN, and the VPN and single sign-on use the same directory account — so revoking it removes access entirely, without a separate procedure in the platform. The value of the scheme is that revocation becomes a property of the system rather than an action that can be forgotten in one of three places. Manual scope import and the model key outside the perimeter are real platform boundaries, but they have nothing to do with ending sessions.

units.title: The loop: how it is done with AI and how it lives on
units.subtitle: Intent, repeatable feedback, the line between machine and human, and an honest reading of signals after publication

lessons.title: Intent as an artefact
lessons.summary: After this chapter you understand why work starts with a written intent, what it must contain, and how it turns into a verifiable platform contract.

cards.heading: Why not start with code
cards.text:
The temptation to start with code is understandable: the model answers quickly, the first result appears within a minute, and it seems the intent can be written up later. In practice "later" never comes. A week on, nobody can say which decision this report was supposed to support, why exactly these breakdowns were chosen and what was considered a sign of success. The report remains, but the reason it is the way it is disappears.

The AI-native SDLC playbook describes the same order for software development: work starts with `intent.md` — a proto-specification written in the initiator's own words: the problem, the proposed outcome, the systems affected, the constraints. After that, every stage ends with an artefact commit, and that commit opens the next stage. The point is not bureaucracy but the fact that an artefact can be handed over — to another person, to another model session, to yourself a month from now.
An intent for a report on the platform is five answers written down before the first line of code or the first request to the model:
list: What decision is made with this report. Not "show sales" but "choose which items to restock first".
Who the reader is and what they can do. A person who opens the report once a week for ten minutes and a person who lives in it every day are two different reports.
What data and from where. Folder, file-name pattern, sheet, columns. Exactly the ones that are actually read, not "roughly sales".
Constraints. How many files of what size actually arrive, what must not be shown, which values must be matched against a reference table.

How we will know it worked. A sign that can be checked: the number agrees with the reference calculation, opening time is below a threshold, a reader's question gets closed without writing to the author.

cards.heading: The fifth point is the hardest
cards.text:
The first four points are usually easy to write. People stumble on the fifth: "how we will know it worked". The temptation is to write "the report will be useful". That is not a sign: it cannot be checked, which means it cannot be failed either.

A sign of success must be such that, a month later, two people independently reach the same verdict. These work: the report total agrees with the reference calculation to a given precision; the report opens faster than the named threshold on real volume; the reader finds the breakdown they need without contacting the author. Anything that depends on someone's mood does not.

There is a side benefit too. A written sign of success is a ready-made statement of the verification task. It almost always turns directly into a gate: "agrees with the reference" becomes a reconciliation run, "opens faster than the threshold" becomes a measurement. An intent whose fifth point is written honestly already contains half of the verification plan.

cards.heading: An intent is not a prompt
cards.text:
A prompt is a consumable: it lives for one session and disappears with it. An intent outlives the code. The difference shows in how the model's context works. Anthropic's documentation on the context window puts it directly: the window is working memory, and as the number of tokens grows, accuracy and recall degrade — an effect it calls context rot. So what matters is not "how much fits" but what exactly is selected.

Hence the practical rule from the material on context engineering: find the smallest set of high-signal tokens that produces the desired outcome. A written intent is exactly such a set. It can be placed in full at the start of any new session, and it costs less than a retelling of the conversation that led to it.

cards.heading: How an intent becomes a contract
cards.text:
On the platform an intent has two formal heirs, and both are data, not prose.

The first is the generator's `manifest.json`. It declares the inputs (file-name pattern, sheet, columns), the outputs (finished HTML or slot files), volume limits and dependencies. An unknown top-level key is a registration error, deliberately: the manifest is treated as a contract, and a typo in it must be visible immediately. A version with a dependency unusable in the browser or with volume above the engine's ceilings is rejected at registration — that is, it stops the administrator, not the analyst in the middle of a run.

The second is `semantics.json`: what the report means. Which canonical tables are derived from the input files, which rules are applied before calculation, how each metric is computed. The platform validates this file when a version is registered: the shape, the identifiers, "read-only" for SQL and a dry run of every query over empty tables. A typo in a column name becomes a 400 error for the author, not an obscure error for an operator a week later.

cards.heading: What an input declaration looks like

cards.text: When `inputs` is non-empty, the engine reads exactly the matching files and skips the rest. This is how intent turns into behaviour: the line "we read the weekly sales exports, the Sales sheet, three columns" stops being a verbal agreement and becomes what is executed. Note the side effect of the declaration: it simultaneously defines both what is read and what the platform will later be able to say something about.

cards.heading: Discrepancies are read against the contract
cards.text:
A contract is useful not at the moment it is written but at the moment of a discrepancy. Every run records which folders are connected, which files were read, which sheets and columns were opened. Matching the declared against the observed gives quality findings such as "declared but not found" — tied to a source, not to the reader's mood.

Without declared inputs there is nothing to compare against. An old generator whose manifest has neither `inputs` nor checks gets only what is visible from the runs themselves: source freshness and changes in row count. Everything about column contents requires a declaration. This is the direct cost of an unwritten intent, expressed in what the platform does not know about your report.

cards.note: The platform is honest about the boundary of observation too: a file taken from cache was not opened by the generator — so nobody knows anything about its columns in this run, and that is exactly what it says. A lack of observation is marked, not substituted with the past.

cards.heading: What carries over beyond the platform
cards.text:
The general mechanics are these. An intent is a specification written before the work and in the customer's terms. A contract is the machine-checkable part of the intent. A discrepancy is the difference between the declared and the observed, and it only makes sense when the declared is written down.

The chain is robust to the executor changing. It does not matter whether the code is written by a model, the generator's author or an analyst a year from now: there is one contract, one check, and a discrepancy reads the same way. This is the reason intent has become more important in working with AI than it used to be: the executor is cheap and fast, so the bottleneck has shifted to formulating the task and accepting the result.

There is also a simple test of an intent's maturity. Try handing it to someone who knows nothing about your task and ask what they would do. If they ask about the data and the sign of success, the intent is not finished. If they ask about the subject domain, the intent is ready; what is needed next is not text but a conversation.

takeaways: An intent is written before code and contains five things: the decision, the reader, the data, the constraints and the sign of success.
A prompt lives for one session, an intent outlives the code; so it is selected as context, not accumulated like a conversation.
On the platform, intent materialises in `manifest.json` (what we read and what we output) and `semantics.json` (what it means); both are validated when a version is registered.
A "declared versus observed" discrepancy becomes a quality finding only where a declaration exists.
An unknown key in the manifest is an error, not a trifle: a contract must break loudly.

sources.title: Effective context engineering for AI agents

checks.q: The author declared the input `{"match": "Sales_*.xlsx", "sheets": [{"name": "Sales", "columns": ["Region"]}]}` in the manifest, but the generator also reads a "Reference" sheet from the same file. Registration passed. What happens next?
options: The run fails on read: the engine gives the generator only the sheets declared in the manifest
Registration should have returned 422: a non-empty `inputs` requires listing every sheet read
The run passes, but the "Reference" sheet stays unobserved: there will be no checks on its columns
The run passes, and the platform completes the declaration itself from the sheets and columns opened
checks.why: The declaration filters files, not sheets inside an already opened file, so the calculation does not break — observation does. The platform can compare declared with observed only along what was declared, and an undeclared sheet stays outside quality and outside the provenance graph. The server does not know whether the declaration is complete and does not fill it in itself: keeping the contract complete is the author's job.

checks.q: Suppose unknown top-level keys in the manifest were silently ignored. Which error would become possible?
options: Volume above the engine's ceilings would stop being rejected, and the analyst would hit the limits instead
A typo in a key would read as "nothing declared", and the feature would silently switch off
A version with a browser-unusable dependency would pass registration and fail for the operator
A dry run of queries over empty tables would stop catching typos in column names
checks.why: Silent ignoring turns a typo into a default, and a default looks like a deliberate decision: the author will see the discrepancy not at registration but on someone else's machine, where the output simply won't be written back. Dependency checks, volume ceilings and the dry run of queries are separate registration gates, and strictness about unknown keys does not replace them.

checks.q: A team wants to pin down a metric's formula so that it cannot quietly drift away from the report. Which solution matches how the platform works?
options: Put the formula in `semantics.json`: it is validated at registration and frozen with the version
Keep the formula in a prompt the analyst pastes into the model session with every question
Describe the formula in a comment in the generator code and require updating it at every review
Create a page of metric descriptions and link to it from the footer of every report publication
checks.why: A code comment and a separate page are not executed, and a prompt is not versioned — all three drift from the calculation unnoticed. A definition in `semantics.json` is validated at registration (shape, read-only SQL, a dry run over empty tables) and frozen together with the version, so a mistake in a column name becomes a 400 response to the author, not a wrong number for the reader.

checks.q: A report has lived for six months, and its author has left. A newcomer sees a number that looks odd and wants to understand whether it should be like that. What gives the answer fastest?
options: Look in the run log at which files were read and which sheets and columns were opened
Read the generator code in full — only it shows exactly how this number was calculated
Compare the number with the previous publication and judge how much it has changed in a month
The written intent and contract: what decision the report serves, what's declared as input and metric
checks.why: Code answers the question "how was it calculated", but not "is this how it was meant to be". Comparing with a previous publication shows a change but not the norm, and the run log describes the observed but not the declared. The intent and the contract together give both the goal and the declared formula, and the platform will show the discrepancy between declared and observed by itself.

checks.q: An author decided not to write an intent and instead to keep the entire conversation with the model "in case of questions". What is wrong here from the standpoint of working with context?
options: The conversation must be compressed into `intent.md`, otherwise the stage isn't closed by an artefact commit
A conversation is low-signal context: it records the path, not the decision, and it hurts recall
A prompt lives for one session, so a saved conversation is useless as context for a new task
The sign of success can't be recovered from a conversation, and without it no gate can be built
checks.why: Context is a finite resource with diminishing returns: the more tokens, the worse the accuracy and recall, and the task is to find the smallest set of high-signal tokens. A conversation stores rejected options and dead ends on a par with the accepted decision, so as context it is worse than a short intent. The other statements are true in themselves, but they are about how stages are formalised and about gates, not about the quality of context.

lessons.title: Feedback you can repeat
lessons.summary: After this chapter you understand why "I eyeballed it" does not scale, what the deterministic gates before hand-over consist of, and what a false signal costs.

cards.heading: Why eyeballing does not scale
cards.text:
Checking by eye has three properties that make it unfit as the main mechanism. It does not repeat: another person will look at something else. It does not compare: "looks fine" yesterday and today are different thresholds. And it does not keep up with an executor that works faster than you: if a model proposes ten versions an hour, the human eye becomes the bottleneck and starts letting things through.

The AI-native SDLC playbook states the requirement for this spot in one sentence: always give the model a way to verify its own work — tests, a build or a screenshot comparison. The point is not trust in the model but that a defect must be detected within the session, not a week later at review.

cards.heading: The cost of detection grows with the stage
cards.text:
This is an old engineering pattern, and the Google SRE chapter on testing frames it in terms of reliability metrics: a test is prevention, and a defect caught before release has zero time to recovery, because there is nothing to recover.

Translate this to our problem. A formula error caught by the semantics gates costs one run. The same error caught at acceptance by the report owner costs back-and-forth, a rerun and waiting. The same error that reaches the reader costs a decision already taken — and trust in all the other numbers in that report, including the correct ones. So gates are placed as early as possible, not as strictly as possible.

cards.heading: Gates before handing over a generator
cards.text: The generator author's guide requires six gates to be green before a bundle is handed over. The first four are the key ones for our topic.
list: Determinism: two runs on the same data give byte-identical sha256 for all outputs.
Contract: file dispositions are correct, a rerun with the same cache marks all files as taken from cache, and a warm run's outputs are byte-identical to a cold one's.
Equivalence under refactoring: aggregates are compared element-wise, detail rows as multisets, against the old version and on the full real volume.
A run on a full year, not a sample: the engine's limits are tested at the maximum the user will see.

cards.heading: Why exactly these three properties
cards.text:
Running with plain Python without a browser is needed because the engine contract is written so that the code knows nothing about the browser. This makes the check cheap: it can be run in a loop rather than with clicks.

Equivalence answers a question that otherwise has no answer: is a discrepancy a mistake or a deliberate change? A discrepancy by itself is not a defect. The defect is publishing it without noticing: the reader will see different numbers and not know why.

Determinism is the precondition for everything else. As long as two runs give different bytes, "equivalence" means nothing: you cannot tell a code change from your own noise. Non-determinism almost always comes from two places — a recorded generation time and an order taken from a set or a dictionary.

cards.heading: Gates go where they are cheapest
cards.text:
Notice exactly where the shape checks sit. A faulty manifest is rejected at version registration — that is, it stops the administrator uploading the bundle, not the analyst in the middle of a run on their own machine. A query from a metric description is checked by a dry run over empty tables right there, at registration: a typo in a column name becomes a response to the author, not an error for the operator.

This is a general technique, and it matters more than the specific implementations. A check is placed at the point where it is cheapest and where the person able to fix it is standing. Moving the same check one step later does not make it softer — it makes it more expensive, because the person fixing it is no longer the one who made the mistake.

cards.heading: Semantics gates
cards.text:
A separate class of gates checks meaning rather than bytes. The gate engine takes metric definitions from `semantics.json` and executes them over real exports, comparing them with the report authors' reference calculation. For the pilot generator such a run reproduced 482 of 482 Grand Total cells, and the merge checkpoints matched row by row.

A blind check looks stronger still: another agent received only the bundle, one real file and a description of the JSON shape — no reference and no hints — and the independent gates passed 12 of 12, including non-obvious selection rules. That is the definition of good feedback: it checks the result, not diligence, and its verdict does not depend on who runs it.

cards.heading: What good feedback for an agent looks like
cards.text:
Anthropic's material on tools for agents gives a short criterion: an error message should name a specific, actionable fix, not a return code. An agent, like a person, fixes what it has understood.

The platform works the same way in several places. The server returns manifest errors as a list in a single response, in readable text — fixed in one pass, not in five rounds. A missing required auxiliary workbook in the folder becomes a diagnostic card before the run starts, not a quiet fallback inside the generator. The answer "the file is missing" is more useful than a report computed on incomplete data.

cards.heading: What good feedback for a person looks like
cards.text:
For a person the criterion is different: feedback must be sufficient to make a decision and must not require taking things on faith. On the report questions screen, next to the number sits the "How it's calculated" panel — the metric definition, the calculation and the sources — and the SQL is available on a separate line before the person agrees with the number.

The answer card's badge names not "confidence in general" but who chose the metric: exact form, the form matched loosely, understood by meaning, SQL from semantics, no answer. This is more honest than a number: shape matching has a single producer, and it returns a hit only when two conditions hold at once — the accumulated weight is not below the threshold and at least twice that of the nearest competitor.

cards.heading: The cost of a false signal
cards.text:
A false signal is more expensive than a missing one, because it spends the loop's most expensive resource — attention — and teaches people to ignore the channel entirely. The Google SRE chapter on monitoring says the same about alerts: a page that fires on harmless events devalues all the others.

On the platform this decision was taken twice, in opposite directions. The threshold for a confident shape match was raised from 2 to 4: a single common word was read as a confident hit on some metric, and an off-topic question got a cheerful wrong answer; on the authors' held-out sample the number of false matches fell from 6 to 1 with no losses on their own question bank. And conversely: if a word from the question was not found in any dimension, the platform stays silent rather than asking a random clarifying question — a false clarification is worse than none.

cards.note: An answer without a number is never drawn as an empty card: instead, a question goes back to the person with options the browser can actually execute — remove the period filter, remove one non-time filter, take a different metric. An empty screen is also a false signal, just a silent one.

takeaways: Checking by eye does not repeat, does not compare and becomes a bottleneck as soon as the executor speeds up.
Determinism is the precondition of all the other gates: as long as two runs give different bytes, equivalence measures nothing.
A discrepancy between the old and new version is not an error in itself; the error is publishing it unnoticed.
Good feedback for an agent names an actionable fix; for a person it shows the definition, calculation and source next to the number.
A false signal is more expensive than silence: it spends attention and devalues the channel, so thresholds are raised and unsure clarifications are not shown.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Testing for Reliability
Writing effective tools for AI agents

checks.q: An author ran the new version twice on the same files: the sha256 of the outputs matched. Then they compared it with the previous version — the aggregates matched, but the detail rows differed in order. What does this mean?
options: Determinism is broken: since the row order drifts, the first gate counts as failed
The aggregate match is accidental: equivalence counts only if the details match row by row
Determinism holds; detail rows are compared as multisets, a different order isn't a defect
Clear the cache and repeat: a warm run must give outputs byte-identical to a cold one
checks.why: The determinism gate compares two runs of the same version, and it is green: the bytes matched, so the order is stable here. The equivalence gate compares different versions and is formulated precisely this way — aggregates element-wise, detail rows as multisets — because row order is not part of the report's meaning. The cache requirement belongs to the contract gate and has nothing to do with this comparison.

checks.q: The requirement to run on a full year of data was removed from the gate set, leaving a check on a one-week sample. What will stop being caught?
options: Hitting engine limits on file count and size, and memory growth — failures only on the full set
Output non-determinism: a recorded time and set order are visible only at large volume
Discrepancies with the old version: aggregates over a week match even if the logic changed
Errors in metric formulas: on a week of data many selection rules simply never fire
checks.why: Formulas, determinism and equivalence can be checked on a sample too: they are about logic, not scale, and a changing timestamp line breaks the byte comparison at any volume. Volume limits and memory consumption are the only class that by construction is visible only at the real maximum, which is why the requirement is written as "a full year, not a sample". The user will hit them first, and that is the most expensive way to find out.

checks.q: A generator can manage without an auxiliary workbook internally: if it is missing, it takes fallback values. The author considers this a convenience. What does the platform suggest doing instead?
options: Abort the run with an exception inside the generator so the author sees the error in the traceback
Catch the substitution with the semantics gates: reconciliation will show a gap in the totals
Declare the file required: the engine checks it before the run and shows a diagnostic card
Keep the fallback values and write a warning in the footer of the published report HTML
checks.why: A quiet fallback yields a report that looks normal but is computed on different data — the worst kind of false signal, and a footer warning does not remove it. Declaring the file required moves detection to before the run, where it costs one click, and turns silence into a named reason. An exception inside the generator and reconciliation against the reference fire later and cost more: a check is placed where the person able to fix it stands.

checks.q: A user's question contains one word that matches a metric's name and nothing else in common with any metric. The confident-match threshold is 4, and the required lead over second place is twofold. What happens, and why is that right?
options: The platform asks a clarifying question and offers a choice between the two closest metrics
The badge shows "understood by meaning", and the answer is computed on the heaviest metric
The answer is given on this metric: the lead over second place is twofold, so the condition holds
There's no confident match: one word doesn't reach the threshold, the question goes to the model
checks.why: An exact shape match returns a hit only when two conditions hold at once, and the first is already not met: one common word gives a weight below the threshold of 4, so the twofold lead decides nothing. This very case was the reason the threshold was raised from 2 to 4: previously an off-topic question got a cheerful wrong answer, and after the change the number of false matches on the held-out sample fell from 6 to 1. Nor will the platform ask a random clarifying question.

checks.q: An author added a line "generated: <current time>" to the footer of the report HTML. All other gates are green. What happens now?
options: A warm run will diverge from a cold one, and the file dispositions in the contract will be wrong
The determinism gate fails: two runs no longer give byte-identical outputs
Nothing changes: the footer isn't part of the calculation, and gates compare only numeric outputs
The equivalence gate against the old version fails, while determinism holds
checks.why: A recorded time is one of the two classic sources of non-determinism, alongside order taken from an unordered set. The determinism gate compares the sha256 of all outputs of two runs, and any changing line breaks it, wherever it sits. Everything that relies on it falls next: without byte equality you cannot tell a code change from your own noise when comparing versions, while file dispositions have nothing to do with it.

lessons.title: What gets automated and what stays with people
lessons.summary: After this chapter you can draw the line between observation and decision, and you can see where that line runs in the platform itself.

cards.heading: The line is not where it seems
cards.text:
The argument is usually framed as "what the model can already do and what it can't yet". That is the wrong axis: it moves every month and explains nothing. The useful axis is different — what is cheap and repeatable, and what costs money, time and reputation.

Machines get observation, generation and shape checking. People keep decisions, priorities, acceptance and accountability. The AI-native SDLC playbook says so directly: automation takes on mechanical verification, a person stays accountable for every decision that requires judgement, and people's attention concentrates on the gates — they review what the agent flagged rather than starting every stage from scratch.

cards.heading: What the platform does without a person
cards.text: Observation is fully automated and needs nobody's attention until a finding appears.
list: Every run records the connected folders, files read, sheets and columns opened — the provenance graph builds itself.
Content checks declared in the manifest are computed alongside the calculation: not-null, unique, range, pattern, value set.
Even without declarations, source freshness and changes in row count are visible — this follows from the runs themselves.
Quality assessment is computed on read, deterministically, over the report's last ten runs, so there is no background scheduler at all.
The contract's shape is checked at version registration: manifest, dependencies, volume limits, a dry run of every semantics query.

cards.heading: Where the machine stops and waits
cards.text:
A finding does not fix itself and does not disappear by itself. It has a stable identifier — built from the kind of check, the source, the generator, the file, the sheet and the column — so the same problem carries the same number from run to run.

The decision is stored next to the finding. A finding accepted as normal stays in the list but stops counting as open; it becomes open again when the acceptance expires or when a newer run reproduces it afresh. This is not cosmetic: attention is not spent twice on the same case already dealt with, and at the same time the decision does not become eternal.

The same goes for baseline value sets: the first run seeds the expected set, later runs report new values, and only a person can extend the set, by an explicit action.

cards.heading: Three places where the line is visible in the interface
cards.text:
First: a number is shown together with how it was obtained. Next to the answer sits the "How it's calculated" panel — definition, calculation, sources — and the SQL opens on a separate line. On the confident shape-match path the page does not put SQL into the editor at all and runs nothing by itself: it chooses the metric, opens its form and fills in the period named in the question. Running it is a human action.

Second: a finding waits for a decision. The platform can notice that a source has not been updated, that a column has gone, that values without a match have appeared, that a reference table version is outdated and the report needs recalculating. Whether to fix it now, schedule it or accept it as normal is not its question.

Third: publication is separated from the run. A run calculates and shows the result; publication is a separate action that makes the new report version current in a single commit. Between them stands a person who looks at the run's warnings — for example, the line about new values that did not make it into the reference table, with the owner's name.

cards.note: Where the platform infers something by itself, it does not pass the inference off as fact. Automatic inference of canonical tables from observations ships with the status of a suggester: the table is marked as inferred and shows its confidence and evidence until a person confirms it, and it can be worked with as a real table only after confirmation.

cards.heading: Shape checks versus content checks
cards.text:
It helps to distinguish two kinds of check, because they are automated differently.

A shape check answers the question "is this legitimately built at all": is the manifest key known, is the dependency usable in the browser, is the declared volume within the engine's ceilings, does the metric query parse and does it write anything. It has a definition of the right answer, it is repeatable, and it is entirely mechanical.

A content check answers the question "is this right in substance": is this the right column, the right period, does this client code mean what we think it does. It has no definition of the right answer inside the system — that lies outside, in the subject domain. The machine can narrow the space: show a discrepancy, list candidates, compute confidence. It cannot choose among the candidates.

So the platform consistently builds interfaces of the form "here is the observation, here are the options, here is the button". A finding with evidence. A card with alternative metrics next to the number already calculated. The difference between declared and observed, naming the file and the column. Every time the last step is left to a person, and every time everything that could be done without them has been done before that step.

cards.heading: Why it is the decision that is not delegated
cards.text:
Formally — because a decision has consequences that cannot be rolled back with a run. Accepting a discrepancy as normal means saying: the number people will see is how it should be. Publishing a version means replacing what readers already refer to.

There is a mechanical justification too. An observation is verifiable: you can repeat the run and get the same result. A decision is not: it has no reference to check it against, because the reference is the very subject of the decision. It only makes sense to automate what has a definition of the right answer.

Hence a practical consequence for working with AI: what should grow is not the list of decisions the machine makes, but the list of observations it brings to a person by the time of the decision.

cards.heading: Even a model check does not decide
cards.text:
The layer where a model checks how the question itself was assembled is telling. Between assembling the intent and showing the number there can be a single advisory model check: do the question, the chosen interpretation and the output format agree. Its negative verdict holds the number back and shows a question — but a "calculate anyway" button stays next to it. An error, a timeout or an unavailable model do not block the answer: the path is designed so that the checker's failure does not become the platform's failure.

And one more boundary in the same place: only names and the question text go to the model, data cells never do. Only the user's browser sees the result. Responsibility for data is not delegated either — it is implemented as a route along which data does not travel.

cards.heading: The feedback loop from people also ends with a person
cards.text:
A vote on an answer ("thumbs up" or "thumbs down") is the only input into the bank of suggestions for improving the phrasings by which a question is recognised. But a vote gets there automatically only with independent confirmation: three "ups" from one person on three different calendar days, or votes from two different people. Three clicks within a minute do not become a candidate.

And even after that the suggestion is not applied by itself: the queue is reviewed by a person who has the right to refresh this report's data, and they have exactly one decision — accept or reject. The machine collects observations, filters out noise and brings a candidate. A candidate is not a change.

takeaways: The line runs between observation (cheap, repeatable, verifiable) and decision (expensive, unique, without a reference).
The platform automates the provenance graph, checks, trends and contract shape checks; a finding waits for a person.
A decision is stored next to the finding by a stable identifier, but stops applying if a newer run reproduced the problem.
Calculation and publication are separated on purpose: human acceptance stands between them.
Automatic inference ships as a suggestion with evidence, and the model check as an advisory one, with the person's right to proceed.

sources.title: Google SRE Book — Monitoring Distributed Systems

checks.q: It is proposed that if the finding "new values without a match" repeats three runs in a row, the platform itself adds these values to the baseline set and closes the finding. Why does this violate how the platform works?
options: Because extending the set is the decision "the values are normal", and repetition doesn't prove it
Because acceptance is always granted for a term, and auto-closing would make the decision indefinite
Because a finding has a stable identifier, and closing it would reset its number between runs
Because a three-run window is too narrow: stability is visible only over the report's ten runs
checks.why: Repetition only says the data is stable, not that it is correct: an unrecognised client code will arrive every week precisely because nobody mapped it. The platform reports new values and lets a person accept them into the baseline set by an explicit action. The window is irrelevant: any window measures stability, not correctness. The identifier and the acceptance term are properties of a decision already taken; they do not create it.

checks.q: What would change if a generator run published the new report version immediately, without a separate human action?
options: The acceptance point would vanish: run warnings would be read only after readers saw the numbers
Publication would stop being atomic: the current version would change piecemeal, not in one commit
Run warnings about values without a match would vanish: only the publication step produces them
The provenance graph would stop being built: its recording is tied to the separate publish action
checks.why: Atomic publication and provenance recording are implementation properties; they would survive, and warnings are produced by the run itself, not by publication. What would be lost is the only place where a person sees the result together with the warnings and can choose not to publish. That is exactly where the decision "these numbers can be shown" is made, and after publication it has already been made by default.

checks.q: A user asked a question, and the shape match turned out to be confident. What happens on screen?
options: The form opens, but the period must be chosen manually: only the metric is taken from the question
The question goes to the model for an advisory check, and the number appears after its verdict
SQL is put into the editor and run immediately, and the number appears with no human involvement
The metric is chosen, its form opened and the period filled in; running it is left to the person
checks.why: On the confident shape path the socket to the model is not opened at all, and the page neither puts SQL into the editor nor runs the calculation automatically. Exactly what the question actually names is filled in: the metric and the period — and pressing run stays a human action, because that is what spends resources and produces the number.

checks.q: Automatic inference proposed treating several similar sheets as one canonical table, with high confidence. Which behaviour matches the decision taken?
options: The table works as a real one at once, and a person can override it manually later if they wish
The table is marked as inferred, shows confidence and evidence, and waits for confirmation
Confidence above a threshold removes the need to confirm: evidence is shown only in disputed cases
The inference isn't shown at all until a person describes the canonical table by hand in the manifest
checks.why: A trial showed real ambiguity: similar sheets are sometimes one table and sometimes different ones, and only a person who knows the subject domain can tell them apart. So the status was declared up front as "suggester": the inference is visible with evidence but becomes a real table only after confirmation, and no confidence threshold overrides that confirmation.

checks.q: The model check on question assembly is unavailable: the service is not responding. How will the platform behave, and why was it decided this way?
options: The number is shown but marked as unchecked, and the "How it's calculated" panel can't be opened
The answer is held back until the service recovers, and the person is shown "calculate anyway"
The question is queued and will be recalculated once the checking model starts answering again
The answer is given as usual: the path is fail-open, an advisory check's failure doesn't block it
checks.why: The check is declared advisory, not prohibitive: even its negative verdict only holds the number back and leaves the person a "calculate anyway" button. An error, a timeout and an unavailable model are handled the same way — answer as usual, without queues or special marks. Blocking would make the availability of answers hostage to the availability of an optional layer.

lessons.title: How to tell that things got better
lessons.summary: After this chapter you read the platform's telemetry with the sampling taken into account, and you know which conclusions must not be drawn from it.

cards.heading: Which signals already exist
cards.text:
The platform collects four independent streams, and they should not be confused.

Perf telemetry: for every request it records the route, status, duration, database time and query count, response size and stage spans. The `/admin/perf` page shows p50/p95/p99 by route, the slowest requests and browser timings over windows from an hour to thirty days.

The error log: 4xx and 5xx from the same log, grouped by report — with the owner, per-status counters, the three worst paths and the time of last occurrence. Status 401 is excluded as authentication noise.

Run statistics and quality: source freshness, changes in row count, the results of declared checks — all of this is computed over the report's last ten runs at the moment the page is read.

cards.heading: Why telemetry is sampled
cards.text:
Recording everything turned out not to be free. With every request recorded and a load of about 2,000 requests per second, the writer thread held the GIL long enough to stall the event loop: a p99 response time of 9.27 ms versus 0.73 ms with telemetry switched off. The instrument was breaking what it measured.

The mechanism was pinned down precisely, and that is instructive. The first hypothesis — rare stalls on batch flush — failed an order-of-magnitude check: the writer wakes up about sixty times per run, one stall affects three or four requests, so all sixty give about two hundred and forty affected requests, while p99 at 2,000 requests per second over 120 seconds is 2,400 requests. Two hundred and forty is p999, not p99. The correct explanation turned out to be continuous contention for the GIL, proportional to the writer's load.

cards.heading: The mechanics of adaptive sampling
cards.text: The solution is a control loop inside the writer thread.
list: The writer estimates the true request rate from the size of its own batches, smoothing it with an exponential average with a coefficient of 0.3.
The recording fraction is computed from the estimate: eff = clamp(target write rate / estimated request rate, floor, ceiling). By default the target is 200 records per second and the floor is 0.01.
The setting that used to be a fixed probability is now read as a ceiling, not as a set fraction.
Every recorded row is stamped with the probability with which it survived. The stamp must equal the gate's decision, so the fraction is read exactly once per request.
The perf report page reconstructs unbiased counters and percentiles by weighting each record as 1/probability.

cards.heading: Why reweighting is mandatory
cards.text:
This is the Horvitz–Thompson estimator: the sum of values divided by their probability of inclusion in the sample. It is unbiased precisely because a rare event that made it into the sample carries the weight of all its twins that did not. Without dividing by the probability you get not "a sample-based estimate" but simply a smaller number, and there is nothing to compare it with: under different loads the fraction differs, so the undercount differs too.

The method has a price, and it is recorded in the decision: the variance of the weighted estimates grows as 1/eff. The more aggressive the sampling, the noisier the summary. Hence a deliberate trade-off at a known rate — the tail cost of telemetry is roughly 3.5 µs of p99 per recorded row per second, so a target of 200 costs about 674 µs of tail at a load of 2,000 requests per second, while a target of 20 costs about 119 µs but in exchange gives percentiles ten times noisier.

cards.heading: The exception that keeps the error log intact
cards.text:
Responses with status 400 and above are always recorded and never stamped. Both halves of the rule are mandatory.

If they were not singled out, a rare 500 on a loaded server would vanish from the log with probability 1 − eff: at eff around 0.1, nine errors out of ten would simply not be recorded. If they were always recorded but stamped, weighting would give each error a weight of 1/eff at an inclusion probability of 1 — and each error would count as ten.

Records with no stamp at all — old files, browser beacons, garbage-collector pause records — get a weight of 1. Backward compatibility rests on this and nothing else.

cards.note: The offline check: on synthetic data of two sets of 100 thousand records, the weighted summary reconstructs the original within ±0.64% on record count, ±2% on p50 and p95 and ±5% on p99. Note the order: the further into the tail, the worse the reconstruction. That is a property of the method, not a defect of the implementation.

cards.heading: Why percentiles from different windows cannot be compared
cards.text:
The most common wrong conclusion looks like this: "after the update p99 doubled, so the build is worse". This has already happened in production. After the update the medians improved — serving time from 242.7 to 207.2 µs, report serving from 0.67 to 0.42 ms — while the p99 of report serving rose from 11.35 to 22.51 ms.

The cause lies in the composition of the window, not in the build. The "after" window started at process start: it contained cold cache builds — 88% hits versus 96% in the old window — and requests for a 15 MB data file that was not in the old window at all. Both windows were also short, 6 and 16 minutes, with a different mix of requests.

The generalisation is simple: a percentile is a function of a distribution, and the distribution is defined by the composition of the load. Percentiles can be compared only between windows of comparable composition. The Google SRE guidance makes the same point about measurement windows: even thirty-day windows are not comparable with each other, because one contains four weekends and another five.

cards.heading: What cannot be concluded from this at all
cards.text: A list of survivorship errors specific to our signals:
list: The error log shows only what reached the server. A report that failed to open because of the network will not appear in it.
The absence of quality findings for an old generator with no declared inputs does not mean the data is fine: only freshness and row count are available for it.
A check that looked at part of the rows is marked as sampled — "zero violations" on a sample does not equal "no violations".
Browser timings arrive as a beacon when leaving the page; sessions closed abnormally do not make it into the statistics.
Telemetry can be switched off with a runtime toggle, and then a window will turn out empty not because there were no requests.

cards.heading: Leading and lagging indicators
cards.text:
The AI-native SDLC playbook divides metrics into two classes. Leading ones measure the process: how much time passes from the first conversation to a written intent, the share of changes that go through on the first pass, the share of successful first check runs. Lagging ones measure the outcome: how many intents survived to the next stage, how much rework after work started, how many defects were caught before merge versus those that reached production.

Translate this to our problem. Leading: how many reports have declared inputs and checks; the share of versions that passed the gates the first time; the time from a finding to a decision on it. Lagging: the number of open findings left unresolved past their deadline; the number of runs that needed recalculating because of an outdated reference table version; reader complaints about the numbers.

The difference is that leading indicators can be improved today, while lagging ones can only be observed. If you measure only lagging ones, you learn about a problem when fixing it is most expensive.

cards.heading: And an honest caveat about scale
cards.text:
The measured load in production is about half a request per second: 487 records in 16 minutes, and not one of them carries a sampling stamp. So sampling never left the ceiling, the counters are exact, and there is no tail cost of telemetry in this setup: the threshold of 200 records per second is three orders of magnitude above the real load.

Hence the most valuable conclusion of the whole chapter. Numbers have an addressee. The pathology for which the entire control loop was built is unreachable in the current setup, and work whose prize is smaller than the instrument's resolution is not started. Measurement exists not to give optimisation a pretext, but to give it an addressee.

takeaways: Telemetry is sampled out of necessity: recording everything under high load itself spoiled response time (p99 9.27 ms versus 0.73 ms).
The recording fraction is computed by a control loop, stamped into every row, and the summary is reweighted as 1/probability — this is the Horvitz–Thompson estimator.
Responses with status 400 and above are always recorded and without a stamp: their inclusion probability is 1, and a stamp would inflate their weight.
Percentiles from windows with different load composition are not comparable: the p99 rise after the update was explained by a cold cache and a new large file, not by the build.
Leading indicators can be improved today, lagging ones can only be observed; both must be measured.
Optimisation must have an addressee: at a measured 0.5 requests per second, some tasks make no sense however elegant they are.

checks.q: The telemetry target write rate is 200 rows per second, the fraction ceiling is 1, the floor 0.01, and the tail cost of recording is about 3.5 µs of p99 per recorded row per second. Load has grown to 2,000 requests per second. What will the recording fraction be, and roughly what will the tail cost of telemetry be?
options: Fraction 0.01: with a tenfold load increase the control loop drops to the sampling floor
Fraction stays at 1.0; cost about 7 ms, since all 2,000 rows are written at 3.5 µs each
Fraction about 0.1; tail cost about 700 µs of p99 — 3.5 µs per row per second
Fraction about 0.1; tail cost about 9.27 ms of p99 — what recording everything used to cost
checks.why: The fraction is computed as 200/2000 = 0.1 and lies between the floor of 0.01 and the ceiling of 1, so the limits do not kick in and the loop does not drop to the floor. The cost is paid for the actual write rate, which equals the target: 200 rows per second times 3.5 µs — about 700 µs. Nine milliseconds belong to recording everything, that is, to 2,000 rows per second, which is not the case here.

checks.q: The summary weights records by the rule "weight = 1/inclusion probability", and the fraction stamp is currently about 0.1. Imagine that responses with status 500 were stamped with this fraction like all others, yet still always recorded. What would become wrong?
options: The summary would undercount errors tenfold, since the 1/eff weight applies only to successes
The error counter would be inflated: at inclusion probability 1 and weight 1/eff, an error counts as ten
Errors would vanish from the log: at eff about 0.1, nine 500s out of ten would not be recorded
Percentiles of successful requests would drift down: errors would get weight 1 and dilute the tail
checks.why: A 1/probability weight is correct only when the stamp equals the true inclusion probability. Forced emission makes that probability one while the stamp says 0.1 — the mismatch multiplies every error by ten, that is, it inflates the counter rather than deflating it. Errors vanishing is the other half of the rule, about the absence of forced emission, and here, by the premise, forced emission is in place.

checks.q: After rolling out a new build the medians improved by 15–37%, but the p99 of report serving rose from 11.35 to 22.51 ms. The "before" window is 6 minutes, the "after" window is 16 minutes and starts at process start: it has 88% cache hits versus 96% in the old window, and it includes requests for a 15 MB data file that was not in the old window at all. How should this be read?
options: The tails aren't comparable: the "after" window has a cold cache — 88% hits versus 96% — and a 15 MB file
Medians matter more than the tail: serving time fell from 242.7 to 207.2 µs, the p99 rise can be ignored
Adaptive sampling caused the p99 rise: at a fraction of 0.1 only rare slow requests land in the tail
The build doubled the tail — from 11.35 to 22.51 ms, and it should be rolled back before investigating
checks.why: A percentile depends on the composition of the window, and here the composition differs on three axes at once: cache warm-up, the presence of a large file and the window length — 6 minutes versus 16. Medians are more robust to composition, so their shift reads as real, but it neither cancels the question about the tail nor replaces it. A comparable tail needs a window without a cold start, that is, after several days of operation.

checks.q: An owner asks for a metric that will show that work on data quality is improving, and show it as early as next week. What should you propose?
options: The share of successful first check runs together with the number of defects reaching production after merge
The number of runs recalculated because of an outdated reference table version, and reader complaints
The share of reports with declared inputs and checks, and the time from a finding to a decision on it
The number of open findings unresolved past their deadline: it will respond to the work within a week
checks.why: Complaints, open findings and forced recalculations are lagging indicators: they measure the outcome and react with a delay of weeks, so nothing will be visible in them next week. The share of reports with a declared contract and the speed of response to a finding are leading: they measure the process and depend on actions taken right now. Both classes must be measured, but only leading ones can be moved.

checks.q: On the perf report page a route shows an estimate of 3,000 requests per hour and, next to it, a raw number of 300. What does this mean?
options: 300 rows were recorded with a probability of about 0.1, and weighting gave an estimate of 3,000
The raw number 300 is database queries, and the 3,000 estimate is HTTP requests on the same route
Of the route's 3,000 requests, 2,700 returned errors and so didn't enter the percentile statistics
The estimate is inflated tenfold: the 1/eff weight was applied to rows that are always recorded anyway
checks.why: A route row shows the weighted estimate next to the raw record count precisely when sampling is active, and the ratio 3000/300 = 10 is exactly 1/probability, that is, a fraction of about 0.1. Errors have nothing to do with it: responses with status 400 and above are always recorded, go without a stamp and are counted with a weight of 1, so they do not enter this multiplier and create no inflation.

checks.q: An administrator lowered the telemetry target write rate from 200 to 20 rows per second to reduce the effect on the tail. Measured at a load of 2,000 requests per second, a target of 200 costs about 674 µs of tail p99, and a target of 20 about 119 µs. What do they get in exchange?
options: Errors will start vanishing from the log: at the new target nine 500s out of ten won't be recorded
Estimates will become biased: a lower fraction pulls the weighted counters down about tenfold
Summary accuracy won't change, and the tail gets exactly ten times cheaper — from 674 to 67 µs
The tail gets cheaper, from 674 to 119 µs, but variance grows as 1/eff — the summary gets noisier
checks.why: No bias appears: weighting by 1/probability stays unbiased at any fraction — only the variance changes, and it grows in inverse proportion to the fraction. Errors are unaffected, because they are always emitted, outside the sampling. The tail cost does not fall exactly tenfold: the stated trade-off is the summary's statistical resolution against the tail at a rate of about 3.5 µs per row per second.
